we obtain coverings with thickness satisfying

$$
{ \frac { 1 } { n } } \log _ { 2 } \Theta \lesssim 0 . 0 8 4 . . . ~ .
$$

These appear to be the most efficient coverings known.

On the other hand these are all extremely poor coverings when compared with the existence results.For Rogers showed in [Rog3] that lattice coverings exist with

$$
\Theta \leqslant c \ n ( \log _ { e } n ) ^ { a }
$$

for some constant $c$ ， where $a =  { \Vdash } \log _ { 2 } ( 2 \pi e )$ ,and in [Rog1] that (possibly nonlattice） coverings exist with

$$
\Theta \leqslant n \log _ { e } n + n \log _ { e } \log _ { e } n + 5 n \ ,
$$

for $n \geqslant 3$ (see also [Erd2l,[Gril1],[Rog7)．As usual these results are nonconstructive,in the sense explained in Chap.1.

In the other direction Coxeter,Few and Rogers [Cox26l showed that any $n$ -dimensional covering satisfies

$$
\Theta \geqslant \tau _ { n } .
$$

This is a companion to Eq.(39) of Chap.1． Again let $_ s$ be a regular simplex of edge 2. Spheres of radius $\{ 2 n / ( n + 1 ) \} ^ { 1 / 2 }$ centered at the vertices of $S$ just cover $S$ ,and $\tau _ { n }$ is the ratio of the sum of the volumes of the intersections of these spheres with $s$ to the volume of $s$ . Thus

$$
\begin{array} { c } { { \tau _ { n } = \left( \displaystyle \frac { 2 n } { n + 1 } \right) ^ { n / 2 } \sigma _ { n } } } \\ { { - \displaystyle \frac { n } { e \sqrt { e } } ~ \mathrm { a s } ~ n \longrightarrow \infty . } } \end{array}
$$

In summary,from (15)-(18),the thinnest coverings satisfy

$$
{ \frac { n } { e { \sqrt { e } } } } \leq \Theta \leqslant n \log _ { e } n + n \log _ { e } \log _ { e } n + 5 n .
$$

Remarks. (i) These bounds are considerably closer together than the corresponding bounds for packings (Chap.1,Eq.(46));on the other hand the best constructions known are further from the bounds.(ii) There are no known examples of nonlattice coverings that are thinner than the best lattice coverings. (ii) One may also consider the covering problem on the sphere $\Omega _ { n }$ (analogous to Chap.1,\$2.3). There are some results in [Fej1, p.325],[Rog6],[Wyn2l,but not much is known about this problem. (iv) Davenport's construction can be adapted to produce binary codes with low covering radius [Gra4].

1.4 Computational difficulties in packings and coverings.Given a generator matrix for an $_ n$ -dimensional lattice A we can find its determinant from Eq.(4)of Chap.1.But anything else is hard! For an arbitrary lattice A the best algorithms known for finding either the packing radius $\pmb { \rho }$ or the covering radius $R$ require a number of steps that grows exponentially with $_ n$ [Diei],[Fin1],[Hel3],[Hel4],[Kan2],[Poh1].The problem of finding the covering radius is known to be in the class of $N P$ -hard problems [Emd1],and finding the packing radius is conjectured to be in this class. Evidence for this conjecture is supplied by the fact that certain closely related coding theory problems are $N P$ -hard [Ber8].Finding the covering radius of a code is also known to be $N P$ -hard[McL2].

Lenstra,Lenstra and Loväsz [Len1] describe an algorithm (the“LLL algorithm"）which finds lattice vectors of moderately small length in a number of steps that grows only as a polynomial function of $\pmb { n }$ . The short vectors in A have length $2 \rho$ ；the LLL algorithm finds lattice vectors that are guaranteed to have length $\leqslant 2 ^ { \left( n + 1 \right) / 2 } \rho$ For modest values of $\pmb { n }$ the algorithm does much better than this and very often finds a vector of minimal length．It has been used on lattices of dimension as large as 100 in connection with breaking certain encryption schemes [Lag4], [Odl4]. The LLL algorithm actually converts the given basis for the lattice into a “reduced basis". One of the reduced basis vectors is then a short vector in the lattice. Many other reduction algorithms are known; the classical Minkowski reduction algorithm is briefly described in Chap.15, $\ S 1 0 . 1$ Reduction algorithms are discussed in [Aff1],[Bab1],[Bar11]-[Bar13], [Dic7],[Doni],[Gru1],[Hel3],[Hel4],[Lag3],[Min1],[Nov1],[Rys2], [Rys3],[Rys8],[Rys14],[Sch4],[Sto1],[Tam1]-[Tam4],[Wae3],[Wae5]. (For three-dimensional lattices see also the crystallographic references mentioned at the end of this section.） Babai[Bab1] has shown that the LLL algorithm can be used to find an upper bound on the covering radius that is $\leqslant 3 ^ { n } R$ ：

There is of course no practicable algorithm known for finding the best lattice packings or coverings of a given dimension. Other algorithms related to the classification of lattices and quadratic forms are discussed in Chap. 15, \$11.

The situation improves when the lattices have some algebraic structure. For the root lattices (Chap.4, $\ S 2 \ r ,$ ）and some related lattices we are able to calculate the exact value of $R$ and find the Voronoi cels in Chap.21．In some other special cases $R$ can be found by Simon Norton's method ([Nor4] $\cong$ Chap.22,[Con37],[Con38],[Con43])．Otherwise if $_ n$ is small one may try to find the Voronoi cells first and then obtain $R$ as the distance of the furthest vertex of a Voronoi cell from the lattice.

Algorithms for computing the Voronoi cells of arbitrary sets of points are described in [Aki2],[Bow2],[Bro3],[Dev1],[Dev2],[Fin5],[Lee1], [Pre2],[Sei4]，[Wat1].References $\qquad \left[ \mathbf { C o n } 2 9 \right] \ \cong$ Chap.20，[Con35], [Con38],[Con40],[For2] describe algorithms for reasonably nice latices that，given an arbitrary point $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ ，identify which Voronoi cell $x$ belongs to,i.e.find the closest lattice point to $x$ .Such algorithms are important for the applications described in $\ S 3$ below and $\ S 1$ of Chap.3. There are many algorithms used by crystallographers for classifying periodic structures in three dimensions - see for example [Ahm1],[Bur1], [Bur2],[Fer1],[Hal5],[Koc2],[Pat1],[San1],[Say2i,[Zim2].See also [Coh4a],[Spe1].

# 2. Lattices, Quadratic Forms and Number Theory

2.1 Thenorm ofavector.Whenstudyinglatticevectors $x = ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) \in \Lambda$ it is generally easier to work,not with their length,but with their squared length or norm．This is denoted by

$$
\begin{array} { r } { N ( x ) = x \cdot x = ( x , x ) = \sum x _ { i } ^ { 2 } . } \end{array}
$$

The minimal squared distance between distinct lattice vectors,or more simply the minimal norm of $\pmb { \Lambda }$ ,is

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \operatorname* { m i n } \ \big \{ \ N ( x - y ) : x , y \in \Lambda , x \ne y \ \big \} } \\ & { = \operatorname* { m i n } \ \big \{ \ N ( x ) \ : \ x \in \Lambda , x \ne 0 \ \big \} . } \end{array}
$$

If the minimal norm is $\pmb { \mu }$ ,the packing radius of $\Lambda$ is given by

$$
\rho = { \sqrt [ { 2 } ] { \mu } } .
$$

Formulae (2O) and (21） are equivalent definitions for the minimal norm of a lattice, for if $_ x$ and $y$ are distinct vectors in $\boldsymbol { \Lambda }$ then $x ^ { \prime } = x - y$ isa nonzero vector of $\pmb { \Lambda }$ .(20)and (22)- but not necessarily (21） - are also valid for nonlattice packings.

2.2 Quadratic forms associated with a lattce. Quadratic forms provide an alternative language for studying lattices,especially useful for investigating arithmetical properties.In this section we show how quadratic forms and lattices are related.Some of the material is rather detailed,and the reader may like to turn at once to $\ S 3$ where we discuss the quantization problem. The classification of quadratic forms and lattices is briefly discussed in $\ S 2 . 4$ ；we shall say much more in Chaps.15-18.

Let $\pmb { \Lambda }$ be a lattice in $_ n$ -dimensional space $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ ，having basis vectors $\nu _ { 1 } , \ldots , \nu _ { n }$ (forming the rows of a generator matrix $M .$ )．The generic lattice vector $x = ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) \in \Lambda$ may be written (see Eq.(2） of Chap.1）as

$$
x = \xi _ { 1 } \nu _ { 1 } + \mathbf { \alpha } \cdot \mathbf { \alpha } \cdot \mathbf { \beta } + \xi _ { n } \nu _ { n } = \xi M ,
$$

where the $\xi _ { i }$ are integers and $\boldsymbol { \xi } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \dots , \xi _ { n } )$ . The norm of this vector is

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { { \displaystyle { \cal N } ( x ) = { \cal N } ( \xi _ { 1 } \nu _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n } \nu _ { n } ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } \xi _ { i } \xi _ { j } \nu _ { i } \cdot \nu _ { j } } } } \\ { { { } } } \\ { { = \xi M M ^ { \prime \prime } \xi ^ { t r } = \xi A \xi ^ { \prime r } = f ( \xi ) ( \mathrm { s a y } ) , } } \end{array}
$$

where $A = M M ^ { \prime \prime }$ is a Gram matrix for $\Lambda$ ． Regarded as a function of the $_ n$ integer variables $\xi _ { 1 } , . . . . , \xi _ { n } , f ( \xi )$ is a quadratic form associated with the lattice.

For example, from the Gram matrix given in Eq.(7) of Chap.1,one quadratic form associated with the hexagonal lattice is

$$
\xi _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \xi _ { 1 } \xi _ { 2 } + \xi _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } .
$$

The $_ n$ -dimensional cubic lattice $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ (Chap.4,\$5） has generator matrix ${ \mathbf { I } } _ { n }$ (the identity matrix),and the corresponding quadratic form is

$$
\xi _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \xi _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n } ^ { 2 } .
$$

It is sometimes simpler to use the $\xi$ coordinates $( \xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n } )$ for lattice vectors rather than the $_ x$ -coordinates. For instance if we start with the quadratic form $f$ we may define the latice by setting the norm of $( \xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n } )$ equal to $f \left( \xi \right)$ .(Or we may factor $\pmb { A }$ as $M M ^ { t r }$ and use $\pmb { M }$ as a generator matrix.)

We recall that congruent lattices are related by Eqs. (22) and (23） of Chap.1 with $c = 1$ and det $U = \pm 1$ ．Quadratic forms corresponding to congruent lattices are called integrally equivalent.Thus there is a one-toone correspondence between congruence classes of lattices and integral equivalence classes of quadratic forms. For example the vectors $\nu _ { 1 } , \nu _ { 2 }$ in Fig. 2.6a and $w _ { 1 } , \ w _ { 2 }$ in Fig.2.6b also span lattices that are congruent to the hexagonal lattice of Fig.1.3a.The Gram matrices for these bases are

$$
\left[ - 1 / _ { 2 } \begin{array} { l l } { { \ - \ i / _ { 2 } } } \\ { { \ - \ i / _ { 2 } } } \end{array} \right] \quad \mathrm { a n d } \quad \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { { \ 3 } } & { { \ - \ d ^ { 3 } / _ { 2 } } } \\ { { \ d ^ { 3 } / _ { 2 } } } & { { \ 1 } } \end{array} \right]
$$

and so the corresponding quadratic forms

$$
\xi _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } - \xi _ { 1 } \xi _ { 2 } + \xi _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \quad \mathrm { a n d } \quad 3 \xi _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + 3 \xi _ { 1 } \xi _ { 2 } + \xi _ { 2 } ^ { 2 }
$$

are integrally equivalent to each other and to (25).

If $\pmb { \Lambda }$ is a lattice of full rank, i.e.a lattice in $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional space that is spanned by $\pmb { n }$ independent vectors,then $M$ has rank ${ n , \ A }$ is a positive definite matrix,and the associated quadratic form is called a positive definite form.

Indefinite quadratic forms (those for which $\pmb { A }$ is an indefinite matrix) may also be studied via lattices,although these are no longer lattices in Euclidean space $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ .One of the most interesting cases occurs when $\pmb { A }$ has signature $\left( n - 1 , 1 \right)$ ，so that the corresponding lattice is in Lorentzian (or hyperbolic） space.We shall say much more about this in Chaps.15,26 and 27.

In view of the equivalence between lattces and quadratic forms,all the geometrical problems described in Chaps.1 and 2 have corresponding formulations in terms of quadratic forms. For example, finding the minimal norm of a lattice is equivalent to finding the minimal value of $f \left( \xi \right)$ over all integral $\xi \neq 0$ ，the so-called homogeneous minimum of the quadratic form [Cas2l. Similarly the inhomogeneous minimum of the form is the square of the covering radius of the lattice.A locally optimal lattice packing,i.e.a lattice $\mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \Lambda }$ whose density $\Delta$ does not increase when A isperturbed slightly，corresponds to an extreme form [Bac2],[Bar4], [Bar6]-[Bar10],[Con42],[Cox10],[Kne2],[Rys15]．We know all the extreme forms in at most 6 variables [Bar6],[Bar7],[Hof1]. Extreme forms in 7 variables have been studied in [Bar9],[Con42],[Lar1],[Sco1], [Sco2],[Shu4],[Sta1], [Sta2].A quadratic form corresponding to a densest lattice packing is called an absolutely extreme form. The results described in Chap.1, $\ S 1 . 5$ mean that the absolutely extreme forms are known for $n \leqslant 8$

![](images/55abd4cdf6a0809474421e83cf634a6720aaf1ff31bf903c81d4a25248558e1e.jpg)  
Figure 2.6． Two congruent versions of the hexagonal lattice.

Much of the research into lattices has been carried out in the language of quadratic forms. However in this book we usually prefer to study lattices geometrically,since the choice of a particular set of basis vectors is often arbitrary and conceals the symmetry of the situation. For example the simplest quadratic form for the $E _ { 8 }$ lattice is

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \xi _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } - \xi _ { 1 } \xi _ { 2 } + \xi _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } - \xi _ { 2 } \xi _ { 3 } + \xi _ { 3 } ^ { 2 } - \xi _ { 3 } \xi _ { 4 } + \xi _ { 4 } ^ { 2 } - \xi _ { 4 } \xi _ { 5 } } \\ { + \xi _ { 5 } ^ { 2 } - \xi _ { 5 } \xi _ { 6 } + \xi _ { 6 } ^ { 2 } - \xi _ { 6 } \xi _ { 7 } + \xi _ { 7 } ^ { 2 } - \xi _ { 5 } \xi _ { 8 } + \xi _ { 8 } ^ { 2 } , } \end{array}
$$

obtained from the basis given in Chap.4,Fig.4.7. The definition given in Chap.4,Eq. (97),reveals much more of the symmetry.

Nevertheless quadratic forms are important for studying certain aspects of lattices,and there is an extensive literature - see the references in $\ S 1$ of Chap.15. Quadratic forms are particularly useful for investigating arithmetical aspects of lattices,as we now show.

2.3 Theta series and connections with number theory.A very old problem asks for the number of ways of writing an integer $m$ as a sum of four squares，or in other words for the number of quadruples of integers $( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , x _ { 3 } , x _ { 4 } )$ such that

$$
x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + x _ { 3 } ^ { 2 } + x _ { 4 } ^ { 2 } = m .
$$

For example when $m = 2$ there are 24 solutions,consisting of all permutations of $( \pm 1 , \pm 1 , 0 , 0 )$ .(We agree to count $2 = 1 ^ { 2 } + 1 ^ { 2 } + 0 ^ { 2 } + 0 ^ { 2 }$ $\bar { 2 } = 1 ^ { 2 } + ( - 1 ) ^ { 2 } + 0 ^ { 2 } + 0 ^ { 2 }$ $2 = 1 ^ { 2 } + \mathrm { \ i } + 1 ^ { 2 } + 0 ^ { 2 }$ etc.asdistinct solutions.)

There is a nice way to state this problem in terms of lattices. For any lattice $\pmb { \Lambda }$ ，let $N _ { m }$ be the number of vectors $x \in \Lambda$ of norm $^ { m }$ ,i.e. with $x \cdot x = m$ .From (24), $N _ { m }$ is also the number of integral vectors $\xi$ such that

$$
\xi A \xi ^ { t r } = m ,
$$

or in other words the number of times the quadratic form associated with $\Lambda$ represents the number $^ m$ .Eq.(30) is an example of a Diophantine equation of degree 2 [Mor6]. Now $x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + x _ { 3 } ^ { 2 } + x _ { 4 } ^ { 2 }$ is the quadratic form associated with the four-dimensional cubic lattice $\mathbf { Z } ^ { 4 }$ So the number of ways of writing $^ { m }$ as a sum of four squares is equal to the number of vectors of norm $^ { m }$ in the lattice ${ \pmb z } ^ { 4 }$

The calculation of these numbers is facilitated by introducing the theta seriesofa lattice $\mathbf { \Delta } \Lambda$ ,which is

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \Theta _ { \mathrm { A } } ( z ) = \displaystyle \sum _ { x \in \Lambda } q ^ { x \cdot x } } } \\ { { = \displaystyle \sum _ { m = 0 } ^ { \infty } N _ { m } \ q ^ { m } , } } \end{array}
$$

where $q = e ^ { \pi i z }$ . For many purposes we can just think of $\Theta _ { \Lambda }$ as a formal power series in an indeterminate $q$ ,although for deeper investigations we must take $q = e ^ { \pi i z }$ ，where $z$ isa complex variable.In this case $\Theta _ { \Lambda } ( z )$ is easily seen to be a holomorphic function of $z$ for $\mathbf { I m } ( z ) \geqslant 0$ [Gun1,p. 71], [Ser1,p. 109].

We can also use (31） to define the theta series of a nonlattice packing A. The commonest examples of this occur when $\mathbf { \boldsymbol { \Lambda } }$ is a translate of a lattice,or a union of translates (e.g.Eq. (35)).

For a periodic packing ${ \mathcal P }$ ,consisting of a union of say $\pmb { \mathscr { s } }$ translates

$$
u _ { j } + \Lambda , ~ j = 1 , . ~ . ~ . ~ , s ,
$$

of a lattice $\pmb { \Lambda }$ (compare Eq. (13) of Chap.1),we define the average theta series to be

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \Theta _ { \pmb { \mathscr { P } } } ( z ) = \frac { 1 } { s } \displaystyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { s } \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { s } \sum _ { x \in \Lambda } q ^ { N ( x + u _ { j } - u _ { k } ) } } } \\ { { = \Theta _ { \Lambda } ( z ) + \frac { 2 } { s } \displaystyle \sum _ { j < k } \sum _ { x \in \Lambda } q ^ { N ( x + u _ { j } - u _ { k } ) } } } \end{array}
$$

[Odl6].If $\mathcal { P }$ is distance invariant (cf.[Mac6,p.40l),i.e. has the property that the number of points of $\mathcal { P }$ at any distance $^ { d }$ from $x \in \mathcal P$ is independent of $_ x$ ,then $\Theta _ { \mathcal { P } } ( z )$ reduces to

$$
\Theta _ { \mathcal { P } } ( z ) = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { s } \sum _ { x \in \Lambda } q ^ { N ( x + u _ { j } - u _ { 1 } ) } .
$$

For example,the theta series of the integers $\mathbf { z }$ is

$$
\Theta _ { \bf Z } ( z ) = \sum _ { m = - \infty } ^ { \infty } q ^ { m ^ { 2 } } = 1 + 2 q + 2 q ^ { 4 } + 2 q ^ { 9 } + 2 q ^ { 1 6 } + { \bf \alpha } \cdot { \bf \cdot } \cdot { \bf \sigma } ,
$$

which is the Jacobi theta function $\theta _ { 3 } ( z )$ (Chap.4， S4.1). The translate $\mathbf { Z } + \iota / _ { 2 } = \{ . . . , - 1 / _ { 2 } , - 1 / _ { 2 } , \iota / _ { 2 } , 1 / _ { 2 } , . . . \}$ has theta series

$$
\Theta _ { { \bf Z } + 1 / 2 } ( z ) = \sum _ { m = - \infty } ^ { \infty } q ^ { ( m + 1 / 2 ) ^ { 2 } } = 2 q ^ { 1 / 4 } + 2 q ^ { 9 / 4 } + 2 q ^ { 2 5 / 4 } + \ \cdot \cdot \cdot \ ,
$$

which is the Jacobi theta function $\theta _ { 2 } ( z )$

We now see one of the advantages of using the norm $N ( x ) = x \cdot x$ in Eq.(31)．Because $N ( \ ( x _ { 1 } , \ \cdot \ \cdot \ , x _ { n } ) \ ) = x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \ \cdot \ \cdot \ + \ x _ { n } ^ { 2 } = \ N ( x _ { 1 } ) +$ $\cdots + N ( x _ { n } )$ ，we have

$$
\Theta _ { \mathbf { Z } ^ { n } } ( z ) = \Theta _ { \mathbf { Z } } ( z ) ^ { n } = \theta _ { 3 } ( z ) ^ { n } .
$$

So the answer to the problem at the start of this section is simply the coefficient of $q ^ { m }$ in the expansion of $\theta _ { 3 } ( z ) ^ { 4 }$ in powers of $q$ ：

To obtain the theta series of the lattice $D _ { n }$ (which consists of the points of $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ whose coordinates sum to an even number,Chap.4, $\ S 7 . \bar { 1 } )$ we introduce the theta function $\theta _ { 4 } . \theta _ { 3 }$ and $\theta _ { 2 }$ may be regarded as assigning unit masses to the integer and half-integer points on the real line respectively.To get $\theta _ { 4 }$ we assign masses of $+ 1$ to the even integers and $^ { - 1 }$ to the odd integers,or formally

$$
\theta _ { 4 } ( z ) = \sum _ { m = - \infty } ^ { \infty } ( - q ) ^ { m ^ { 2 } } = 1 - 2 q + 2 q ^ { 4 } - 2 q ^ { 9 } + 2 q ^ { 1 6 } - \cdot \cdot \cdot .
$$

Then

$$
\Theta _ { D _ { n } } ( z ) = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \left\{ \theta _ { 3 } ( z ) ^ { n } + \theta _ { 4 } ( z ) ^ { n } \right\} .
$$

We cannot resist giving two more examples. It is not difficult to show that the translate $( \mathbb { \gamma } _ { 2 } , \ldots , \mathbb { \gamma } _ { 2 } ) + D _ { n }$ has theta series $\psi _ { 2 } \theta _ { 2 } ( z ) ^ { n }$ .The packing

$$
D _ { n } ^ { + } = D _ { n } \cup ( \nmid _ { 2 } , \dots , \nmid _ { 2 } ) + D _ { n }
$$

is the diamond packing in three dimensions and the $E _ { 8 }$ lattice in eight dimensions.  (See Chap.4, $\ S 7 . 3$ ， $D _ { n } ^ { + }$ is a lattice if and only if $\pmb { n }$ is even, and ${ D } _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ is congruent to $\mathbf { Z } ^ { 4 }$ ） Thus we have the appealing formulae ([Slo17])

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \Theta _ { \mathrm { d i a m o n d } } ( z ) = 1 / _ { 2 } \left( \theta _ { 2 } ( z ) ^ { 3 } + \theta _ { 3 } ( z ) ^ { 3 } + \theta _ { 4 } ( z ) ^ { 3 } \right) , } \\ & { \Theta _ { E _ { 8 } } ( z ) = 1 / _ { 2 } \left( \theta _ { 2 } ( z ) ^ { 8 } + \theta _ { 3 } ( z ) ^ { 8 } + \theta _ { 4 } ( z ) ^ { 8 } \right) . } \end{array}
$$

Many other theta series will be given in later chapters. We calculate the theta series of the hexagonal lattice in Chap.4, $\ S 6 . 2$ ，to illustrate one general method of obtaining the theta series from the quadratic form.A more general theta function that includes $\theta _ { 2 } , \theta _ { 3 }$ and $\theta _ { 4 }$ as special cases is the Jacobi theta function $\theta _ { 3 } ( \xi \mid z )$ (Chap.4,Eq. (6))．However most of the lattices we encounter can be handled using $\theta _ { 2 } , \theta _ { 3 } , \theta _ { 4 }$ and other simpler functions defined in $\ S 4 . 1$ of Chap. 4.

We note that the theta series of a lattice tell us the packing radius $\pmb { \rho }$ the kissing number $\tau$ and the density $\Delta$ ,since

$$
\Theta _ { \Lambda } ( z ) = 1 + \tau q ^ { 4 \rho ^ { 2 } } + \ \cdot \ \cdot \ \cdot \ ,
$$

$$
\Delta = \operatorname * { l i m } _ { r  \infty } ( \frac { \rho } { r } ) ^ { n } \sum _ { m \leqslant r ^ { 2 } } N _ { m } .
$$

We also obtain the theta series of the dual lattice $\Lambda ^ { * }$ by a simple substitution:

$$
\Theta _ { \Lambda ^ { * } } ( z ) = ( \operatorname * { d e t } \Lambda ) ^ { 1 / 2 } \left( \frac { i } { z } \right) ^ { n / 2 } \Theta _ { \Lambda } \left( - \frac { 1 } { z } \right)
$$

一 see Chap.4, Eq.(19)． Here for the first time we must use $z$ rather than $q$ ．There is also a generalization of (43）which applies to nonlattice packings that are the union of translates of a lattice [Odl6l. Two illustrations are given in Example 6 of Chap.7.

The actual values of the theta series are also of importance in chemistry (for example in calculating the Madelung constant,see [Bor6l, [Gel2], [Gla7],[Gla8],[Zuc1l)，and in communication theory．The error probability when a lattice is used as a code for a particular Gaussian channel can be estimated by the value of $\Theta _ { \Lambda } ( q )$ for a particular choice of q- see Eq.(35) of Chap.3.

The theta series is determined by the lattice,but not conversely. Witt [Wit4] observed that in 16 dimensions $D _ { 1 6 } ^ { + }$ and the direct sum ${ E _ { 8 } \oplus E _ { 8 } }$ are inequivalent lattices of determinant 1 with the same theta series. It is easy to verify this,and the verification illustrates how identities between theta functions have lattice-theoretic proofs. First, since $D _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ is congruent to ${ \pmb Z } ^ { 4 }$ ,we have the identity $1 / 2 \left( \theta _ { 2 } ( z ) ^ { 4 } + \theta _ { 3 } ( z ) ^ { 4 } + \theta _ { 4 } ( z ) ^ { 4 } \right) = \theta _ { 3 } ( z ) ^ { 4 }$ ,i.e.

$$
\theta _ { 3 } ( z ) ^ { 4 } = \theta _ { 2 } ( z ) ^ { 4 } + \theta _ { 4 } ( z ) ^ { 4 } .
$$

We must show that the theta series of $D _ { 1 6 } ^ { + }$ and ${ E _ { 8 } \oplus E _ { 8 } }$ are equal, i.e. that

$$
\frac { 1 } { 2 } \left( \theta _ { 2 } ( z ) { } ^ { 1 6 } + \theta _ { 3 } ( z ) { } ^ { 1 6 } + \theta _ { 4 } ( z ) { } ^ { 1 6 } \right) \ = \ \frac { 1 } { 4 } \left( \theta _ { 2 } ( z ) { } ^ { 8 } + \theta _ { 3 } ( z ) { } ^ { 8 } + \theta _ { 4 } ( z ) { } ^ { 8 } \right) ^ { 2 }
$$

(from (37)-(4o))．This follows immediately by eliminating $\theta _ { 3 } ( z )$ using (44)and expanding both sides.

Similarly Kneser [Kne5] observed that $D _ { 1 2 }$ and $D _ { 4 } \oplus E _ { 8 }$ are inequivalent l2-dimensional lattices of determinant 4 with the same theta series.(This identity also follows immediately from (44).） Later Kitaoka [Kit2] gave an example of two 8-dimensional lattices of determinant 81 with the same theta series,and examples are now known in dimension 5. In dimension 2,on the other hand,the theta series determines the lattice uniquely (see for example [Wat2O]).(Some related references are [Con43i], [Hsi5],[Hsi7],[Kit1],[Li1].)

2.4 Integral lattices and quadratic forms.The class of integral lattices includes many important examples. In this book we shall call a lattice or quadratic form integral if the inner product of any two lattice vectors is an integer,or in other words if the Gram matrix $A$ has integer entries.(The term classically integral is sometimes used - see the discussion of integrality notions in Chap.15.）Equivalently,a lattice $\Lambda$ is integral if and only if

$$
\Lambda \subseteq \Lambda ^ { * } ;
$$

and for many geometrical purposes this is the best form of the definition. Most of the lattices encountered so far in this chapter are integral when suitably scaled.Our general policy (for example when selecting basis vectors in Chap.4) is to choose the scale so as to make the determinant as small as possible while making the lattice integral. For example the hexagonal lattice $\ b { A } _ { 2 }$ as defined by Eq.(8)of Chap.1 is integral,although the equivalent lattice defined by (6) is not.

An important group associated with an integral lattice $\Lambda$ is its dual quotient group $\Lambda ^ { * } / \Lambda$ ，which has order det $\Lambda$ For example $A _ { 2 } ^ { * } / A _ { 2 }$ isa cyclic group of order 3．The three cosets of $\pmb { A } _ { 2 }$ in $\boldsymbol { A } _ { 2 } ^ { * }$ are indicated by the letters $a , b , c$ in Fig. 1.3b.

Note that an integral latice $\Lambda$ has the property

$$
\Lambda \subseteq \Lambda ^ { * } \subseteq { \frac { 1 } { \operatorname* { d e t } \Lambda } } \Lambda .
$$

(Forif $x \in \Lambda ^ { * }$ ， $\begin{array} { r l } { x = \xi \left( M ^ { - 1 } \right) ^ { t r } = } & { { } \xi \left( M ^ { - 1 } \right) ^ { t r } M ^ { - 1 } M = ( \mathrm { d e t \ \Lambda } \Lambda ) ^ { - 1 } \xi \mathrm { a d j } ( A ) M } \end{array}$ $\mathbf { \Sigma } = ( \operatorname* { d e t } \Lambda ) ^ { - 1 } \boldsymbol { \xi } ^ { \prime } M$ ,where $\xi , \xi ^ { \prime } \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ and adj $\left( { \cal A } \right)$ is the adjoint of $\pmb { A }$ ）

An integral lattice with |de ${ \textbf { t } } \Lambda | = 1$ ，or equivalently with $\Lambda = { \Lambda } ^ { * }$ ，is called unimodular or self-dual. (We have written $| { \tt d e t } \Lambda |$ rather than det $\Lambda$ so that the definition also applies to Lorentzian lattices.） If $\Lambda$ is integral then $x \cdot x$ is necessarily an integer for all $x \in \Lambda$ If $x \cdot x$ isan even integer for all $x \in \Lambda$ ，then $\Lambda$ is called even; otherwise odd.Even unimodular lattices (also called Type I latices） are especially interesting. $E _ { 8 }$ and $\Lambda _ { 2 4 }$ are even unimodular lattices,while $\mathbf { Z } , \ \bar { \mathbf { Z } } ^ { 2 } , \ \mathbf { Z } ^ { 3 } , . .$ are odd unimodular (or Type I) lattices.

It is known that if a unimodular lattce has the property that the norm of every lattice vector is a multiple of some positive integer $^ { c }$ ，then $c$ is either1or 2[O'Mel,p.324].

The classification of odd and even unimodular lattices is an important problem in number theory and other parts of mathematics [Bri2],[Dol1], [Hazl],[Hir4],[Nik2l,and the known results are summarized in Table 2.2.Even unimodular lattices exist if and only if the dimension is a multiple of 8 (Cor.18 of Chap.7),while odd unimodular lattices exist in all dimensions. $E _ { 8 }$ is the unique even unimodular 8-dimensional latice, and ${ E _ { 8 } \oplus E _ { 8 } }$ and $D _ { 1 6 } ^ { + }$ are the only two such 16-dimensional lattices [Wit4].The even unimodular 24-dimensional lattices were enumerated by Niemeier [Nie2],who found that there are 24 such lattices,23 with minimal norm 2 and one,the Leech lattice $\Lambda _ { 2 4 }$ ，with minimal norm $4 \ : -$ see Table 16.1 of Chap.16. Three separate verifications of Niemeier's result will be given in Chaps.16 and 18.

Table 2.2． The number of $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional unimodular lattices. $a _ { n }$ is the number of unimodular lattices of dimension $n$ containing no vectors of norm 1.If $n \equiv 0 { \pmod { 8 } }$ ， ${ \pmb a } _ { n }$ is written as $d _ { n } + e _ { n }$ ，where $d _ { n }$ is the number of odd lattices and $e _ { n }$ is the number of even lattices.Similarly $b _ { n }$ is the total number of unimodular lattices of dimension $\pmb { n }$ (including those with vectors of norm 1).   
![](images/b6a33c4e1a803fa59daf28f69c0174f1a7831e1605afc81be44c6a90ce2dccaf.jpg)

Kneser[Kne4] (see also [HerO],[Ko1],[Mor3],[Smi6]) enumerated the odd unimodular lattices in dimensions $n \leqslant 1 6$ ，the authors ([Con27], [Con34],Chap.16） extended this to $n \leqslant 2 3$ ，and Borcherds ([Bor1], $\left[ { \tt B o r 3 } \right] = { \tt C h a p . \ 1 7 } )$ recently enumerated the 24- and 25-dimensional odd lattices. If $\Lambda$ is a unimodular lattice so is $\mathbf { Z } ^ { i } \oplus \mathbf { { } } \mathbf { {  { \Lambda } } }$ for all $_ i$ , so it is simplest to record how many lattices are not of the form $\mathbf { Z } \oplus \mathbf { \Lambda } \mathbf { \Lambda } ^ { \prime }$ for some $\Lambda ^ { \prime }$ ,i.e. do not contain a vector of norm 1． The numbers $\left( a _ { n } \right)$ of lattices of this type are given in the first row of Table 2.2,while the second row $( b _ { n } )$ gives the total number. If $_ n$ is not a multiple of 8 the table simply gives the number of odd unimodular lattices;if $n \equiv 0$ (mod 8） the numbers are writen to show the division into odd and even lattices.For $1 \leqslant n \leqslant 8$ there is only one odd unimodular lattice, $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ ，while for $n = 9$ ,10,11,..there is also $E _ { 8 } \oplus \mathbf { Z } ^ { n - 8 }$ In dimension 12 a'third odd lattice $( D _ { 1 2 } ^ { + } )$ appears,and so there are three odd unimodular l2-dimensional lattices, $\mathbf { Z } ^ { 1 2 }$ ， ${ \cal E } _ { 8 } \oplus \mathbf { Z } ^ { 4 }$ and $D _ { 1 2 } ^ { + }$ . This explains the first twelve columns of Table 2.2. The enumeration is extended to dimension 24 in Chaps.16 and 17. See also the remarks on extremal self-dual lattices in Chap.7.

The Minkowski-Siegel mass formulae provide a powerful check that these enumerations are correct. Let $| \dot { \bf A u t } ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } ) |$ be the order of the automorphism group of a lattice $\mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \Lambda }$ (defined in $\ S 4 . 1$ of Chap.3)．The mass formula gives an explicit constant $\scriptstyle a _ { 0 }$ such that

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \sum \frac { 1 } { \left| \mathbf { A u t } \left( \Lambda \right) \right| } = a _ { 0 } , } \end{array}
$$

where the sum is over all inequivalent lattices from a given genus (for example all $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional odd unimodular lattices)．A slightly more general formula gives an explicit formula for

$$
\sum _ { \Lambda } \frac { \Theta _ { \Lambda } ( z ) } { | \operatorname { A u t } ( \Lambda ) | } .
$$

We illustrate by using the mass formula to check that the first nine columns of Table 2.2 are correct. First we consider even unimodular lattices.In dimension 8 the constant $a _ { 0 } = 1 / 6 9 6 7 2 9 6 0 0$ isgiven in Chap.16,Table 16.4,and indeed

$$
{ \frac { 1 } { \left| \operatorname { A u t } ( E _ { 8 } ) \right| } } = { \frac { 1 } { 6 9 6 7 2 9 6 0 0 } }
$$

(see Chap.4,S8.1). The values of $a _ { 0 }$ for odd unimodular lattices are given in Chap.16,Table 16.2．For $1 \leqslant n \leqslant 8$ ， $a _ { 0 } = 1 / ( 2 ^ { n } n ! )$ ， confirming that $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ is the unique odd unimodular lattice (since $\left| \mathbf { A u t } ( \mathbf { Z } ^ { n } ) \right| = 2 ^ { n } n !$ Chap.4, \$5)．However, for $n = 9$ ， $a _ { 0 } = 1 7 / 2 7 8 6 9 1 8 4 0 0$ ,and indeed there are two 9-dimensional lattices, ${ \cal E } _ { 8 } \oplus { \cal Z }$ and $\mathbf { Z } ^ { 9 }$ ,and

$$
\frac { 1 } { | \mathbf { A u t } ( E _ { 8 } \oplus \mathbf { Z } ) | } + \frac { 1 } { | \mathbf { A u t } ( Z ^ { 9 } ) | }
$$

$$
= { \frac { 1 } { 2 \cdot 6 9 6 7 2 9 6 0 0 } } + { \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { 9 } \cdot 9 ! } } = { \frac { 1 7 } { 2 7 8 6 9 1 8 4 0 0 } } .
$$

We shall say more about these formulae in Chap.16. The most dramatic application of the mass formulae is the verification of Niemeier's list of 24-dimensional even unimodular lattices given in Chap.16, $\ S 2$

The mass formulae also provide a lower bound on the number of inequivalent lattices of each dimension (since $\left| \mathbf { A u t } ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } ) \right| \geqslant 2$ in (47)).It follows from Chap.16,Table 16.4,for example that there are at least 80000000 distinct even unimodular 32-dimensional latices，so it is extremely unlikely that Niemeier's work will ever be extended to 32 or higher dimensions.

This book also has results on the classification of (positive definite) quadratic forms of other small determinants (2,3,..） in Chap.15,and contains some information about indefinite forms (Chaps.15,26,27).

2.5 Modular forms. Further connections between lattices and number theory arise because the theta series of an integral lattice is a modular form.We do not state the general theorem here; some important special cases will be found in Chap.7,Theorems 7 and 17． There is a brief account of the general theory of the connections between quadratic forms and modular forms in Cassels [Cas3，p.382l,and numerous other references:[Gun1]，[Har4],[Hec2]，[Hec3]，[Kit3]，[Kno1],[Lan9], [Ogg1],[Pet4],[Ran6],[Sch6],[Sch7],[Vig1].

The main consequence of this theory is that there are only a limited number of possibilities for the theta series when the determinant is small. From this it is sometimes possible to derive explicit expressions for the coefficients $N _ { m }$ in the theta series,or to obtain accurate numerical estimates for the coefficients. We shall give five samples of such results; many others will be found in the above references.

(i)In dimensions $n \leqslant 7$ ，as we have mentioned,the lattice $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ with quadratic form (26) is the unique unimodular lattice. From this it follows that when $_ n$ is even there are simple formulae for the coeffcients of the theta series,or in other words for the number of ways of writing a number as a sum of $\pmb { n }$ squares. For example the final answer to our original questions is that the number of ways of writing $^ { m }$ as a sum of four squares is equal to

$$
8 \sum _ { d | m , 4 \rangle d } d
$$

(cf.Chap.4,Eq.(49)).

(ii) There are many other beautiful identities that arise in connection with the particular modular forms known as Eisenstein series,whose coefficients involve the arithmetical function $\sigma _ { k } \left( m \right)$ ，the sum of the $k$ th powers of the divisors of $^ { m }$ .For example the theta series of $E _ { 8 }$ ,Eq.(40), is also equal to

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \Theta _ { E _ { 8 } } ( z ) = 1 + 2 4 0 \displaystyle \sum _ { m = 1 } ^ { \infty } \sigma _ { 3 } ( m ) q ^ { 2 m } } } \\ { { = 1 + 2 4 0 q ^ { 2 } + 2 1 6 0 q ^ { 4 } + 6 7 2 0 q ^ { 6 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot } } \end{array}
$$

- see Chap. 4, $\ S 8 . 1$ and Chap. 7.

(iii) Let us define

$$
\begin{array} { c l } { { \Delta _ { 2 4 } ( z ) = q ^ { 2 } \displaystyle \prod _ { m = 1 } ^ { \infty } ( 1 - q ^ { 2 m } ) ^ { 2 4 } = \displaystyle \sum _ { m = 0 } ^ { \infty } \tau ( m ) q ^ { 2 m } \quad \mathrm { ( s a y ) } } } \\ { { = q ^ { 2 } - 2 4 q ^ { 4 } + 2 5 2 q ^ { 6 } - 1 4 7 2 q ^ { 8 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot , } } \end{array}
$$

in which the function $\pmb { \tau }$ is called Ramanujan's function. It now follows from modular form theory that there is a simple expression for the coefficients of the theta series of the Leech lattice $\Lambda _ { 2 4 }$ Let

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \displaystyle \Theta _ { \Lambda _ { 2 4 } } ( z ) = \sum _ { m = 0 } ^ { \infty } N _ { m } q ^ { m } } \\ { = 1 + 1 9 6 5 6 0 q ^ { 4 } + 1 6 7 7 3 1 2 0 q ^ { 6 } + \cdots . } \end{array}
$$

Then, for $m > 0$

$$
N _ { 2 m } = \frac { 6 5 5 2 0 } { 6 9 1 } \ ( \sigma _ { 1 1 } ( m ) - \tau ( m ) )
$$

- see Chap.4, \$11.

(iv）The second term on the right-hand side of (53) is much smaller than the first.In fact it is known from Deligne's work [Deg1],[Deg2],[Kat3] that

$$
\left| \tau ( m ) \right| \leqslant m ^ { 1 1 / 2 } d \left( m \right) ,
$$

where $d ( m )$ is the number of divisors of $m$ ,and so

$$
\tau ( m ) = O \left( m ^ { 1 1 / 2 + \epsilon } \right)
$$

for every positive $\epsilon$ . Since $\sigma _ { 1 1 } ( m ) > m ^ { 1 1 }$

$$
N _ { m } \approx \frac { 6 5 5 2 0 } { 6 9 1 } \ \sigma _ { 1 1 } \ \left( \frac { m } { 2 } \right)
$$

is a very good approximation. This is typical of the estimates that can be obtained for the coeffcients of theta series (see for example [Ran6,\$4.5], [Ran7],and $\ S 1 . 4$ of Chap.3),at least for dimensions $n \geqslant 4$

(v) The theta series of any even unimodular lattice can be writen as a polynomial in $\Delta _ { 2 4 } ( z )$ and the theta series of $E _ { 8 }$ (Th.17 of Chap.7). Consider for example the 48-dimensional lattices $P _ { 4 8 p }$ and $P _ { 4 8 q }$ mentioned in Table 1.3. Knowing only that they are even unimodular lattices of minimal norm 6 we can immediately deduce from this theorem that both have theta series equal to

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \Theta _ { E _ { 8 } } ( z ) ^ { 6 } - 1 4 4 0 \ \Theta _ { E _ { 8 } } ( z ) ^ { 3 } \Delta _ { 2 4 } ( z ) + 1 2 5 2 8 0 \ \Delta _ { 2 4 } ( z ) ^ { 2 } } \\ & { = 1 + 0 q ^ { 2 } + 0 q ^ { 4 } + 5 2 4 1 6 0 0 0 q ^ { 6 } + 3 9 0 0 7 3 3 2 0 0 0 q ^ { 8 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot \ . } \end{array}
$$

The kissing number 5241600o is obtained with almost no extra work! Further information about this and similar examples will be found in Chaps.7 and 19.

2.6 Complex and quaternionic latices. The lattices defined so far in this chapter are subgroups of real $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional space $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ that are generated by $\pmb { n }$ linearly independent vectors. They are closed under the operations of addition,subtraction, and multiplication by integers $\textbf { \textit { m } } \in \textbf { \textit { Z } }$ ,or in other words are Z-modules.There are several possible generalizations,for example by using complex or quaterninic vectors instead of real vectors.These more general lattices are of interest in their own right,and sometimes lead to simpler constructions of real lattices.They are introduced in this section; further examples will be found for example in Chaps.7, 8 and_in [Cas3,Chap.7],[Cha1],[Con36],[Hsi6al,[Kar1],[Lew1],[O'Me1], [Ong1],[Ong2],[Otr1],[Que4],[Que6],[Rog9],[Rogi1],[Ser2],[Smi11].

Let C denote the field of complex numbers $\left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { z = x + i y } &  : \ x , y \in \mathbf { R } \ \right\} \nonumber \end{array}$ ，where $i ^ { 2 } = - 1$ ，and let $\mathbf { H }$ denote the (skew) field of quaternions $\{ z = u + i \nu + j w + k x$ $u , \nu , w , x \in \mathbb { R } \ )$ ,where

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { i ^ { 2 } = j ^ { 2 } = k ^ { 2 } = - 1 , } } \\ { { i j = - j i = k , j k = - k j = i , k i = - i k = j } } \end{array}
$$

([Bir1],[Cox8],[Cox17],[Her1]).The conjugate $\bar { z }$ of $\pmb { z }$ is defined to_be $x - i y$ (in $\mathbf { C } )$ or $u - i \nu - j w - k x$ (in $\mathbf { H } )$ ,and the norm of $z$ is $N ( z ) = z { \overline { { z } } }$ ，which is $x ^ { 2 } + y ^ { 2 }$ or $u ^ { 2 } + \nu ^ { 2 } + w ^ { 2 } + x ^ { 2 }$ ． Similarly the norm of a vector $z = ( z _ { 1 } , \dots , z _ { n } )$ is

$$
N ( z ) = z _ { 1 } { \overline { { z } } } _ { 1 } + \ \cdot \ \cdot \ + \ z _ { n } { \overline { { z } } } _ { n } .
$$

Besides changing the field we also change what we mean by an integer. There are many possibilities,but here we shall just consider three rings of integers to be used instead of $\mathbf { z }$ .These are the Gaussian and Eisenstein integers

$$
\begin{array} { l l } { \pmb { \mathcal { G } } = \{ a + i b : a , b \in \mathbf { Z } \} \subset \mathbf { C } , } \\ { \pmb { \mathcal { E } } = \{ a + \omega b : a , b \in \mathbf { Z } \} \subset \mathbf { C } , } \end{array}
$$

where $\omega = ( - 1 + i \sqrt { 3 } ) / 2$ is a complex cube root of unity [Cox10,p.421], [Cox21, p.145l，[Fei2],[Har5，p.179],[LanO,II，pp.5，16l,and the Hurwitz quaternionic integers [Hurl],[Cox18]

$$
{ \mathcal { H } } { = } \{ a + i b + j c + k d ~ : ~ a , b , c , d \in { \bf Z } ~ \mathrm { o r } ~ a , b , c , d \in { \bf Z } + \nu _ { 2 } ~ \} \subset { \bf H } .
$$

Let $J$ be one of the rings of integers ${ \mathbf { z } } , ~ { \mathcal { G } } , ~ { \mathcal { E } } , ~ { \mathcal { H } } ,$ and let $\pmb { K }$ be the corresponding field (R,C,C,H respectively)．A $\pmb { J }$ -lattice isdefined as follows. Take $_ n$ vectors $\nu _ { 1 } , \dotsc , \nu _ { n } \in K ^ { n }$ that are linearly independent over $\pmb { K }$ .Then the $J$ -latticeA generated by these vectors consists of all linear combinations

$$
\xi _ { 1 } \nu _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n } \nu _ { n } ,
$$

where $\xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n } \in J$ . Since $\pmb { J }$ isa ring, $\Lambda$ is closed under addition,subtraction and multiplication (on the left,in the quaternionic case) by elements of $\pmb { J }$ ,i.e. is a $J$ -module.

Aside.Other choices for $\pmb { J }$ that lead to interesting examples include the rings of algebraic integers $\left\{ a + b \theta : a , b \in \mathbf { Z } \right\}$ ,where $\pmb \theta$ is one of

$$
{ \sqrt { - 2 } } , { \sqrt { - 5 } } , { \frac { - 1 + { \sqrt { - 7 } } } { 2 } } , { \frac { - 1 + { \sqrt { - 1 1 } } } { 2 } } , { \frac { 1 + { \sqrt { 5 } } } { 2 } } ,
$$

or the ring of _cyclotomic integers Zl5l where $\zeta = e ^ { 2 \pi i / m }$ (see Chap.8,[Bay1l, [Con36],[Cos1],[Cra2]-[Cra5],[Que6l)．However,one must be careful.If $J$ is not a principal ideal domain (e.g.when $\theta = \sqrt { - 5 } )$ $\pmb { \Lambda }$ may be $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional but not have $\pmb { n }$ generators,i.e.may not be a free $\pmb { J }$ -module;these are called non-principal lattices. If $\pmb { J }$ contains an irrational real number (as in the last example in (62)) then $\pmb { \Lambda }$ is dense in $K ^ { n }$ ,i.e.is not a (discrete） lattice.Nevertheless these examples can still be used to produce lattice packings by redefining the norm or the associated quadratic form (see e.g. $\ S 4$ of Chap.8)．By restricting ourselves in this section to the special rings mentioned above we avoid these complications.

Let A be a $\boldsymbol { J }$ -latice. Just as in the case of real lattices we may now define a generator matrix $M$ (Eq.(1）of Chap.1）and Gram matrix $\dot { A } = M \overrightarrow { M } ^ { \prime }$ (cf. Chap.1,Eq.(3))． The main difference from the real case is that the inner product of vectors $x = ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ ， $y = ( y _ { 1 } , \ldots , y _ { n } )$ is now defined to be the hermitian inner product

$$
x \cdot \overline { { { y } } } = x _ { 1 } \overline { { { y } } } _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + x _ { n } \overline { { { y } } } _ { n } .
$$

The determinant of $\Lambda$ is given by Eq. (4) of Chap.1,the minimal norm $\mu$ by Eq.(21）above,the packing radius $\pmb { \rho }$ by Eq.(22),the covering radius by a formula analogous to Eq.(3),the theta series by

$$
\Theta _ { \Lambda } ( z ) = \sum _ { x \in \Lambda } q ^ { N ( x ) } , \quad q = e ^ { \pi i z } ,
$$

(cf.Eq. (31)),and the dual lattice by

$$
{ \textstyle \Lambda ^ { * } = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { { \textstyle x \in K ^ { n } } } & { { : \ x \cdot \overline { { u } } \in J \ \mathrm { f o r \ a l l } \ u \in \Lambda } } \end{array} \right\} }
$$

(cf.Chap.1,Eq. (24)). $\pmb { \Lambda }$ is integral if $\Lambda \subseteq \Lambda ^ { * }$ ,and unimodular or self-dual if $\Lambda = { \Lambda ^ { * } }$ ：

f $\mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \Lambda }$ is a complex $\pmb { J }$ -lattice in $\mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ there is a corresponding real lattice $\mathbf { \delta } \mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \mathbf { r e a l } }$ in $\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 n }$ consisting of the vectors

$$
( \mathbf { R e } ( z _ { 1 } ) , \mathbf { I m } ( z _ { 1 } ) , \mathbf { \pi } . \mathbf { \pi } . \mathbf { \pi } . , \mathbf { R e } ( z _ { n } ) , \mathbf { I m } ( z _ { n } ) )
$$

for $( z _ { 1 } , \dots , z _ { n } ) \in \Lambda$ Also

$$
\operatorname * { d e t } \Lambda _ { \mathrm { \small { r e a l } } } = \partial ^ { n } 4 ^ { - n } ( \operatorname * { d e t } \Lambda ) ^ { 2 } ,
$$

where ä,the absolute value of the discriminant of $\pmb { J }$ ,is equal to 3 if $J = { \pmb { \mathcal { E } } }$ or4if $\boldsymbol { J } = \boldsymbol { \mathcal { G } }$ .The theta series of the dual lattice is

$$
\Theta _ { \Lambda ^ { * } } ( z ) = ( \operatorname * { d e t } \Lambda ) ^ { 2 } ~ \left( \frac { 2 i } { z \sqrt { \partial } } \right) ^ { n } \Theta _ { \Lambda } ~ \left[ - \frac { 4 } { z \partial } \right] .
$$

If $\pmb { \Lambda }$ is a quaternionic $\pmb { \mathcal { H } } ^ { \dagger }$ lattice in $\mathbf { H } ^ { n }$ the corresponding real lattice $\mathbf { \delta } \mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \mathbf { r e a l } }$ in $R ^ { 4 n }$ is obtained by replacing every component $u + i \nu + j w + k x$ of every vector in A by $( u , \nu , w , x )$ .In this case

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } \Lambda _ { \mathrm { \small { r e a l } } } = 4 ^ { - n } ( \operatorname* { d e t } \Lambda ) ^ { 4 } .
$$

In all cases $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { r e a l } }$ has the same packing and covering radii as $\pmb { \Lambda }$ ,and we define the density, kissing number and thickness of $\mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \Lambda }$ to be equal to the corresponding values for Areal·

In the case where $\pmb { \Lambda }$ is an $\pmb { \delta }$ -lattice (where $\pmb { \mathcal { E } }$ is the ring of Eisenstein integers), multiplication of vectors in $\pmb { \Lambda }$ by $\omega$ is a fixed-point-free automorphism of order 3 of $\pmb { \Lambda }$ and $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { r e a l } } ;$ only the zero vector is fixed.Conversely,a real lattice in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 n }$ with a fixed-point-free automorphism of order 3 can be regarded as an $\pmb { \mathcal { E } }$ -latticein $\mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ If A has generator matrix $M = X + i Y \left( X , Y \right)$ eal),then $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { r e a l } }$ has generator matrix

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { X } & { Y } \\ { \nu _ { 2 } ( X + \sqrt { 3 } Y ) } & { \nu _ { 2 } ( Y - \sqrt { 3 } X ) } \end{array} \right] . } \end{array}
$$

Similarly if $\mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \Lambda }$ isa $\pmb { \mathcal { G } }$ -lattice (where $\pmb { \mathcal { G } }$ is the ring of Gaussian integers), multiplication by $i$ is an automorphism $\pmb { \sigma }$ of $\Lambda$ and $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { r e a l } } , ~ \sigma$ has order 4,and the powers $\sigma , ~ \sigma ^ { 2 } , ~ \sigma ^ { 3 }$ have no fixed points except 0.If $\pmb { \Lambda }$ has generator matrix $M = X + i Y \left( X , Y \right.$ real),then $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { r e a l } }$ has generator matrix

$$
\left[ \begin{array} { c c } { { X } } & { { Y } } \\ { { - Y } } & { { X } } \end{array} \right] .
$$

The situation is a little more complicated if $\pmb { \Lambda }$ is an $\pmb { \mathcal { H } } ^ { \pmb { \mathcal { L } } }$ lattice (where $\pmb { \mathcal { H } }$ is the ring of Hurwitz integers). $\pmb { \mathcal { H } }$ contains 24 integers of norm 1,or units,namely

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \pm 1 , \pm i , \pm j , \pm k , \pm \omega , \pm \omega ^ { i } , } } \\ { { { } } } \\ { { \pm \omega ^ { j } , \pm \omega ^ { k } , \pm \overline { { \omega } } , \pm \overline { { \omega } } ^ { i } , \pm \overline { { \omega } } ^ { j } , \pm \overline { { \omega } } ^ { k } , } } \end{array}
$$

where

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \omega = \gamma _ { 2 } \left( - 1 + i + j + k \right) , } \\ { \qquad } \\ { \overline { { \omega } } = \gamma _ { 2 } \left( - 1 - i - j - k \right) , } \end{array}
$$

and

$$

Asa multiplicative group this set of units is isomorphic to $2 \mathsf { A } _ { 4 }$ ，where $\mathbb { A } _ { 4 }$ is the alternating group of degree 4. Let $L _ { \pi }$ denote left multiplication of vectors in $\mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \Lambda }$ by $\pi$ ，where $\pmb { \pi }$ is one of the 24 units in $\pmb { \mathcal { H } } .$ If $\pi \neq 1$ ， $L _ { \pi }$ is a fixed-point-free automorphism of $\pmb { \Lambda }$ and $\mathbf { \delta } \mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \mathbf { r e a l } }$ Conversely,if $L$ is a real lattice in $\mathbf { R } ^ { 4 n }$ which is a left $( 2 A _ { 4 } )$ -module,and every nontrivial element of $2 \mathsf { A } _ { 4 }$ acts in a fixed-point-free manner,then $\pmb { L }$ can be regarded as an $\pmb { \mathcal { H } }$ lattice in $\mathbf { H } ^ { n }$ If $\pmb { \Lambda }$ has generator matrix $M = U + i V + j W + k X$ (U,v,W, $X$ real), then $\mathbf { \delta } \mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \mathbf { r e a l } }$ has generator matrix

\left[ \begin{array} { c c c c c } { { U ^ { \prime } } } & { { } } & { { V ^ { \prime } } } & { { W ^ { \prime } } } & { { } } \\ { { - V } } & { { U } } & { { - X } } & { { W } } \\ { { - W } } & { { X } } & { { U } } & { { - V } } \\ { { - X } } & { { - W } } & { { V } } & { { U } } \end{array} \right] .
$$

where $\omega M = U ^ { \prime } + i V ^ { \prime } + j W ^ { \prime } + k X ^ { \prime }$

Examples. If $\Lambda = \mathcal { G }$ in $\mathbf { C } ^ { 1 }$ ， $\Lambda _ { \tt r e a l }$ is the square lattice $\mathbf { Z } ^ { 2 }$ ；if $\Lambda = \mathcal { E }$ ， $\pmb { \Lambda } _ { \mathrm { r e a l } }$ is thehexagonal lattice (Fig.1.3a);and if $\Lambda = \mathcal { H } , \Lambda _ { \mathrm { r e a l } }$ is $D _ { 4 }$ (Chap. 4, $\ S 7 . 2 )$ ：

The densest six-dimensional lattice $E _ { 6 }$ hasa simple description as an Eisenstein lattice. If $\Lambda$ is the $\pmb { \delta }$ -lattice in ${ \bf C } ^ { 3 }$ with generator matrix

$$
\left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { \theta } & { 0 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { \theta } & { 0 } \\ { 1 } & { 1 } & { 1 } \end{array} \right]
$$

where $\theta = \omega - \overline { { \omega } } = \sqrt { - 3 } ,$ then $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { r e a l } }$ .s $\scriptstyle { E _ { 6 } }$

Similarly the densest eight-dimensional lattice $\scriptstyle { E _ { 8 } }$ has a simple description as a Hurwitzian lattice. If $\pmb { \Lambda }$ is the $\pmb { \mathcal { H } }$ lattice in $\mathbf { H } ^ { 2 }$ with generator matrix

$$

The Leech lattice can be constructed in all three ways,as a $\mathcal { G } , \mathcal { E } \mathrm { . }$ or $\pmb { \mathcal { H } } .$ lattice - see $\ S 1$ of Chap.6and Example 12 of Chap.7.

Finally,we briefly discuss the existence of even complex lattices.The norm of $\pmb { \Lambda }$ ，denoted by $\mathcal { M } ( \mathbf { \Phi } )$ ，is the subgroup of the real numbers generated by $\left\{ N ( x ) : x \in \mathbf { \Lambda } \right\}$ ．We have already seen that if $\pmb { \Lambda }$ is a real self-dual lattice then $\mathcal { M } ( \Lambda )$ iseither $\mathbf { z }$ or 2Z[O'Mel,pp.227,324l． The same proof shows that this result also holds for complex lattices．Lattices for which $\mathcal { M } ( \mathbf { \boldsymbol { \Lambda } } ) = 2 \mathbf { Z }$ are called even.Even self-dual $\pmb { \mathcal { G } }$ -lattices exist in $\mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ if and only if $_ n$ is a multiple of 4; there are no even self-dual $\pmb { \delta }$ -lattices [Ger5,Th.3.6l. There are however even self-dual lattices over other rings of integers- see for example $\ S 4$ of Chap. 8.

# 3. Quantizers

3.1 Quantization,analog-to-digital conversion,and data compression. As mentioned at the end of $\ S 1 . 4$ of Chap.1，although this book primarily discusses geometrical problems,many of them have direct application to other branches of science.In this section and in $\ S 1$ of Chap.3 we describe two of the principal applications,to vector quantizers and to the design of signals for use over a noisy channel.

The real world is full of nasty numbers like O.79134989..,，while the world of computers and digital communication deals with nice numbers like O and 1. A quantizer,or analog-to-digital converter,is a device for converting nasty numbers into nice numbers. Quantizers are found in digital measuring instruments or recording devices, and in digital communication systems(including most medium- or long-distance telephone networks,those that use pulse code modulation for example 一 see $\ S 1 . 1$ of Chap.3)．We must add,however,that most existing quantizers are one-dimensional; the $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional quantizers described here are not yet in general use.

Figure 2.7． An example of a (hypothetical) two-dimensional quantizer. Eleven representative points $P _ { 1 } , \ldots , P _ { 1 1 }$ have been chosen in advance. Any point $_ x$ in the plane is then“rounded off,or quantized,to the closest point $P _ { i }$ ．The illustration also shows the Voronoi cells around each $P _ { i }$ ．For example,any point $_ x$ falling in the Voronoi cell of $P _ { 4 }$ (the shaded region） is rounded off to $P _ { 4 }$

![](images/d1028b351080bee8a704086e599bf7a9070f257c10f2953085aeae2b179728cd.jpg)  
Figure 2.8. An $_ n$ -dimensional quantizer.

to the quantizer is a pair of real numbers $( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } )$ ， which we regard as a point $x$ in the plane,and the output is the closest one of $P _ { 1 } , \ldots , P _ { 1 1 }$ to $x$ ： Any point $x$ in the plane is thus replaced by (or rounded-off to) the closest point $P _ { i }$ ．This process is also called data-compression; the output could equally well be the index $_ i$ of the closest $P _ { i }$

The formal definition of an $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional quantizer is as follows (Fig. 2.8). $M$ points $P _ { 1 } , \dots , P _ { M }$ are chosen in $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ . The input $x$ is an arbitrary point of $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ ； the output is the closest $P _ { i }$ to $_ x$ . If the closest $P _ { i }$ is not unique,one of the closest $P _ { i }$ is chosen at random to be the output.

The action of this quantizer may also be described by saying that the space $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ is_partitioned into the Voronoi cells (\$1.2) $V ( P _ { 1 } )$ ， $V ( P _ { 2 } ) _ { } , \ldots$ around the $P _ { i }$ ； if the input $_ x$ belongs to $V ( P _ { i } )$ ，the output is $P _ { i }$ (see Fig. 2.7).

Quantizing introduces errors， the magnitude of the error being measured by the Euclidean distance from $_ { x }$ to the closest $P _ { i }$ The $P _ { i }$ should therefore be chosen according to the probability distribution of $_ x$ so as to be representative or“typical” points. More precisely we shall attempt to choose the $P _ { i }$ so as to minimize the mean squared error (or m.s.e.)，the average value of $N ( x - P _ { i } ( x ) )$ ，where $P _ { i } \left( x \right)$ denotes the closest point to $x$ ：

If $_ x$ has probability density function $p ( x )$ , the average mean squared errorper dimension is

$$
E = \frac { 1 } { n } \intop _ { \pmb { R } ^ { n } } N \left( x - P _ { i } \left( x \right) \right) p \left( x \right) d x ,
$$

which,since the Voronoi cells partition $\pmb { { \cal R } } ^ { n }$ , can be written as

$$
E = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { M } \int _ { V ( P _ { i } ) } N ( x - P _ { i } ) p ( x ) d x .
$$

Remarks. (i) (78) and (79) assume the probability that the input $_ x$ lies exactly on the boundary of a Voronoi cell to be negligibly small. (ii) The factor $1 / n$ is to ensure a fair comparison between quantizers of different dimensions. (ii) The mean squared error criterion is only one of many possible distortion measures; it has the advantage of being widely used and is mathematically the simplest. For applications to speech or picture processing the correct choice of distortion measure is a difficult problem. See for example [Ata1]-[Ata3],[Fla1], [Sch10].

The main theorem in this subject is due to P.L. Zador,who showed in 1963([Zad1],[Zad2l) that it is possible to reduce the average mean squared error per dimension by using higher-dimensional quantizers. In other words it is more efficient to wait until several numbers have arrived at the quantizer,and then to quantize them all at once by regarding them asspecifying a point in some high-dimensional space.It pays to procrastinate.

Unfortunately Zador's result, like others we have mentioned,is nonconstructive,and the problem of explicitly finding good multidimensional quantizers is still unsolved. But the lattices shown in Table 1.1 perform very well if the input $x$ has a uniform distribution,as we shall see.

We now give a more precise account of Zador's result. Given the dimension $_ n$ ,the number of points $M$ ,and the probability density function $p \left( x \right)$ of the input,we wish to find the infimum

$$
E \left( n , M , p \right) = \operatorname * { i n f } _ { \{ P _ { i } \} } E ,
$$

i.e. the smallest error attainable by any set of $M$ points $P _ { 1 } , \ldots , P _ { M } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ Zador ([Zad1],[Zad2]; see also [Buc2],[Buc3],[Ger2],[Yam1l)showed under quite general assumptions about $p \left( x \right)$ that

$$
\operatorname * { l i m } _ { M  \infty } M ^ { 2 / n } { \cal E } ( n , M , p ) = G _ { n } ( \int _ { R ^ { n } } p ( x ) ^ { n / ( n + 2 ) } d x ) ^ { \frac { n + 2 } { n } } ,
$$

where $G _ { n }$ only depends on $_ n$ ．Zador also showed that

$$
\frac { 1 } { \left( n + 2 \right) \pi } \Gamma \left( \frac { n } { 2 } + 1 \right) ^ { 2 / n } \leqslant G _ { n } \leqslant \frac { 1 } { n \pi } \Gamma \left( \frac { n } { 2 } + 1 \right) ^ { 2 / n } \Gamma \left( 1 + \frac { 2 } { n } \right) .
$$

For large $_ n$ the upper and lower bounds in (82)agree, giving

$$
G _ { n } \to { \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi e } } = 0 . 0 5 8 5 5 0 . . . \mathrm { a s } \ n \to \infty .
$$

Since the probability density function $p \left( x \right)$ only appears in the last term of (81),we may choose any convenient $p \left( x \right)$ when attempting to find $G _ { n }$ ．The simplest choice,and one which is of considerable interest in its own right, is to assume that $_ x$ is uniformly distributed over a large region of $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ (a large ball,for example)．With a uniformly distributed input the mean squared error is minimized if each point $P _ { i }$ lies at the centroid of its Voronoi region $V ( P _ { i } )$ [Ger2l. We are most interested in the case when $M$ ， the number of points,is very large.This enables us to ignore boundary effects,and leads to simpler answers. If the input is uniformly distributed, (79）and(81） become

$$
E = \frac { \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { M } \int _ { V ( P _ { i } ) } N ( x - P _ { i } ) d x } { \displaystyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { M } \int _ { V ( P _ { i } ) } d x } ,
$$

$$
G _ { n } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { M \to \infty } \frac { E \left( n , M , p \right) } { \left[ \frac { 1 } { M } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { M } \int _ { V \left( P _ { i } \right) } d x \right] ^ { 2 / n } } ,
$$

where $E ( n , M , p ) = \operatorname { i n f } E$ .Equations (84) and (85) can be interpreted as saying that,for optimal quantization of a uniformly distributed input using a large number of points, $G _ { n }$ is the average mean squared error per dimension,scaled so as to be a dimensionless quantity (independent of the choice of scale of the $P _ { i } )$ .

3.2 The quantizer problem.From now on we assume that the input $\pmb { x }$ has a uniform distribution over a large ball in $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ ，and that $M$ ,the number of points $P _ { i }$ ,is large. The quantizer problem is to choose points $P _ { 1 } , \dots , P _ { M }$ in $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ so as to minimize

$$
\frac { 1 } { n } \cdot \frac { \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { M } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { M } \int \displaylimits _ { V ( P _ { i } ) } N ( x - P _ { i } ) d x } { \displaystyle \left\{ \frac { 1 } { M } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { M } \mathrm { V o l } ( V ( P _ { i } ) ) \right\} ^ { 1 + \frac { 2 } { n } } } ,
$$

where $V ( P _ { i } )$ is the Voronoi cell of $P _ { i }$ ．Then (from (84),(85)) $G _ { n }$ is equal to the limit as $M  \infty$ of the infimum of (86) over all choices of the $P _ { i }$ By the previous section the solution to the quantizer problem gives both the optimal quantizer for uniformly distributed inputs and,via (81),the error probability for an optimal quantizer when the input has an arbitrary probability density function $p ( x )$ ：

If all the Voronoi cells $V ( P _ { i } )$ are congruent (as in the case when the $P _ { i }$ form a lattice),(86) can be simplified. Suppose the Voronoi cells are congruent to a polytope $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ .If we place the origin of coordinates at the centroid of $\mathbf { I }$ ，(86）becomes

$$
{ \frac { { \frac { 1 } { n } } \int _ { \Pi } \mathbf { \boldsymbol { x } } \cdot \mathbf { \boldsymbol { x } } \ d \mathbf { \boldsymbol { x } } } { \mathbf { V o l } { ( \Pi ) } ^ { 1 + { \frac { 2 } { n } } } } } = G \left( \Pi \right) ,
$$

the normalized second moment of $\mathbf { I I }$ defined in $\ S 1 . 2$ If the points $P _ { i }$ form (a large segment of) a lattice $\mathbf { \boldsymbol { \Lambda } }$ ，with Voronoi cells congruent to a polytope $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ we write $G \left( \Lambda \right) = G \left( \Pi \right)$ . The lattice quantizer problem is to find an ndimensional lattice $\Lambda$ for which $G \left( \Lambda \right)$ is a minimum.

3.3 Quantizer problem-summary of results. It is not difficult to show that the solution to the one-dimensional quantizer problem is to place the points $P _ { i }$ uniformly along the real line,so as to form (a large segment of) the integer lattice $\mathbf { z }$ The Voronoi cells are intervals of length 1,and we take $\Pi$ to be the interval $[ - 1 / 2 , \ 1 / 2 ]$ .From (87) we have

$$
G _ { 1 } = { \frac { \displaystyle \int _ { - 1 / 2 } ^ { 1 / 2 } x ^ { 2 } d x } { \displaystyle \int _ { - 1 / 2 } ^ { 1 / 2 } d x } } = { \frac { 1 } { 1 2 } } = 0 . 0 8 3 3 3 3 \ldots .
$$

This is a familiar result in quantization theory: if uniformly distributed numbers are quantized one at a time,the average squared error is $1 / 1 2$ Zador's thesis shows that this error can be reduced by using higher-dimensional quantizers.

For the two-dimensional problem Fejes Tóth ([Fej8l; see also [Fej10], [Ger2],[Newll) showed that the points should form the hexagonal lattice; correspondingly

$$
G _ { 2 } = G \left( { \mathrm { r e g u l a r ~ h e x a g o n } } \right) = { \frac { 5 } { 3 6 { \sqrt { 3 } } } } = 0 . 0 8 0 1 8 7 5 _ { \cdots }
$$

(see Chap.21, $\ S 2 \mathrm { I } )$ ．As usual the problem is unsolved in higher dimensions.

The solution to the lattice quantizer problem is known in three dimensions [Barl6l: the best lattice quantizer is the bcc lattice,and

$$
{ \cal G } \left( \mathrm { b c c } \right) = { \cal G } \left( \mathrm { t r u n c a t e d ~ o c t a h e d r o n } \right) = \frac { 1 9 } { 1 9 2 \cdot 2 ^ { 1 / 3 } } = 0 . 0 7 8 5 4 3 . . . ~ .
$$

It is shown in [Barl6] that the bcc lattice is the only lattice at which $G ( \pi )$ is even a local minimum．For comparison

$$
G \left( { \mathrm { f c c } } \right) = G \left( { \mathrm { r h o m b i c ~ d o d e c a h e d r o n } } \right) = 2 ^ { - 1 1 / 3 } = 0 . 0 7 8 7 4 5 . . .
$$

(Chap.21,Eq. (26)),but this can be reduced by perturbing the lattice slightly.In higher dimensions even the best lattice quantizers are not known.

In [Con39] we conjecture a new lower bound on $G _ { n }$ whichis significantly stronger than Zador's lower bound. The conjecture is that $G _ { n }$ is at least

$$
\frac { n + 3 - 2 H _ { n + 2 } } { 4 n \left( n + 1 \right) } \left\{ \left( n + 1 \right) \left( n ! \right) ^ { 4 } F _ { n } ^ { 2 } \left[ \frac 1 2 \cos ^ { - 1 } \frac 1 n \right] \right\} ^ { \frac 1 n } ,
$$

where $H _ { m } = 1 ^ { - 1 } + 2 ^ { - 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + m ^ { - 1 }$ $( m = 1 , 2 , \ldots )$ is a harmonic sum, and $F _ { n } \left( \alpha \right)$ isdefined in Eq.(64) of Chap.1.This bound is also given in Table 2.3 and Fig.2.9. Although no formal proof has been found,there are plausible geometrical reasons for believing that the bound is correct. The conjectured new bound is analogous to the Rogers bound for the sphere packing problem (Eq.(39）of Chap.1),the Coxeter-Few-Rogers bound (16) for the covering problem,and the Coxeter-Boroczky bound for spherical codes (Eq.(63)of Chap.1).

It is worth remarking that the best $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional quantizers presently known are always the duals of the best packings known. However,we do not expect that this will always be the case. It would be nice to have more data.What is $G \left( \Lambda \right)$ for Dickson's four-dimensional lattices mentioned in $\ S 1 . 3$ ,or for the Barnes-Trenerry lattices also mentioned there?
