2.1 The 2-point-homogeneous spaces. To start with we choose a group $G$ ， whose properties will determine everything that follows. Although Kabatiansky and Levenshtein's theory is somewhat more general,we shall restrict ourselves here to two classes of compact groups: finite groups and connected compact groups.We shall use Examples E1,E2 and E3 of the previous section as illustrations (these are the settings for error-correcting codes， constant weight codes and spherical codes respectively). The appropriate groups $G$ are as follows.In Example El we take $G$ to be the automorphism group ofthe $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional cube，called the hyperoctahedral group,or $[ 3 ^ { n - 2 }$ ,4l in Coxeter's notation (see [Cox28l)．It has order $2 ^ { n } \cdot n !$ (E2) $G$ is the symmetric group $\ S _ { n }$ ,of order n!. (E3) $G$ is the special orthogonal group $S O \left( n \right)$ ,i.e. the group of isometries of $\Omega _ { n }$ with determinant 1.

Next we need a 2-point-homogeneous $G$ -space M[Hel6,p.289]. This implies three things.(i) M is a set on which $G$ acts,so that there is an element $g ( x ) \in \mathbf { M }$ forevery $g \in G$ and $\textbf { \em x } \in \textbf { M }$ ，and furthermore $g _ { 2 } ( g _ { 1 } ( x ) ) = ( g _ { 2 } g _ { 1 } ) ( x )$ and $1 ( x ) = x$ for all $x$ ,where $g _ { 1 } , g _ { 2 }$ are arbitrary elements of $G$ and $1 \in G$ is the identity element. (i) $\mathbf { M }$ is a metric space with a distance function $\boldsymbol { \tau }$ defined on it. (iii) $\tau$ is strongly invariant under $G$ :for any $x , x ^ { \prime } , y , y ^ { \prime } \in \mathbf { M } ,$ $\tau \left( x , y \right) = \tau \left( x ^ { \prime } , y ^ { \prime } \right)$ if and only if there is an element $g \in G$ such that $g ( x ) = x ^ { \prime }$ and $g ( y ) = y ^ { \prime }$ . We let $T \subseteq \mathbf { C }$ denote the range of $\pmb { \tau }$

Assumption (ii) certainly implies that $G$ acts transitively on M. In fact $G$ is as close to being doubly transitive as it can be without changing the distances $\tau ( x , y )$ between the points of M.

Let $H$ be the subgroup of $G$ that fixes a particular element $x _ { 0 } \in \mathbf { M }$ (any $x _ { 0 }$ will do, since $G$ is transitive)．Then $\mathbf { M }$ can be identified with the space $G / H$ of left cosets $g H$ (with the point $x _ { 0 }$ corresponding to $H$ itself) .

Examples (continued). (E1） For M we take the set of vertices of the $_ n$ dimensional cube, $\{ ( - 1 ) ^ { x } : = ( ( - 1 ) ^ { x _ { 1 } } , \ldots , ( - 1 ) ^ { x _ { n } } ) \}$ for $x = ( x _ { 1 } , \dots ,$ $\boldsymbol { x } _ { n } ) \in \mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n } \}$ ，which of course we will often identify with $\mathbf { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n }$ We let $\tau \left( \left( - 1 \right) ^ { x } , \left( - 1 \right) ^ { y } \right)$ be the Hamming distance between $_ x$ and $y$ ，so that

$T = \{ 0 , 1 , \ldots , n \}$ .A typical element of $G$ has the form $g = \sigma \pi$ ，and consists of a permutation $\pi \in \ S _ { n }$ followed by a sign change $\sigma =$ diag $\{ ( - 1 ) ^ { a _ { 1 } } , \ldots , ( - 1 ) ^ { a _ { n } } \}$ ， $a _ { i } = 0$ or1.The subgroup $H$ fixing the vertex $x _ { 0 } = \left( 1 , 1 , . . . , 1 \right)$ is ${ \mathsf { S } } _ { n }$ itself,and the natural map $G  G / H \cong \mathbf { M }$ sends $\pmb { g }$ to $( - 1 ) ^ { a }$ ：

(E2) $\textbf { M } =$ Johnson space $\mathbf { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n , w }$ with $w \leqslant n / 2$ ， $\tau ( x , y ) = \mathbb { 1 } / 2$ Hamming distance between $x$ and $y$ ， $T = \left\{ 0 , 1 , \ldots \ldots , w \right\}$ ， $H \cong \mathbb { S } _ { n - w } \times \mathbb { S } _ { w }$ (E3) ${ \bf M } = \Omega _ { n }$ ， $\tau ( x , y ) = x \cdot y$ ， $T = [ - 1 , 1 ]$ ， $H = S O \left( n - 1 \right)$ (In this case $\cos ^ { - 1 } \left( x \cdot y \right)$ is the metric on $\mathbf { M }$ ,but it is simpler to work with $x \cdot y$ ）

The final assumption we shall make about $G$ is that (a) if $G$ is infinite, then $\mathbf { M }$ is a connected Riemannian manifold and $\tau$ is a constant times the natural distance on the manifold,and (b） if $G$ isfinite,and $d _ { 0 } = \operatorname* { m i n } \tau \left( x , y \right)$ for $x , y \in \mathbf { M } , x \neq y$ ，then $\mathbf { M }$ has the structure of a graph in which $_ x$ is adjacent to $y$ if and only if $\tau ( x , y ) = d _ { 0 }$ and furthermore $\boldsymbol { \tau }$ is a constant times the natural distance in the graph.

These assumptions are quite restrictive. In fact if $G$ is infinite then Wang ([Wan2l;see also [Hel6,p.535],[Tit1],[Wol1,Th.8.12.2]) has proved that the following are the only possibilities for the space M:

(a)the sphere $\Omega _ { n }$ ，   
(b)real projective space $\mathbf { P } ^ { n } \left( \mathbf { R } \right) = S O \left( n + 1 \right) / O \left( n \right)$   
(c) complex projective space $\mathbf { P } ^ { n } ( \mathbf { C } ) = S U ( n + 1 ) / U ( n )$ ，   
(d) quaternionic projective space ${ \bf P } ^ { n } \left( { \bf H } \right) = S p \left( { n + 1 } \right) / ( S p \left( { n } \right) \times S p \left( { 1 } \right) ) ,$   
(e)the Cayley projective plane $\mathbf { P } ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { C a y } )$ ：

These are the compact Riemannian symmetric spaces of rank one,and $( G , H )$ is an example of a Gelfand pair ([BouO],[Gell],[Kra2],[Let1], [Let2]).

The finite 2-point-homogeneous spaces M have not yet been completely classified,although they have been the subject of an enormous amount of research in connection with distance-transitive graphs,strongly regular graphs,two-weight codes and association schemes (see [Banl1],[Ban12], [Big2],[Big3a],[Big4],[Big5],[Bum1],[Cal1],[Cam2],[Coi1],[Coi2], [Cur1],[Del9],[Del11],[Del12],[Del14],[Dun1]-[Dun9],[Goe4],[Gor1], [Hub1],[Kan5],[Leo10],[Leoli],[Lin12],[McK1],[Sei1]-[Sei3],[Slo5], [Smi1]-[Smi3l, [Sta4], [Sta8]). Some of the most important examples are:

(f) Hamming space $\mathbf { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n }$ ，or more generally the space $\mathbf { F } _ { q } ^ { n }$ of $\pmb { n }$ -tuples from $\mathbf { F } _ { q }$ ，with $\mathbf { \nabla } _ { \tau } ( \boldsymbol { x } , \boldsymbol { y } ) =$ Hamming distance,   
(g) Johnson space $\mathbf { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n , w }$ as in Example E2,   
(h) the space whose elements $x , y , \ldots$ are $k$ -dimensional subspaces of ${ \bf F } _ { q } ^ { n }$ where $k \leqslant n / 2$ ，with $\tau ( x , y ) = { \mathrm { r a n k } } ( x \cap y )$ ，   
(i) the space of maximal totally isotropic subspaces of an orthogonal, unitary,or symplectic geometry over a finite feld,with $\boldsymbol { \tau } \left( x , y \right) =$ rank $( \boldsymbol { x } \ \cap \ y )$ ,and

(j) the spaces of bilinear,alternating bilinear,or hermitian forms over a finite feld,with $\tau \left( x , y \right) = { \mathrm { r a n k } } \ \left( x - y \right)$ ，

but this list is by no means complete.It is remarkable that the bounds obtained in $\ S 3$ apply to subsets of any one of these spaces.

2.2 Representations of $G$ . Since $G$ is compact,it has a unique normalized measure $\pmb { \mu }$ ，Haar measure,which is invariant under $G$ (see for example [Hal6l). This induces a unique invariant measure on M, which will also be denoted by $\pmb { \mu }$ .We assume that $\pmb { \mu }$ is normalized so that $\mu \left( \mathbf { M } \right) = 1$ In Example (E1), $\mu \left( x \right) = 2 ^ { - n }$ for each $x \in \mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n }$ ,and in (E2) $\mu \left( x \right) = 1 / ( \phantom { | } _ { w } ^ { n } )$ for each $x \in \mathbf { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n , w }$ In (E3) $\pmb { \mu }$ is normalized Lebesgue measure on the sphere,with $\mu ( \Omega _ { n } ) = 1$

Let $L ^ { 2 } ( G )$ denote the vector space of complex-valued functions $\pmb { u }$ on $_ G$ satisfying

$$
\int _ { G } | u ( g ) | ^ { 2 } d \mu ( g ) < \infty ,
$$

with the inner product

$$
( u _ { 1 } , u _ { 2 } ) = \int _ { G } u _ { 1 } ( g ) \ \overline { { { u _ { 2 } ( g ) } } } \ d \mu ( g ) .
$$

Those $u \in L ^ { 2 } ( G )$ that are constant on left cosets of $H$ can be regarded as belonging to $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { M } )$ ,which is defined similarly and has the inner product

$$
( u _ { 1 } , u _ { 2 } ) = \int _ { \bf M } u _ { 1 } ( x ) \ \overline { { { u _ { 2 } ( x ) } } } \ d \mu ( x ) .
$$

We shall study how $G$ acts on the functions in $L ^ { 2 } ( G )$ and $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { M } )$

The left regular representation of $G$ on $L ^ { 2 } ( G )$ is given by

$$
g  R ( g ) , \quad g \in G ,
$$

where

$$
R ( g ) u ( f ) = u ( g ^ { - 1 } f ) , \mathrm { f o r } u \in L ^ { 2 } ( G ) , f \in G .
$$

Then $\boldsymbol { R } \left( \boldsymbol { g } \right)$ is a unitary representation with respect to our scalar product, i.e. satisfies

$$
( R ( g ) u _ { 1 } , \ R ( g ) u _ { 2 } ) \ = \ ( u _ { 1 } , u _ { 2 } )
$$

for all $u _ { 1 } , u _ { 2 } \in L ^ { 2 } ( G )$ (see [Vil1, p. 28]).

By the Peter-Weyl theorem ([Coil],[Coi2],[Grol],[Vil],[War3]) the space $L ^ { 2 } ( G )$ decomposes into a countable direct sum of mutually orthogonal subspaces $\{ V ^ { ( m , i ) } , m = 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots ; i = 1 , 2 , \ldots , d _ { m } ^ { \prime } \}$ with the following properties. $V ^ { ( m , i ) }$ is a vector space of continuous functions, of dimension $d _ { \ m } ^ { \prime }$ ,and affords an irreducible unitary representation of $G$ The spaces V(m,D), V(m,2), $V ^ { ( m , 2 ) } , \ldots , \ V ^ { ( m , d ^ { \prime } _ { m } ) }$ are isomorphicand afford equivalent representations of $G$ . Finally every irreducible unitary representation of $G$ is obtained in this way.

To obtain the decomposition of $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { M } )$ we must consider only those ireducible representations of $G$ which are of “class 1 with respect to $H ^ { \prime \prime }$ i.e. those representations $\rho ( g )$ on a space $V ^ { ( m , i ) }$ which have the property that there is a nonzero vector $a ~ \in ~ \tilde { V } ^ { ( m , i ) }$ with $\rho ( h ) a = a$ for all $\textbf { \textit { h } } \in \textbf { \textit { H } }$ (see[Vil1],pp.29,52l).For the groups we are considering it is known (cf.[Coi,Th.3.5],[Coi2,Chap.2,\$4],[Gan1,Prop.3.4],[Hig2],[Tra1]) that if such an invariant vector $^ { a }$ exists then it is unique apart from a scale factor (a subgroup $H$ with this property is called“massive).

Then (see [Vil1,p.54]) $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { M } )$ decomposes into a countable direct sum of mutually orthogonal subspaces $\{ V ^ { ( k ) } , \stackrel { \bar { k } = 0 } { = } 1 , \stackrel { 1 } { \dots } \}$ Each $V ^ { ( k ) }$ is one of the spaces $V ^ { ( m , i ) }$ mentioned above,and is a space of continuous functions of dimension $d _ { k } = d _ { m } ^ { \prime }$ $V ^ { ( k ) }$ affords an irreducible representation $\pmb { \rho } ^ { ( k ) } ( \pmb { \sigma } )$ of $G$ which is of class 1 with respect to $H$ ,and each such representation arisesjustonceinthedecomposition,the $V ^ { ( k ) }$ beingmutually nonisomorphic.We take $V ^ { ( 0 ) }$ to be the space of constant functions,and $d _ { 0 } = 1$ ：

Let $\{ e _ { i } ^ { k } ; i = 1 , \ldots , d _ { k } \}$ be an orthonormal basis for $V ^ { ( k ) }$ ,chosen so that $e _ { 1 } ^ { k }$ is an invariant vector $\pmb { a }$ Let $\rho ^ { ( k ) } ( g )$ be represented with respect to this basis by the matrix $\left( \rho _ { i j } ^ { ( k ) } ( g ) \right)$ ， where

$$
\rho ^ { ( k ) } ( g ) \ e _ { i } ^ { k } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { d _ { k } } \rho _ { j i } ^ { ( k ) } ( g ) e _ { j } ^ { k } .
$$

It is clear that $\rho _ { 1 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( h ) = 1$ for $\textit { \textbf { h } } \in \textit { \textbf { H } }$ . The functions $\rho _ { i 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( g )$ are constant on left cosets of $H$ ,and can be written as $\rho _ { i 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( x )$ ， $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbf { M }$ [Vil1, p. 53]. Then

$$
\sqrt { d _ { k } } \rho _ { 1 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( x ) , . . . , \sqrt { d _ { k } } \rho _ { d _ { k } 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( x )
$$

is an orthonormal basis for $V ^ { ( k ) }$ [Coi2, Th.1.10]. Any element of $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { M } )$ hasa“Fourier expansion"

$$
u \left( x \right) = \sum _ { k } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d _ { k } } c _ { i 1 } ^ { ( k ) } \rho _ { i 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( x ) , x \in \mathbf { M } ,
$$

where the series converges in the norm of $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { M } )$ ,and

$$
c _ { i 1 } ^ { ( k ) } = d _ { k } \intop _ { \mathbf { M } } u \left( x \right) \overline { { \rho _ { i 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( x ) } } d \mu \left( x \right)
$$

(see [Vil1,p. 54]).

2.3 Zonal spherical functions. To each space $V ^ { ( k ) }$ we associate the function

$$
J _ { k } ( x , y ) = d _ { k } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d _ { k } } \rho _ { i 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( x ) \overline { { \rho _ { i 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( y ) } } , x , y \in \bf { M } ,
$$

which has a number of interesting properties.

(i) It is immediate from the definition that $J _ { k } ( x , y )$ is positive definite, in the sense that, for any $u \in L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { M } )$ ，

$$
\int \int J _ { k } \left( x , y \right) u \left( x \right) \widehat { u \left( y \right) } d \mu \left( x \right) d \mu \left( y \right) \geqslant 0 ,
$$

or alternatively for any integer $\pmb { n }$ ，any points $x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } \ \in \mathbf { M }$ and any complex numbers $a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n }$ the relation

$$
\sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } J _ { k } ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) \ a _ { i } { \overline { { a } } } _ { j } \geqslant 0
$$

holds.(Conditions (1O） and(11） are equivalent - see for exampleBochner [Boc1].)

(ii） Since the representation ${ \bf \Gamma } _ { \rho } ( g )$ afforded by $V ^ { ( k ) }$ is unitary,it also follows from (9） that $J _ { k } ( x , y )$ is independent of the particular choice of basis for $V ^ { ( k ) }$ ,and furthermore that

$$
J _ { k } \left( g x , g y \right) = J _ { k } \left( x , y \right)
$$

for all $x , y \in \mathbf { M }$ ， $g \in G$ ，i.e. $J _ { k } ( x , y )$ is invariant under $G$ ，and so depends only on $\tau ( x , y )$ . Thus we can write

$$
J _ { k } ( x , y ) = d _ { k } \ \Phi _ { k } ( \tau ( x , y ) ) ,
$$

where

$$
\Phi _ { k } \left( \tau \left( x , y \right) \right) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d _ { k } } \rho _ { i 1 } ^ { \left( k \right) } \left( x \right) \overline { { \rho _ { i 1 } ^ { \left( k \right) } \left( y \right) } } .
$$

The function $\Phi _ { k } ( t )$ ，which is a continuous function of $t$ defined on the set $_ T$ (the range of $\tau )$ ,is called the zonal spherical function associated with $V ^ { ( k ) }$ (see[Coi2],7],d],G],ul],ta,i)e let $\tau ( x , x ) = \tau _ { 0 } .$ then

$$
\Phi _ { k } \left( \tau _ { 0 } \right) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { d _ { k } } \ \left| \ \rho _ { i 1 } ^ { \left( k \right) } \ \right| ^ { 2 } = 1 ,
$$

since $\{ \rho _ { i 1 } ^ { ( k ) } \} _ { i }$ is the first column of a unitary matrix. Also $\Phi _ { 0 } ( t ) = 1$

(ii) From (9), $J _ { k } ( x , y ) = { \overline { { J _ { k } ( y , x ) } } } ,$ and(13）and $\tau \left( x , y \right) = \tau \left( y , x \right)$ then imply that $J _ { k } \left( x , y \right)$ and $\Phi _ { k } ( t )$ are real.

(iv） The orthogonality of the spaces $V ^ { ( k ) }$ implies that the $\Phi _ { k } ( t )$ are orthogonal and satisfy

$$
\int _ { T } \Phi _ { k } ( t ) \ \Phi _ { l } ( t ) \ d \tilde { \mu } ( t ) = { \frac { \delta _ { k l } } { d _ { k } } } ,
$$

where $\tilde { \pmb { \mu } }$ is the measure on $T$ given by

$$
\tilde { \mu } \left( A \right) = \mu \left\{ x \in \mathbf { M } ; \tau \left( x _ { 0 } , x \right) \in A \right\} .
$$

(v）An alternative expression for $\Phi _ { k } ( t )$ may be obtained as follows ([Coi2, p.38],[Vil,p.30l)．By definition,

$$
\rho _ { 1 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( g ) = ( \rho ^ { ( k ) } ( g ) a , a ) ,
$$

where $_ { a }$ is the unit vector in $V ^ { ( k ) }$ fixed by $H$ .Furthermore it is easy to see that ([Vill,p.30])

$$
\rho _ { 1 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( h _ { 1 } \ g \ h _ { 2 } ) = \rho _ { 1 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( g )
$$

for any $h _ { 1 } , h _ { 2 } \in H$ ， $g \in G$ Thus $\rho _ { 1 1 } ^ { ( k ) }$ is constant on the double cosets $H g H$ If $g _ { x }$ and $g _ { y }$ are any elements of $G$ such that

$$
g _ { x } ( x _ { 0 } ) = x , g _ { y } ( x _ { 0 } ) = y ,
$$

then

$$
\Phi _ { k } \left( \tau \left( x , y \right) \right) = \rho _ { 1 1 } ^ { \left( k \right) } ( g _ { y } ^ { - 1 } g _ { x } ) .
$$

In the literature $\rho _ { 1 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( g )$ ， $F _ { k } \left( x , y \right)$ and $\Phi _ { k } \left( t \right)$ are all referred to as zonal spherical functions (or kernels).The name comes from the identification of points $x \in \mathbf { M }$ with left cosets $g H$ . Then $H x$ represents a“sphere”in M centered at $x _ { 0 }$ and passing through $x$ ,and is identified with the double coset $H g H$ From (18) $\rho _ { 1 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( x )$ is constant on these spheres.

Example E1 (see [Dun1], [Dun8]). $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { M } )$ consists of the complex-valued functions on the vertices of the $_ n$ -cube,and has a basis consisting of the monomials $\phi _ { 1 } ^ { a _ { 1 } } \ldots \phi _ { n } ^ { a _ { n } }$ where $( a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } ) \in \mathbf { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n }$ and $\phi _ { i }$ is theith coordinate function （with $\phi _ { i } ^ { 2 } \ = \ 1$ ). $G$ permutes and/or negates the $\phi _ { \textit { i } }$ while $H$ just permutes them.Also $V ^ { ( k ) }$ consists of thepolynomials of degree $k$ in $\phi _ { 1 } , . . . , \phi _ { n }$ ，with $d _ { k } = { \binom { n } { k } }$ ，for $k = 0 , 1 , \ldots , n$ The fixed vector $a = e _ { 1 } ^ { k }$ in $V ^ { ( k ) }$ is $\Sigma \phi _ { 1 } ^ { a _ { 1 } } \ldots \phi _ { n } ^ { a _ { n } }$ the sum being over all $( a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } )$ with weight $k$ (i.e.which contain $k$ ones). Then $\Phi _ { k } ( t )$ is a special case of a Krawtchouk polynomial (see [Mac6l,[Sze1]):

$$
\Phi _ { k } \left( t \right) = K _ { k } \left( t , n \right) = { \binom { n } { k } } ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { k } ( - 1 ) ^ { j } \ { \binom { t } { j } } \left( { \binom { n - t } { k } } \right) ,
$$

for $k = 0 , 1 , \ldots , n$

Example E2 (see [Dell2],[Dun2l). $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { M } )$ consists of the complex-valued functions on the $w$ -subsets of an $\pmb { n }$ -set,and decomposes into orthogonal subspaces $\{ V ^ { ( k ) } , 0 \leqslant k \leqslant w \}$ $V _ { k }$ has dimension ${ \dot { d } } _ { k } = \left( { \frac { n } { k } } \right) - \left( { \frac { n } { k } } { \frac { \ l } { - 1 } } \right)$ and is described explicitly in [Dell2] (where it is denoted by $\mathrm { H a r m } ( k ) )$ $V _ { k }$ affords the irreducible representation of $S _ { n }$ corresponding to the tworowed Young tableau $[ n - k , k ]$ (cf.[Mil3, $\ S 4 . 2 ] )$ The corresponding zonal spherical function is

$$
\Phi _ { k } \left( t \right) = Q _ { k } \left( w - t \right) ,
$$

where

$$
Q _ { k } ( t ) = \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { k } ( - 1 ) ^ { i } { \frac { \binom { k } { i } \left( n + 1 - k \right) \binom { t } { i } } { \binom { w } { i } \left( n - w \right) } }
$$

is a particular kind of Hahn polynomial [Kar2].

Example E3 (the most extensively studied case: see for example [Coi2l, [Del16],[Dun7],[Erd1],[Hob1],[Koo1]，[Mul1]，[Vil1，Chap.IX]). $L ^ { 2 } ( \Omega _ { n } )$ decomposes into an infinite direct sum of orthogonal subspaces $\{ V ^ { ( k ) } , k = 0 , 1 , \ldots \}$ ： $V ^ { ( k ) }$ consists of all functions in $L ^ { 2 } ( \Omega _ { n } )$ which are represented by homogeneous polynomials $f ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ of total degree $k$ in variables $x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n }$ that satisfy Laplace's equation

$$
\nabla ^ { 2 } f = { \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } f } { \partial x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } } } + \cdots + { \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } f } { \partial x _ { n } ^ { 2 } } } = 0 .
$$

$V ^ { ( k ) }$ is usually denoted by $\mathrm { H a r m } ( k )$ and its elements are called spherical harmonics．It has dimension

$$
d _ { k } = { \binom { n + k - 1 } { n - 1 } } - { \binom { n + k - 3 } { n - 1 } } .
$$

The corresponding zonal spherical function isa Gegenbaueror ultraspherical polynomial,which is a special case of a Jacobi polynomial. To avoid confusion of notation we write it as a Jacobi polynomial, using the standard notation of [Abr1]:

$$
\Phi _ { k } \left( t \right) = \frac { P _ { k } ^ { \left( \alpha , \beta \right) } \left( t \right) } { \left( { k + \alpha } \right) } , k = 0 , 1 , . . . ,
$$

where $\alpha = \beta = ( n { - } 3 ) / 2$ .(The normalization is determined by (15), remembering that $\tau _ { 0 } = \tau \left( x , x \right) = x \cdot x = 1 . .$

Many of the other 2-point-homogeneous spaces that we listed in Section 2.1 have also been studied in detail - see [Coi2l,[Del9],[Del1],[Del12], [Del14],[Dun2]-[Dun6],[Koo1]-[Koo3],[Sta4]-[Sta11],[Vil1].For the projective spaces $\mathbf { P } ^ { n } \left( \mathbf { R } \right) , \mathbf { P } ^ { n } \left( \mathbf { C } \right) , \mathbf { P } ^ { n } \left( \mathbf { H } \right)$ and $\mathbf { P } ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { C a y } )$ the zonal spherical functions are Jacobi polynomials

$$
\Phi _ { k } ( t ) = \frac { P _ { k } ^ { ( \alpha , \beta ) } \left( 2 t ^ { 2 } - 1 \right) } { \left( { k \atop k } + { \alpha } \right) } ,
$$

where $\alpha = ( n - 2 ) / 2$ and $\beta = - \psi _ { 2 , \ 0 , \ 1 }$ and 3 respectively.For the finite 2-point-homogeneous spaces many (but not all) of the zonal spherical functions belong_to a general family found by Askey and Wilson (see [Ask4],[Leo10],[Leo11]).

2.4 Positive-definite degenerate kernels. We have seen that the zonal spherical function $J _ { k } ( x , y )$ is a continuous，positive-definite,degenerate (because of (9)） kernel or p.d.k．on M. It is also invariant under $G$ by (12)．It is easy to see that the product of two p.d.k.'s is a p.d.k.,and a sum of p.d.k.'s with positive coefficients is a p.d.k. The p.d.k.'s that are given by the zonal spherical functions are called elementary，and clearly any sum

$$
F ( x , y ) = \sum _ { k } \lambda _ { k } \ J _ { k } ( x , y )
$$

with $\lambda _ { k } \geqslant 0$ and $\Sigma _ { k } \lambda _ { k } d _ { k } < \infty$ of elementary p.d.k.'s is also an invariant p.d.k.It is surprising that the converse holds:any invariant p.d.k.can be written in the form (25) as a sum of elementary p.d.k.'s with positive coefficients. This was first proved for Example E3 by Schoenberg [Sch5], and generalized to include all the groups considered here and many others by Bochner [Bocl] and later writers [Bin1],[Gel1],[Kre1] (see also [Kab1, Th. 2]).

It is a corollary that the product of any two zonal spherical functions $\Phi _ { i } ( t )$ and $\Phi _ { j } ( t )$ can be expanded as a sum

$$
\Phi _ { i } ( t ) \Phi _ { j } ( t ) = \sum _ { k } c _ { i j k } \ \Phi _ { k } ( t )
$$

with $c _ { i j k } \geqslant 0$ ([Koo3]).Of course this applies to those Krawtchouk,Hahn and Jacobi polynomials given above.Such expansions with positive coefficients have been extensively studied [Ask1],[Ask2],[Gas1].

# 3．The linear programming bounds

3.1 Codes and their distance distributions.Having constructed the zonal spherical functions $\phi _ { k } ( t )$ we can now proceed to derive the linear programming bounds.We shall study finite subsets $c$ of any of the 2- point-homogeneous spaces M; such subsets will be called codes,since they generalize the notions of error-correcting codes and spherical codes. Of course we are not interested in arbitrary subsets,but only those in which the distances between vectors are restricted in some way.We assume that a subset $\textit { S } \subseteq T$ has been specified,and that we wish to find codes $C$ for which $\tau ( x , y ) ~ \in ~ \mathbf { S }$ for all $x , y \in C$ ， $x \not = y$ ； such a code is called an $s$ code,and the largest cardinality $| C |$ of an $s$ -code will be denoted by $A \left( \mathbf { M } , S \right)$ ：

Example E1. If we take $S = \left\{ d , d + 1 , \ldots , n \right\}$ then an $s$ -code is an ordinaryerror-correctingcodeofminimaldistance $d$ ，and $A \left( \mathbf { M } , S \right) = A \left( n , d \right)$ (E2) If $S = \left\{ \delta , \delta + 1 , \ldots , n \right\}$ an $s$ -code isa constantweightcodewithminimaldistance2δ,and $A \left( \mathbf { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n , 2 } , S \right) = A \left( n , e , w \right)$ (E3) If $S = [ - 1 , \cos \theta ]$ ,an $s$ -code is a spherical code with minimal angle $\pmb \theta$ and $A \left( \Omega _ { n } , S \right) = A \left( n , \theta \right)$ ：

The distance distribution $\{ \alpha _ { t } \}$ of any code $c$ is defined by $\alpha _ { t } = { \frac { 1 } { | C | } }$ · (number of ordered pairs $x , y \in C$ with $\tau ( x , y ) = t )$

It is immediate that

$$
\begin{array} { c } { { \alpha _ { \tau _ { 0 } } = 1 , } } \\ { { \alpha _ { t } \geqslant 0 \mathrm { f o r } t \in T , } } \\ { { \sum _ { t } \alpha _ { t } = | C | , } } \end{array}
$$

but there are some additional inequalities.

Theorem 1.Let $\beta _ { k } = \vert C \vert ^ { - 1 } \cdot \sum _ { t } \alpha _ { t } \ \Phi _ { k } ( t ) , k = 0 , 1 , . . . ,$ denote the "transform"of the distance distribution by the zonal spherical functions. Then $\beta _ { k } \geqslant 0$ for all $k$ ：

Proof.

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \displaystyle \beta _ { k } = \frac { 1 } { | C | } \sum _ { t } \alpha _ { t } \ \Phi _ { k } ( t ) = \frac { 1 } { | C | ^ { 2 } } \sum _ { x , y \ \in { \cal C } } \Phi _ { k } ( \tau ( x , y ) ) } \\ { \displaystyle \geqslant 0 \quad \mathrm { ~ b y ~ } ( 1 1 ) . } \end{array}
$$

If $G$ (and M) are finite this result is due to Delsarte[Del8],[Del9l; in the infinite case it can be found (implicitly or explicitly）in [Del16l, [Kab1],[Llo1],[Odl5]．See also [Dun5].In Example E1 $\{ \beta _ { k } \}$ is the Krawtchouk transform of $\{ \alpha _ { t } \}$ If $C$ is a linear code then $\{ \alpha _ { t } \}$ is its weight distribution and by the MacWilliams identity (Eq. (5O) of Chap.3) $\{ { \beta } _ { t } \}$ is the weight distribution of the dual code.

3.2 The linear programming bounds. Theorem 1 and (27)-(29） make it possible to regard the problem of bounding $A \left( \mathbf { M } , S \right)$ as a linear programming problem:

Primal problem: Choose a natural number $\pmb { \mathscr { s } }$ ,a subset $\{ \tau _ { 1 } , \ldots , \tau _ { s } \}$ of $s$ ， and real numbers $\alpha _ { \tau _ { 1 } } , \ldots , \alpha _ { \tau _ { s } }$ so as to

$$
\operatorname* { m a x i m i z e } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { s } \alpha _ { \tau _ { i } }
$$

subject to

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } & { } & { \alpha _ { \tau _ { i } } \geqslant 0 , i = 1 , . . . , s , } \\ & { } & { \underline { { s } } } \\ & { } & { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { s } \alpha _ { \tau _ { i } } \Phi _ { k } ( \tau _ { i } ) \geqslant - 1 , k = 0 , 1 , . . . } \end{array}
$$

This is a linear programming problem with perhaps infinitely many unknowns $\alpha _ { t } \left( t \in S \right)$ and constraints (32)．If $C$ is an $s$ -code then its distance distribution $\{ \alpha _ { t } \}$ certainly satisfies the inequalities (31),(32).So if the maximal value of the sum (3O) that can be attained (for any choice of $\pmb { \mathscr { s } }$ and $\tau _ { 1 } , \dots , \tau _ { s } )$ is $A ^ { * }$ ,then $\angle ( \mathbf { M } , S ) \leqslant 1 + A ^ { * }$ .(The extra 1 arises because the term $\alpha _ { \tau _ { 0 } } = 1$ does not occur in (30).)

The dual problem is as always more convenient,and reads as follows (cf.[Duf1],[Dun9],[Sim0]).

Dual problem. Choose a natural number $N$ and real numbers $f _ { 1 } , \dots , f _ { N }$ so as to

$$
{ \mathrm { m i n i m i z e } } \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { N } f _ { k }
$$

subject to

$$
\begin{array} { c } { f _ { k } \geqslant 0 , k = 1 , . . . , N , } \\ { \overset { N } { \underset { k } { \sum } } \int _ { k } \Phi _ { k } ( t ) \leqslant - 1 , \mathrm { f o r } t \in S . } \end{array}
$$

Thus we have proved:

Theorem 2. If $A ^ { * }$ is the optimal solution to either of the primal or dual problems then $\smash { \cal A } \left( \mathbf { M } , \boldsymbol { S } \right) \leqslant 1 + \boldsymbol { A } ^ { * }$ ：

The reason for preferring the dual problem is that by the duality theorem any feasible solution to the dual problem is an upper bound to the optimal solution of the primal problem,or in other words:

Theorem 3.If $f _ { 1 } , \dots , f _ { N }$ satisfy (34) and (35) then $A \left( \mathbf { M } , S \right)$ $\leqslant 1 + f _ { 1 } + \mathrm { ~ \cdots ~ } + f _ { N }$

This can be restated in an equivalent form which is sometimes easier to use.

Theorem 4. Suppose the space M, the zonal spherical functions $\Phi _ { k } ( t )$ and a subset $S \subseteq T$ ，are given,and we wish to bound the cardinality $A \left( \mathbf { M } , S \right)$ of the largest subset $C$ of $\mathbf { M }$ such that $\tau ( x , y ) \in S$ for all $x , y \in C , x \neq y$ ．If we can find a linear combination

$$
f ( t ) = \sum _ { k = 0 } ^ { N } f _ { k } \Phi _ { k } ( t ) ,
$$

for some $N$ ，which satisfies $f _ { 0 } > 0 , f _ { k } \geqslant 0$ for $k { = } 1 , \ldots , N$ ，and $f ( t ) \leqslant 0$ for $t \in S$ ，then

$$
\begin{array} { r } { A ( \mathbf { M } , S ) \leqslant f ( \tau _ { 0 } ) / f _ { 0 } . } \end{array}
$$

Theorem 2,3 and 4 are the general linear programming bounds we were seeking.

As a consequence of Theorem 1 any code $C$ must satisfy further inequalities,the so-called mean inequalities.Let $F ( x , y )$ be any invariant p.d.k. on $\mathbf { M }$ By $\ S 2 . 4$ we can write $F ( x , y ) = f ( \tau ( x , y ) )$ ，where

$$
f ( t ) = \sum _ { k } f _ { k } \Phi _ { k } ( t ) , \ f _ { k } \geqslant 0 ,
$$

and the sum converges for all $\textit { \textbf { t } } \in \textit { \textbf { T } }$ . The mean of $F$ over $C$ and over M are defined by

$$
F ( C ) = { \frac { 1 } { | C | ^ { 2 } } } \sum _ { x , y \ \in \ C } F ( x , y ) ,
$$

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle F ( \mathbf { M } ) = \int _ { \mathbf { M } } \int _ { \mathbf { M } } F ( x , y ) ~ d \mu ( x ) ~ d \mu ( y ) } } \\ { { \displaystyle } } \\ { { \displaystyle = \int _ { \mathbf { M } } F ( x , y ) ~ d \mu ( x ) , ~ \mathrm { f o r ~ a n y } ~ y \in \mathbf { M } , } } \end{array}
$$

since $F ( x , y )$ only depends on $\tau ( x , y )$ . Thus $F ( \mathbf { M } ) = f _ { 0 }$ using(16）and $\Phi _ { 0 } ( t ) = 1$ ：

Theorem 5 (The mean inequality [Kab1l, [Lev5], [Sid3l)． For any invariant p.d.k. $F$ we have

$$
F \left( C \right) \geqslant F \left( \mathbf { M } \right)
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac { 1 } { | C | ^ { 2 } } \sum _ { x , y \ \in C } f ( \tau ( x , y ) ) \geqslant f _ { 0 } .
$$

Proof.From Theorem 1, $\beta _ { k } \geqslant \delta _ { k , 0 }$ Multiplying by $f _ { k }$ and summing on $k$ we obtain (41).

This gives an immediate proof of Theorem 4,avoiding the use of linear programming.

Second proof of Theorem 4. Let $c$ be any $s$ -code.From Theorem 5

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle f _ { 0 } = F ( { \bf M } ) \le F ( C ) = \frac { 1 } { \mid C \mid ^ { 2 } } \sum _ { x , y \in C } F ( x , y ) } } \\ { { \displaystyle \leqslant \frac { 1 } { \mid C \mid ^ { 2 } } \sum _ { x \in C } F ( x , x ) = \frac { 1 } { \mid C \mid } f ( \tau _ { 0 } ) } . } \end{array}
$$

Note that the only properties of zonal spherical functions used to prove Theorems 2-4 are that they are positive-definite kernels invariant under $G$ ： The theorem quoted in $\ S 2 . 4$ ，that the most general continuous functions with these properties are positive sums of zonal spherical functions,(a) justifies our restriction to functions of the form (36),and (b) is used to derive the mean inequality and therefore in the second proof of Theorem 4.

In general the value of the linear programming bound $1 + A ^ { * }$ (see Theorem 2) is unknown．Nor is it known in general how close the bound comes to the true value of $A \left( \mathbf { M } , S \right)$ .For small problems it is usually very close and occasionally does give the exact value of $A \left( \mathbf { M } , S \right)$

3.3Bounds for error-correcting codes.In Example E1 there are just $n { + 1 }$ distinct $\Phi _ { k } \mathbf { ' s }$ ，and so we may take $N = n$ in (33)and(36)(and similarly in all the cases where $G$ and $\mathbf { M }$ are finite)．Theorem 4 now states that if

(iii） We shall prove that the Nadler code is optimal [Bes3]. (the remaining inequalities (32） being redundant). Unfortunately the solution only gives $A \left( 1 3 , 6 \right) \leqslant 4 0$ .However there is an additional inequalitythatwecanimpose.Wemustcertainlyhave $\alpha _ { 1 2 } ( u ) \leqslant A \left( 1 3 , 6 , 1 2 \right) \ = A \left( 1 3 , 6 , 1 \right) = 1$ ，forall $\textbf { \em u } \in { \boldsymbol { C } }$ ，and $\alpha _ { 1 0 } ( u )$ $\leqslant A \left( 1 3 , 6 , 1 0 \right) \ = A \left( 1 3 , 6 , 3 \right) = 4$ Furthermore these can be combined. Forif $\alpha _ { 1 2 } ( u ) = 1$ then $\alpha _ { 1 0 } ( u ) = 0$ so $\alpha _ { 1 0 } ( u ) + 4 \alpha _ { 1 2 } ( u ) \leqslant 4$ and averaging over $u \in C$ gives

$$
\alpha _ { 1 0 } + 4 \alpha _ { 1 2 } \leqslant 4 .
$$

Solving the primal problem by the simplex method with this additional inequality gives $A \left( 1 3 , 6 \right) \leqslant 3 2$ Therefore $A \left( 1 3 , 6 \right) = 3 2$ and the Nadler code is optimal. By analyzing the solution to this linear program in more detail,Goethals [Goe3] has shown that the code is unique.

(iv） The best available bounds on $A \left( n , d \right)$ for $n \leqslant 2 4$ and $d \leqslant 1 0$ are given in Table 9.1; many of the upper bounds were obtained from Theorem 2 and the simplex algorithm,with the addition of extra inequalities (as in the previous example) whenever possible.

(v）Returning to Theorem 4，the best choice for a linear polynomial is $f ( t ) = K _ { 0 } ( t ; n ) + n K _ { 1 } ( t ; n ) / ( 2 d - n ) = 2 ( d - t ) / ( 2 d - n )$ for $2 d > n$ This satisfies the constraints of the theorem and proves that

$$
A \left( n , d \right) \leqslant \frac { 2 d } { 2 d - n } , \mathrm { f o r } \ 2 d > n .
$$

Thisis the Plotkin bound (see [Mac6,Chap.2，Th.1l)．Bya combinatorial argument (see [Mac6,p. 41l) it may be improved to

$$

for $^ { d }$ even and $2 d > n$ . Similarly one can show that

$$
A \left( 2 d , d \right) \leqslant 4 d , \quad \mathrm { f o r ~ } d \ \mathrm { e v e n } .
$$

Provided Hadamard matrices of the appropriate orders exist,Levenshtein has shown that equality holds in (45)and (46) (Lev1],[Mac6,Chap.2, Th.8l)．Thus $A \left( n , d \right)$ is essentially known for $n \leqslant 2 d$ ：

(vi) For $_ n$ slightly greater than $2 d$ McEliece (see [Mac6,Chap.17,Th. 38l） has obtained bounds on $A \left( n , d \right)$ using Theorem 4．Tietävainen [Tie1] has found considerably stronger bounds using analytic arguments and some of the inequalities of Theorem 1.Other bounds on $A \left( n , d \right)$ obtained by linear programming can be found in [Bes1]-[Bes3].

(vii)As we have already discussed in Section 1,for large $\pmb { n }$ and $d$ the best upper bound on $A \left( n , d \right)$ presently known is the JPL bound． The simpler part,given in (2),is obtained from Theorem 4 by using a polynomial of the form

$$
f ( t ) = \frac { 1 } { a - t } \{ K _ { k + 1 } ( t ; n ) K _ { k } ( a ; n ) - K _ { k } ( t ; n ) K _ { k + 1 } ( a ; n ) \} ^ { 2 }
$$

for suitably chosen values of $^ { a }$ and $k$ ．The details can be found in [McE2],[McE4] or[Mac6,Chap.17].Equation (26）plays a crucial role. The more complicated part of their bound will be mentioned in the next section．The JPL bounds have been generalized to tree codes in[Aal1].

3.4 Bounds for constant-weight codes. Exanple E2.continued. The function $A ( n , d , \mathbf { \Omega } _ { n ^ { \prime } } )$ is important in its own right,and because it can be used to derive additional inequalities satisfied by the weight distribution of a code，as wehaveseen in example(ii） oftheprevioussection.Tablesof $A \left( n , d , w \right)$ for $n \leqslant 2 4$ and $d \leqslant 1 0$ are given in [Bes3],and many of the upper bounds there were obtained using Theorem 2 and the simplex method (again with the addition of extra inequalities whenever possible). The more complicated part of the JPL bound,Eq.(1),is obtained by using Theorem 4 to bound $A \left( n , d , w \right)$ and converting this to a bound for $A \left( n , d \right)$ via Elias's inequality

{ \cal A } \left( n , 2 \delta \right) \leqslant \frac { 2 ^ { n } { \cal A } \left( n , 2 \delta , w \right) } { \binom { n } { w } } , \mathrm { f o r } 0 \leqslant w \leqslant n

(see[Bas1],[Bas2],[McE2],[Mac6,Chap.17,Th.33])．For the details of the proof of (1） see [McE2].

# 4.Other bounds

(i)Lovasz [Lovl] has solved a coding problem of long standing by determining the “capacity”(see [Sha4]) of the pentagon.His method, which gives a new way to bound the capacity of any graph,turns out to be closely related to Delsarte's linear programming bound for subsets of an association scheme (see [McE2],[McE3],[Sch9]).

(ii） An unusual method for obtaining lower bounds on $A \left( n , d , w \right)$ was given in [Gra2] (see also [Gra1],[Gra3],[Hon2],[Hon3], $[ \mathsf { K l } \phi 1 ] )$ .This yields

$$
A \left( n , 4 , w \right) \geqslant { \frac { 1 } { n } } { \binom { n } { w } } ,
$$

which implies

$$
{ \cal A } \left( n , 4 , w \right) \sim n ^ { w - 1 } / w ! ~ \mathrm { a s } ~ n \longrightarrow \infty ;
$$

and

$$
A \left( n , 2 \delta , w \right) \gtrsim n ^ { w - \delta + 1 } / w ! \mathrm { a s } n \longrightarrow \infty .
$$

(iii) For codes in some of the other 2-point-homogeneous spaces mentioned in thispaper see[Big1],[Big3],[Cam3],[Del15],[Ham3],[Ham4], [Kan4],[Sta6],[Tha1],[Tha2].

(iv）Lloyd [Llol] has presented another method for deriving linear programming bounds for spherical codes,by defining an association scheme on $\Omega _ { n }$ ． Yet another way of approaching these problems has been given by Neumaier [Neul]. Urakawa [Ural] derived a bound on $\Delta _ { n }$ that is equivalent to Levenshtein's 1979 bound [Lev7] by considering the spectrum of Laplace-Beltrami operators.

(v） Recently Tsfasman,Vladut and Zink [Tsf2l and others have shown that codes over $\mathbf { F } _ { q }$ ，for $q = p ^ { 2 }$ $p \geqslant 7$ ，constructed from algebraic curves give an asymptotic improvement over the Gilbert bound (see $\ S 2 . 1 1$ of Chap. 3).

# 10

# Three Lectures on Exceptional Groups

J. H. Conway

The first lecture records certain exceptional properties of the groups $L _ { 2 } ( p )$ and gives a description of the Mathieu group $M _ { 1 2 }$ and some of its subgroups,followed by a digression on the Janko group $J _ { 1 }$ of order 175560. With the exception of the Janko group material, all the structure described appears within the Mathieu group $M _ { 2 4 }$ ，which is the subject of the second lecture,where $M _ { 2 4 }$ is constructed and its subgroups described in some detail．The information on $M _ { 2 4 }$ is then found useful in the third lecture, on the group $C o _ { 0 } = \cdot 0$ and its subgroups. An appendix describes the exceptional simple groups.

This chapter is based on lectures given in Oxford,England in 1970. The groups of the title have been caled the sporadic groups since [Con2], but we have preferred not to update the language in this chapter.

# 1． First lecture

1.1 Some exceptional behavior of the groups $L _ { n } ( q )$ .The general linear group $G L _ { n } ( q )$ is the group of all linear automorphisms of an $_ n$ -dimensional vector space over the feld $\mathbf { F } _ { q }$ $q$ being any prime power．The special linear group is the normal subgroup consisting of the automorphisms of determinant 1. The center of either of these groups consists of operations of the form $x \to k x$ (for $k \in \mathbb { F } _ { q } .$ ,and we obtain the corresponding projective groups $P G L _ { n } ( q )$ and $P S L _ { n } ( q )$ by factoring out these centers. $P S L _ { n } ( q )$ is a simple group (for $n \geqslant 2 ,$ ）except in the two cases ${ \pmb n } = 2$ and $q = 2$ or3.It was called by Dickson [Dic1l the linear fractional group $L F ( n , q )$ ，but we shall use Artin's abbreviation $L _ { n } ( q )$ [Art1].

When $n = 2$ ，we take a basis $y , z$ for the space,so that the operations of the group $S L _ { n } ( q )$ have the form $y  a y + b z$ ， $z  c y + d z$ (with $a d - b c = 1 )$ ．The projective line $P L \left( q \right)$ consists of the $q + 1$ values of the formal ratio $x = y / z$ (which are conveniently thought of as the $q$ field elements together with the formal ratio $\infty$ ）and,on the projective line,

$L _ { 2 } ( q )$ becomes the group of all operations of the form

$$
x  { \frac { a x + b } { c x + d } }
$$

with $a d - b c = 1$ ，or equivalently with $a d - b c$ any non-zero square in $\mathbf { F } _ { q }$ . We use the following names for subsets of $P L ( q )$

$$
\begin{array} { c c c } { { \Omega = P { \cal L } ( q ) , } } & { { \Omega ^ { \prime } = { \bf F } _ { q } = \Omega \backslash \{ \infty \} , } } & { { Q = \{ x ^ { 2 } \colon x \in { \bf F } _ { q } \} , } } \\ { { { \cal N } = \Omega \backslash Q , } } & { { Q ^ { \prime } = Q \backslash \{ 0 \} , } } & { { { \cal N } ^ { \prime } = { \cal N } \backslash \{ \infty \} . } } \end{array}
$$

In fact $L _ { 2 } ( q )$ is generated by three operations

$$
\alpha : x \to x + 1 , \qquad \beta : x \to k x , \qquad \gamma : x \to - x ^ { - 1 } ,
$$

provided that $Q ^ { \prime }$ is the set of powers of the feld element $k$ ; for $\beta ^ { b } \alpha ^ { a }$ takes $x$ to $k ^ { b } x + a$ ，while $\beta ^ { b } \alpha ^ { a } \gamma \alpha ^ { c }$ takes $_ x$ to $c - ( k ^ { b } x + a ) ^ { - 1 }$ ，andplainly every operation of $L _ { 2 } ( q )$ can be expressed in one of these forms.

The necessary set of defining relations varies slightly with the structure of $q \colon$ when $q$ is a prime congruent to 3 modulo 4 we have

$$
L _ { 2 } ( q ) = < \alpha , \beta , \gamma : \alpha ^ { q } = \beta ^ { 1 / 2 } { } ^ { ( q - 1 ) } = \gamma ^ { 2 } = \alpha ^ { \beta } \cdot \alpha ^ { - k } = ( \beta \gamma ) ^ { 2 } = ( \alpha \gamma ) ^ { 3 } = 1 > ,
$$

since it is easy to see that these relations enable us to put every function of $\alpha , \beta , \gamma$ into one of the two forms above. $( \alpha ^ { \beta }$ denotes $\beta ^ { - 1 } \alpha \beta .$ ）In the cases $q = 3 , 5 , 7 , 1 1$ ， we shall take $k = 1 , 4 , 2 , 3$ ；for $p = 5$ ，therelation $( \alpha \beta \gamma ) ^ { 5 } = 1$ completes the above set.

It was proved by Galois (in a letter to Chevalier written on the eve of his fatal duel) that $L _ { 2 } ( p )$ cannot have a non-trivial permutation representation on fewer than $p + 1$ symbols if $p > 1 1$ [Hup1,p. 214]. However, for $p = 3 , 5 , 7 , 1 1$ there exist transitive representations on exactly $p$ symbols,and by studying these we shall illuminate some of the “unexpected" isomorphisms

$$
\begin{array} { r } { L _ { 2 } ( 3 ) \cong \mathsf { A } _ { 4 } , \qquad L _ { 2 } ( 4 ) \cong L _ { 2 } ( 5 ) \cong \mathsf { A } _ { 5 } , \qquad } \\ { L _ { 2 } ( 7 ) \cong L _ { 3 } ( 2 ) , \quad L _ { 2 } ( 9 ) \cong \mathsf { A } _ { 6 } , \quad L _ { 4 } ( 2 ) \cong \mathsf { A } _ { 8 } \ , } \end{array}
$$

where $\mathsf { A } _ { n }$ is the alternating group of degre $_ n$ .These isomorphisms are visible inside the Mathieu groups,and in the second lecture we shall find the pieces fittng together. This study is also interesting as an example of a common but puzzling phenomenon: the four cases have much in common but in each particular case there is something peculiar to that case,so that there is no completely general pattern.

It happens that the $p$ objects permuted by $L _ { 2 } ( p ) \ ( p = 3 , 5 , 7 , 1 1 )$ can in each case be taken as $p$ involutory permutations of the set $\pmb { \Omega }$ .For $p = 3 , 5 , 7 , 1 1$ ,respectively,define $\pmb { \pi }$ to be

$$

$$

and define $\pi _ { i }$ as $\alpha ^ { - i } \pi \alpha ^ { i }$ . (Mnemonic: $\pmb { \pi }$ interchanges $\infty$ with O,and takes $x$ to $_ { n x }$ or $x / n$ according as $x \in Q ^ { \prime }$ or $x \in N ^ { \prime }$ ，where $n = 2 , 4 , 3 , 6$ in the respective cases.） It is convenient to define $\pi _ { \infty }$ to be the identity permutation of $\pmb { \Omega }$ ：

Theorem 1. The group $L _ { 2 } ( p ) ( p = 3 , 5 , 7 , 1 1 )$ leaves invariant the set ⅡI consisting of the $p$ involutions $\boldsymbol { \pi } _ { i } ( i \in \Omega ^ { \prime } )$ ：

Proof. $\mathbf { I }$ is obviously invariant under $\alpha$ and the mnemonic shows it to be invariant under $\beta$ also. So we need only check invariance under $\gamma$ Here the miraculous enters - we find that $( \pi _ { i } ) ^ { \gamma } = \pi _ { i \delta }$ ，where $\delta$ is

in the four cases.

We now discuss the cases separately.

1.2 The case $p = 3$ .Here the $\pmb { \pi } _ { i }$ are the elements of a Klein 4-group which is contained in $L _ { 2 } ( 3 )$ ,and being invariant,is a normal subgroup of $L _ { 2 } ( 3 )$ , which is therefore not simple. In this case the representation on $p$ letters is not faithful, since we observe that $\delta$ is the identity.Since $L _ { 2 } ( 3 )$ is of order 12 and contains only even permutations of $\pmb { \Omega }$ ，we have the isomorphism $L _ { 2 } ( 3 ) \cong \mathsf { A } _ { 4 }$

1.3 The case $p = 5$ The group $L _ { 2 } ( 5 )$ induces only even permutations of $\Pi$ and being of order 6O,can only be the alternating group on $\mathbf { I I }$ and we have the isomorphism $L _ { 2 } ( 5 ) \cong \mathsf { A } _ { 5 }$ .Transforming $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ by the operations of the symmetric group $\ S _ { 6 }$ on $\pmb { \Omega }$ ,we obtain just 6 such sets of five involutions. Each permutation of $\ S _ { 6 }$ defines a permutation of these six sets,and so $\ S _ { 6 }$ can be regarded as a permutation group on two distinct systems of six objects.The $\updownarrow _ { 5 }$ fixing $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ is generated by the permutations $\tilde { \pi _ { j } ^ { - 1 } } \pi _ { i } \pi _ { j }$ and contains the original $L _ { 2 } ( 5 )$ ，and so does not fix any element of $\pmb { \Omega }$ It follows that the two permutation representations of $\ S _ { 6 }$ on six objects are essentially distinct，in the sense that they are related by an outer automorphism of $\ S _ { 6 }$ It is known that only for $n = 6$ does $\ S _ { n }$ possess an outer automorphism.

The details are as follows. Let $\Pi _ { i } = \pi _ { i } ^ { - 1 } \Pi \pi _ { i } \ ( i \in \Omega )$ . The sets $\Pi _ { i }$ are the six sets of five involutions,and the permutation $\pi _ { i }$ of $\pmb { \Omega }$ induces the permutation $( \Pi _ { \infty } , \Pi _ { i } )$ of these six sets,and symmetrically the permutation $( \infty , i )$ induces the permutation taking $\Pi _ { x }$ to $\Pi _ { x \pi _ { i } }$ So there is an outer automorphism $\pmb \theta$ interchanging $( \infty , i )$ with $\pi _ { i }$ ，and hence all the 15 involutions of shape $( a b ) ( c ) ( d ) ( e ) ( f )$ with those of shape $( { \boldsymbol { u } } \nu ) ( { \boldsymbol { w } } x ) ( y z )$ The former class corresponds to Sylvester's duads [Syl1], the latter to his synthemes，and the six sets $\Pi _ { i }$ are the synthematic totals. We have $\theta ^ { 2 } = 1$ ，and $( i , j ) ^ { \theta } = \pi _ { i , j }$ ，where $\begin{array} { r l r } { \pi _ { i , j } } & { { } = \pi _ { j } ^ { - 1 } ~ \pi _ { i } ~ \pi _ { j } } & { = \pi _ { i } ^ { - 1 } ~ \pi _ { j } ~ \pi _ { i } } \end{array}$ except that $\pi _ { \infty , i } = \pi _ { i , \infty } = \pi _ { i }$ ：

1.4 The case $p = 7$ . In this case the $\Pi _ { i }$ are the elements of an elementary abelian group $E$ of order 8. $L _ { 2 } ( 7 )$ acts as a subgroup of the automorphism group $L _ { 3 } ( 2 )$ of $\textbf { \textit { E } } ( L _ { 3 } ( 2 )$ because we can regard $E$ as a 3-dimensional vector space over $\mathbf { F } _ { 2 } )$ , and since $\left| L _ { 3 } ( 2 ) \right| = \left| L _ { 2 } ( 7 ) \right|$ we have the isomorphism $L _ { 2 } ( 7 ) \cong L _ { 3 } ( 2 )$ ：

The group $E$ generates together with $L _ { 2 } ( 7 )$ a subgroup $F$ of $\textsf { A } _ { 8 }$ of order 8·168,and so of index 15 in $\textsf { A } _ { 8 }$ Since $\ L _ { 2 } ( 7 )$ is generated by $\alpha , \beta , \gamma$ and is transitive on $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ ，the group $F$ is generated by $\alpha , \beta , \gamma , \pi _ { 0 }$ But (a miracle!) we observe that $\gamma \delta = \pi _ { 0 }$ so that $F$ is equally generated by $\alpha , \beta , \delta , \pi _ { 0 }$ The group $F$ therefore contains two subgroups $L _ { 3 } ( 2 )$ complementary to $E$ ， namelythe“original” $L _ { 2 } ( 7 ) = < \alpha , \beta , \gamma >$ ，andthe“exceptional” $L _ { 2 } ( 7 ) = L _ { 3 } ( 2 ) = < \alpha , \beta , \delta >$ .These are not conjugate in $F$ ，for one of them is transitive on $\pmb { \Omega }$ ，while the other fixes $\infty$ .It is exceptional for the holomorph of an elementary abelian group to exhibit this behavior.

Theorem 9. There exist 8-element ${ \pmb \mathcal { C } }$ -sets，called (special） octads，and each non-empty ${ \pmb \mathcal { C } }$ -set is the symmetric difference of a strictly smaller $\mathscr { C }$ -set with an octad. Each 5-element set is.contained in just one octad.

Any $\mathscr { C }$ -set with at least 5 points is therefore the symmetric difference of an octad containing those 5 points and a strictly smaller $\mathscr { C }$ -set. If some nonempty $\mathscr { C }$ -set had fewer than 5 elements,every set of the same cardinal would be a $\mathscr { C }$ -set,by Theorem 5,and by taking symmetric differences we should obtain every two-element set,and so every set of even cardinal, as a $\mathscr { C }$ -set,which cannot be. It follows that the octads are the smallest nonempty $\mathscr { C }$ -sets,for from any smaller non-empty one we could obtain a still smaller one,and so on．No 5-element set can be contained in two distinct octads,for then their symmetric difference would be a $\mathscr { C }$ -set with at most 6 members.

Theorem 13. Every subset of $\pmb { \Omega }$ is congruent modulo $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ either to a unique set of cardinal at most 3 or to each of 6 distinct sets of cardinal 4.

Proof. If a subset $S$ has 5 or more members we obtain a congruent set with fewer members by taking the symmetric difference with an octad containing 5 members of $S$ .If $s$ has 4 members we obtain 5 more

4-element sets congruent to $S$ by taking the symmetric differences of $s$ with the 5 octads that contain it (Theorem 11). If two distinct sets of 4 or fewer elements are congruent modulo $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ ，their symmetric difference is an octad,and so they must be disjoint and have 4 elements each,so the theorem is best possible.

Thus $4 0 9 6 = 1 + 2 4 + ( \begin{array} { c } { { 2 4 } } \\ { { 2 } } \end{array} ) + ( \begin{array} { c } { { 2 4 } } \\ { { 3 } } \end{array} ) + \frac 1 6 ( \begin{array} { c } { { 2 4 } } \\ { { 4 } } \end{array} )$ In other words $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ is a triple-error-correcting code with covering radius 4.

2.5 The maximal subgroups of $M _ { 2 4 }$ .The complete list of maximal subgroups of $M _ { 2 4 }$ is known．J.A.Todd[Tod3] observed eight distinct types in his paper on $M _ { 2 4 } .$ ，and a further type,the octern group of order 168 described below,has since been discovered．Chang Choi[Chol] and Curtis[Cur2]-[Cur5] have given proofs that these nine groups are inded the only conjugacy classes of maximal subgroups of $M _ { 2 4 }$ .With two exceptions these groups are easily described in terms of the Golay code $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ ，and we describe them in some detail.We shall give a further description of these groups in terms of the MOG in Chap.11.

A 12-element $\mathscr { C }$ -set is called an (umbral) dodecad,and a complementary pair of umbral dodecads is a duum. A triplet of mutually disjoint octads is a trio,and a system of 6 tetrads with the property that the union of any two is an octad is a sextet.(Mnemonics: duum $= 2$ umbrals,trio $\ l = 3$ octads, sextet $= 6$ tetrads.） In general, we use $_ n$ -ad for an $_ n$ -element subset of $\pmb { \Omega }$ ，except that the terms octad and dodecad usually presuppose the corresponding adjectives special and umbral.

The maximal subgroups $M _ { 2 4 }$ can now be described as the stabilizers of the concepts monad,duad,triad,octad,sextet, trio,duum,along with two further groups $L _ { 2 } ( 2 3 )$ ， $L _ { 2 } ( 7 )$ (compare Table 11.1 of the following chapter)．The $L _ { 2 } ( 2 3 )$ is the group we started from,and the $L _ { 2 } ( 7 )$ is the last maximal subgroup. We give theorems asserting the exact amount of transitivity of each of these groups on various configurations in $\pmb { \Omega }$ . We say that a group is $a + b$ transitive on two sets $\pmb { A }$ and $B$ if it contains elements taking any $^ { a }$ elements of $\pmb { A }$ ,and simultaneously any $^ { b }$ elements of $B$ ，to preassigned positions.

Theorem 14. The group $2 ^ { 4 } \mathsf { A } _ { 8 }$ fixing an octad is $6 + 1 , 3 + 2$ and $1 + 3$ transitive on the octad and its complement.

Proof. The stabilizer of an octad and one point in its complement is the group $H = \mathsf { A } _ { 8 }$ ，sextuply transitive on the octad,and,in its role as $\pmb { { \cal L } } _ { 4 } ( 2 )$ ， doubly transitive on the remaining 15 points of the complement,which can be regarded as the involutions of a group $2 ^ { 4 }$ acted upon by $\pmb { L _ { 4 } ( 2 ) }$ .The stabilizer of two points of the complement is therefore a group $2 ^ { 3 } L _ { 3 } ( 2 )$ ， which can only be the group we met in the first lecture,triply transitive on the octad. The stabilizer of one point in the octad together with two of the complement is $L _ { 3 } ( 2 )$ ，and is easily seen to be transitive on the remaining 14 points of the complement.

Theorem 17. $M _ { 2 4 }$ is transitive on sextets.The stabilizer of a sextet is a group $2 ^ { 6 } \cdot 3 \cdot 5 _ { \mathrm { ~ 6 ~ } }$ ，and the subgroup $2 ^ { 6 } \cdot 3$ fixing the tetrads individually is $2 ~ + ~ 1 ~ + ~ 1 ~ + ~ 0 ~ + ~ 0 ~ + ~ 0 ~$ transitive on the tetrads (in any order).

The transitivity $2 ~ + ~ 1 ~ + ~ 1 ~ + ~ 0 ~ + ~ 0 ~ + ~ 0 ~$ is also established. Theorem 18. $M _ { 2 4 }$ is transitive on trios. The stabilizer of a trio is a group $2 ^ { 6 } ( \mathbb { S } _ { 3 } \times L _ { 3 } ( 2 ) )$ ，and the subgroup $2 ^ { 6 } L _ { 3 } ( 2 )$ fixing the octads separately is $2 + 1 + 1$ and $3 + 1 + 0$ transitive on the three octads (in any order).

Proof. The element $\left( a b c d e \right) \left( f g h \right) \left( i \right) \left( j k l . . . x \right)$ of shape 13 5 15 permutes the 30 octads disjoint from $\{ a , b , c , d , e , f , g , h \}$ (Theorem 11） in two orbits of size 15,consisting of those containing,and those not containing,the point $i$ ．Each octad therefore belongs to 15 trios,and $M _ { 2 4 }$ is transitive on the trios,of which there must be $7 5 9 \cdot 1 5 / 3 = 3 7 9 5$ .Since the tetrads of a sextet can begrouped to form 15 distincttrios, and since $1 7 7 1 \cdot 1 5 = 3 7 9 5 \cdot 7$ ,，each trio can be refined into 7 distinct sextets. Now each sextet corresponds naturally to an element of $P ( \Omega ) / \mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ (Theorem 13),and the 7 sextets refining a trio must therefore,together with the empty set, form a 3-dimensional vector space over $\mathbf { F } _ { 2 }$ (a subspace of $P ( \Omega ) / \dot { \mathcal { C } } _ { 2 4 } \dot { ) }$ .The stabilizer of a trio has therefore two interesting normal subgroups - one fixing the octads individually,and another fxing each of the 7 sextets refining the trio. The quotient by the first is ${ \ S } _ { 3 }$ since all permutations of the three octads are induced,and the quotient by the second is $L _ { 3 } ( 2 )$ or a subgroup thereof,since the permutations of the 7 sextets must preserve the vector space structure. The index of their intersection therefore divides 6·168,and so the intersection,fixing both the octads and the sextets individually，has order of form $6 4 n$ (since $6 4 { \cdot } 6 { \cdot } 1 6 8 { \cdot } 3 7 9 5 = 2 4 4 8 2 3 0 4 0 )$ ．But the intersection is a subgroup of the group described in the previous theorem,and since an element $1 ^ { 6 } 3 ^ { 6 }$ cannot fix 7 sextets,it has order at most 64. This gives the structure of the group.

We make only the following remarks about the transitivity. If we fix the three octads individually,and then also a point of one of them，we obtain a subgroup $2 ^ { 3 } L _ { 3 } ( 2 )$ of index 8 in $2 ^ { 6 } L _ { 3 } ( 2 )$ ,which is represented on 7 points of the frst octad (with kernel $2 ^ { 3 }$ ）and in two distinct ways on the 8 points of the other'two octads (faithfully in each case,related by the outer automorphism of the frst lecture)． Fixing a point of the second octad in addition,we come down to a group $L _ { 3 } ( 2 )$ ,represented on 7 points in the first and second octads,on 8 points in the third,and doubly transitively in each case.

Thus the new maximal subgroup of $M _ { 2 4 }$ is easily described as the centralizer in $M _ { 2 4 }$ of the permutation $\mathbf { I I }$ ，itself not in $M _ { 2 4 }$ So it is the octern stabilizer,the cycles of $\Pi$ being ordered triads,or terns.

In Chang Choi's analysis,subgroups of $M _ { 2 4 }$ are divided into three classes - intransitive,transitive but imprimitive,and primitive - and his arguments for the second and third classes are very short. Here we present a quick way to deal with the intransitive groups.

Theorem 21. Any intransitive subgroup of $M _ { 2 4 }$ fixes a monad, dyad, triad, octad,dodecad, or sextet,and is socontained inone of the groups of Todd's list.

Proof. Let $s$ be a non-empty proper subset of $\pmb { \Omega }$ invariant under the group. If $S \in \mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ then $s$ or its complement is an octad or dodecad fixed by the group. Otherwise $s$ is congruent modulo $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ to a unique monad, dyad or triad,or to the six tetrads of a sextet,fixed by the group,as we see from Theorem 13.

Similar ideas enable us to deal with some of the imprimitive groups,as we shall see in a moment. They also enable us to give a complete classification of the subsets of $\pmb { \Omega }$ under the action of $M _ { 2 4 }$

# 2.6 The structure of $\mathbf { P } ( \Omega )$

Theorem 22.The subsetsof $\pmb { \Omega }$ fall into 49 orbits under $M _ { 2 4 }$ ,related as in Fig.l0.l． Each node corresponds to one orbit,and the nodes are joined by lines indicating the number of ways a set of one type can be converted to one of another type by the addition or removal of a single point. Thus in an umbral heptad $( U _ { 7 } )$ ，there is one point whose removal leaves a special hexad $( S _ { 6 } )$ ， while the removal of any of the six others leaves an umbral hexad $( U _ { 6 } )$ .In the complement of an umbral heptad there are two points whose addition gives a transverse octad $( T _ { 8 } )$ ,and 15 that yield umbral octads $( U _ { 8 } )$ ：

Proof.We discuss 8-element sets as an example.Each 8-element set $s$ is congruent modulo $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ to one of

(i) the empty set,   
i) a unique 2-element set $T$   
(ii) each of the tetrads $T _ { 0 } , \dots , T _ { 5 }$ of a sextet.

In case (i), $s$ is a special octad $S _ { 8 }$ ， $M _ { 2 4 }$ is transitive on these.

In case (ii), $s$ is obtained from the special octad $S + T$ by adding one point and subtracting another. Since the stabilizer of a special octad is $1 + 1$ transitive on it and its complement, $M _ { 2 4 }$ is transitive on sets of this type,which we call transverse octads $T _ { 8 }$

In case (ii) $S + T _ { i }$ is a special octad if $T _ { i }$ contains two points of $S$ and two points of its complement,and an umbral dodecad if $T _ { i }$ is disjoint from $S$ ．Counting points of $s$ shows that there are four tetrads of the first kind and two of the second,so that $s$ can be obtained (in two ways） by removing four points from an umbral dodecad. Since the stabilizer of an umbral dodecad is quadruply transitive on the dodecad, $M _ { 2 4 }$ is transitive on sets like $s$ (which we call umbral octads $U _ { 8 } )$ ：

Figure 10.1. The action of $M _ { 2 4 }$ on $\pmb { P } ( \pmb { \Omega } )$ (Theorem 22).

In general,a set of cardinal $n < 1 2$ is called special $( S _ { n } )$ if it contains or is contained in a special octad,otherwise umbral $( U _ { n } )$ if it is contained in an umbral dodecad,and transverse $( T _ { n } )$ if not.A non-umbral dodecad is extraspecial $( S _ { 1 2 } ^ { + } )$ if it contains three special octads,special $( S _ { 1 2 } )$ if it contains just one,penumbral $( U _ { 1 2 } ^ { - } )$ if it contains all but one of the points of an umbral dodecad,and transverse $( T _ { 1 2 } )$ in all other cases. Sets of more than 12 points are described by the same adjectives as their complements.

Figure 10.1 enables us to read off many interesting relationships at a glance. Thus on removing any point from a $U _ { 8 }$ we find a $U _ { 7 }$ ，in which there is a unique further point whose removal leaves an $S _ { 6 }$ .The 8 points of a $U _ { 8 }$ therefore split into 4 sets of 2 in a natural manner,so that the stabilizer of a $U _ { 8 }$ acts imprimitively on the $U _ { 8 }$ .We can also see from the diagram that the stabilizer of any 8-element set also stabilizes a special octad.For $S _ { 8 }$ ,this is the $S _ { 8 }$ itself; for $T _ { 8 }$ ，the unique $S _ { 8 }$ sharing7 points with the $T _ { 8 }$ and for $U _ { 8 }$ ，the union of the two tetrads whose addition separately would convert the $U _ { 8 }$ to a $U _ { 1 2 }$

Theorem 23. If a subgroup of $M _ { 2 4 }$ has two imprimitivity sets of size 12, or three of size 8,it is contained in one of the groups of Todd's list.

Proof. If the 12-ads are umbral,this is obvious. If not,they are congruent modulo $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ to (the same) one of the sets of size 1,2,or 3,or to the six tetrads of a sextet.In the other case,we observe that the group stabilizes the three corresponding special octads. If the union of these is $\pmb { \Omega }$ ，they form a fixed trio,and if not,the group is intransitive.

In a similar way,with more complicated arguments,one can handle the case of four sets of size 6,or six sets of size 4,but other ideas are needed beyond this point.

All maximal subgroups of the Mathieu groups $M _ { 2 3 }$ $M _ { 2 2 }$ $M _ { 1 2 }$ $M _ { 1 1 }$ are also known． Table 10.3 gives descriptions． The left hand column gives the action on the set $\pmb { \Omega }$ ，with semicolons separating the orbits of the Mathieu group under discussion. The symbol [1; 1;7,i5] for example indicates a subgroup of $M _ { 2 2 }$ (fixing the two 1's) that has orbits of size 7 and 15 on the remaining 22 points. In this case there are two conjugacy classes according to which of the two fixed points completes the orbit of size 7 to an octad．Again,the symbol [8,16] indicates a group with two orbits of sizes 8 and 16,while $[ 4 ^ { 6 } ]$ means that the group is transitive,with six imprimitivity sets of size 4.(Thus $[ 4 ^ { 6 } ]$ is not the same as [4,4,4,4,4,4].) The symbol $6 \times 2$ denotes a set of 12 points with at the same time six imprimitivity sets of size 2 and two of size 6,so forming a $6 \times 2$ table in a natural way. It is very easy to recognize the groups from this information, so we refrain from further comment.

3.9 A connection between $\mathbf { \nabla } \cdot \mathbf { 0 }$ and Fischer's group $F i _ { 2 4 }$ ·O can be regarded as a permutation group on the 196560 vectors of $\Lambda ( 2 )$ . It has a subgroup $N = \overline { { 2 } } ^ { 1 2 } M _ { 2 4 }$ that permutes these in three orbits of sizes $2 ^ { 7 } \cdot 7 5 9 , \ 2 ^ { \bar { 1 2 } } \cdot 2 \bar { 4 } ,$ and $2 ^ { 2 } ( ^ { 2 4 } _ { 2 }$ The elementary part $2 ^ { 1 2 }$ of $N$ is permuted by $M _ { 2 4 }$ like the binary Golay code $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ The extension $2 ^ { 1 2 } M _ { 2 4 }$ is split.

The group $F i _ { 2 4 }$ of B.Fischer[Fis1] is a permutation group on 306936 objects (the involutions in a certain conjugacy class).It has a subgroup $N ^ { * } = 2 ^ { 1 2 } M _ { 2 4 }$ that permutes these in three orbits of sizes $2 ^ { 5 } { \cdot } 7 5 9 , \ 2 ^ { 0 } { \cdot } 2 \bar { 4 } .$ and $2 ^ { 1 0 } ( 2 ^ { 2 4 } )$ The elementary part $2 ^ { 1 2 }$ of $N ^ { \ast }$ is permuted by $M _ { 2 4 }$ like the quotient $\bar { P } ( \Omega ) / \mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ The extension $2 ^ { 1 2 } M _ { 2 4 }$ is non-split.

These facts suggest that there is a relation between the two groups,and this is borne out by the fact that the subgroups of $M _ { 2 4 }$ corresponding to the three orbits are identical,while the elementary subgroups are dual. The appropriate name for this relationship - whatever it is -is twinning, as we see from the following parable. “Once upon a time there was an egg (the elementary group $P \left( \Omega \right)$ of order $2 ^ { 2 4 }$ ),which after fertilization (by the action of $M _ { 2 4 } )$ split into two (the group $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ and its quotient $P ( \Omega ) / \mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 } )$ ， which grew into two healthy twins (·O and $F i _ { 2 4 . }$ .”

That the parable is meaningful is suggested by the existence of similar structure relating $\cdot 0$ to itself via its subgroup $6 \ : S u z$ ,with elements of order 3 like $\omega$ taking the place of Fischer's involutions.The elementary $2 ^ { 1 2 }$ in the subgroup $N ^ { * }$ of $F i _ { 2 4 }$ has 24 of Fischer's 3-transpositions (the special involutions of his group)，permuted in the natural way by $M _ { 2 4 }$ ，the centralizer of any one being a group $2 F i _ { 2 3 }$ .In a similar way $^ { . 0 }$ has a group $3 ^ { 6 } . 2 M _ { 1 2 }$ in which the $3 ^ { 6 }$ has 12 special subgroups of order 3 (isomorphic to the groups $V _ { i }$ of the first lecture） permuted naturally by $M _ { 1 2 }$ ,the centralizer of any one being the group $6 \ : S u z$ ：

The Monster group $M$ ，which was discovered a few years after these lectures were given,led to the discovery of several additional simple groups and casts further light on some of those already known. These groups usually arise from studying the structure of centralizers of suitable elements of the Monster.Here we consider elements of prime order,and write $F _ { p + } , F _ { p - }$ etc.for the nonabelian composition factor in the centralizer of an element in the conjugacy class of $M$ called $p + , p -$ etc. in [Con16], [Conl7]. Some of the groups that are obtained in this way are shown above.

$M = F _ { 1 }$ ，the Monster,or Fischer-Griess group,or Friendly Giant,was discovered independently by Fischer and Griess in 1973,and constructed by Griess in 1980 [Gri4]-[Gri8].A simplified construction is described in Chap.29. The baby Monster $B = F _ { 2 + }$ was discovered by Fischer slightly earlier and was constructed by Leon and Sims [Leo9],[Sim3].

The existence of the Thompson group $T h = F _ { 3 | 3 }$ (constructed by J. G. Thompson and P.E. Smith [Tho2l) and of the Harada-Norton group $H N = F _ { 5 + }$ (constructed by Norton [HarO],[Har1],[Nor2],[Nor8]） was suggested by that of the Monster,although the entirely analogous groups of Fischer $( F i ^ { \prime } { } _ { 2 4 } = F _ { 3 + } )$ and Held $( H e = F _ { 7 + } )$ were already known [Heli], [Hel2]. All of these groups are best understood in terms of their relationship with the Monster. We remark that $C o _ { 1 } = F _ { 2 - }$ ， $S u z = F _ { 3 - }$ $H J = J _ { 2 } = F _ { 5 - }$ $M _ { 1 2 } = F _ { 1 1 + }$

# 11

# The Golay Codes and The Mathieu Groups

J. H. Conway

This chapter contains a detailed description of the binary Golay code of length 24,the Steiner system $S \left( 5 , 8 , 2 4 \right)$ ,and the Mathieu group $M _ { 2 4 }$ The MOG (Miracle Octad Generator） and the hexacode are computational tools that make it easy to perform calculations with these objects. The MINIMOG and the tetracode perform similar services for the ternary Golay code of length 12,the Steiner system $S ( 5 , 6 , 1 2 )$ ,and the Mathieu group $M _ { 1 2 }$

# 1． Introduction

The Golay code $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ ，the Steiner system $S \left( 5 , 8 , 2 4 \right)$ ，and the Mathieu group $M _ { 2 4 }$ are beautiful combinatorial objects with a great wealth of structure and applications. The MOG,and its companion-at-arms the hexacode,are computational tools that enable one to perform mental calculations on these objects with great ease.In particular,one can check at sight that a word is in $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ ，complete an octad of $S \left( 5 , 8 , 2 4 \right)$ from any five of its points,or write down many permutations of $M _ { 2 4 }$ in a few moments. There is also a MINIMOG，with companion the tetracode, which together perform similar services for $M _ { 1 2 }$ .Some discoveries about the“lexicography”of $M _ { 2 4 }$ and $M _ { 1 2 }$ indicate that these devices may have some theoretical as well as practical value.

Many calculations in the larger sporadic simple groups reduce to calculations inside $M _ { 2 4 }$ ，which has consequently been used in a number of constructions. In particular,we mention the construction of the Conway groups via the Leech latice (see Chap.1O),the Fischer groups $F i _ { 2 4 } , F i _ { 2 3 }$ $F i _ { 2 2 }$ (83.9 of Chap.lO),the Janko group $\boldsymbol { J } _ { 4 }$ [Con12],[Nor3],and most recently Griess's construction of the Monster group (see [Gri4]-[Gri8l and Chap. 29).

The MOG array was invented by R.T.Curtis [Cur2],[Cur3] in the course of his work on the Leech lattice,and he and others have made valuable use of it for many other investigations involving $M _ { 2 4 }$ . The special virtues of the approach via the hexacode emerged much later,during the construction by Norton，Parker，Benson,Conway and Thackray of the largest Janko group $\scriptstyle J _ { 4 }$ [Conl2],[Nor3]． Although that company included several practiced MOG users,it was found that the hexacode effected still greater simplifications in the enormous number of $M _ { 2 4 }$ -related calculations that were required in the course of the construction．More recently,it has performed a similar role for the many calculations with the Leech lattice that were carried out in the determination of its covering radius and the enumeration of its deep holes (see Chap. 23).

There are almost as many different constructions of $M _ { 2 4 }$ as there have been mathematicians interested in that most remarkable of all finite groups．Usually,when one constructs a large group from some“simpler” object,the construction itself will have a smaller group of symmetries,and one finds that elements inside this “visible subgroup”are “easy” to understand,and the others“hard.’ It is a remarkable fact that the MOG construction manages to have several “visible groups,”each of them a maximal subgroup of $M _ { 2 4 } .$ ！We shall construct it here in a way that is specially related to the sextet group $2 ^ { 6 } { : } 3 ^ { \cdot } \mathsf { S } _ { 6 }$ ，since that offers maximal opportunities for the use of the hexacode,which is the main topic of this chapter.However,we feel that the reader should be aware that the MOG was first used by Curtis in connection with the octad group $2 ^ { 4 } { : } \mathsf { A } _ { 8 }$ ，that when he wrote it up it seemed easiest to use the trio group $2 ^ { 6 } \colon ( \mathbb { S } _ { 3 } \times L _ { 2 } ( 7 ) )$ ， and that still later the triad group $P \Gamma L _ { 3 } ( 4 )$ was found to be just as simply related to the MOG.In fact much of its power stems from the ability to switch groups while seeking the element one desires.

In the first part of the chapter we shall describe the construction of the hexacode and MOG,and show how to use them for the basic calculations that arise in every investigation with $M _ { 2 4 }$ ．The later part has a section for each maximal subgroup,described where possble in close relation to the hexacode or MOG.

# 2.Definitions of the hexacode

As usual ${ \bf F } _ { 4 } = \left\{ 0 , 1 , \omega , \overline { { \omega } } \right\}$ , with the relations

$$
\begin{array} { r } { + \infty = \overline { { \omega } } \ , 1 + \overline { { \omega } } = \omega \ , \omega + \overline { { \omega } } = \omega \overline { { \omega } } = 1 \ , \omega ^ { 2 } = \overline { { \omega } } \ , \overline { { \omega } } ^ { 2 } = \omega \ , \omega ^ { 3 } = 1 \ . } \end{array}
$$

The hexacode $\mathscr { C } _ { 6 }$ (\$2.5.2 of Chap.3） is a 3-dimensional code of length 6 over $\mathbf { F _ { 4 } }$ .In order to display certain symmetries,we usually group the 6 digits of a hexacodeword into 3 couples. The code may be defined in several different ways:

Definition 1. $\mathscr { C } _ { 6 }$ is generated by the words $\begin{array} { r } { \omega \overline { { \omega } } \omega \overline { { \omega } } \omega \overline { { \omega } } , \quad \omega \overline { { \omega } } \overline { { \omega } } \omega \overline { { \omega } } \omega , \quad \overline { { \omega } } \omega \omega \overline { { \omega } } \overline { { \omega } } \omega , \quad \overline { { \omega } } \omega \overline { { \omega } } \overline { { \omega } } \omega \overline { { \omega } } , } \end{array}$

Definition 2. $\mathcal { C } _ { 6 }$ has a word $W ( \phi ) = a b$ cd ef for each quadratic function $\phi \left( x \right) = a x ^ { 2 } + b x + c $ defined over $\mathbf { F } _ { 4 }$ The frst three digits $( a , b , c )$ specify the function $\phi$ ,and the last four $( c , d , e , f )$ give its values at $0 , 1 , \omega , \varpi$ ：

$$
c = \phi \left( 0 \right) , d = \phi \left( 1 \right) , e = \phi \left( \omega \right) , f = \phi \left( \overline { { \omega } } \right) .
$$

Definition 3. Each word ab cd ef of $\mathcal { C } _ { 6 }$ has a slope,s. Then ab cd ef is a word of $\mathcal { C } _ { 6 }$ with slope $s$ if and only if it satisfies the following relations:

The 1-rule: $a + b = c + d = e + f = s ,$

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { a + c + e = a + d + f = b + c + f = b + d + e = \omega s , } \\ & { b + d + f = b + c + e = a + d + e = a + c + f = \overline { { \omega } } s . } \end{array}

(Thus the digits of each couple add to $s$ ，while three digits from distinct couples add to $\boldsymbol { \omega } \pmb { S }$ or $\overline { { \omega } } s$ according as it is the left or right possibility that is chosen an odd number of times.)

The code under any of these definitions is 3-dimensional; in the first case because the four given words add to zero,but obey no further linear relation; in the second case obviously;and in the third case since the relations

$$
a + b = c + d = e + f = s , a + c + e = \omega s
$$

between the seven quantities $a , b , c , d , e , f , s$ imply all the rest. (The frst three of these imply that the replacement of any digit by its mate will alter the sum by $s$ ）

Given the 3-dimensionality，the identity of the three codes follows readily by checking that some 3 independent words can be found in all three codes.We suggest that the reader checks this for the generators of the second version:

$$
W ( x ^ { 2 } ) = 1 0 0 1 \ \overline { { { \omega } } } \omega \ , W ( x ) = 0 1 \ 0 1 \ \omega \overline { { { \omega } } } \ , W ( 1 ) = 0 0 \ 1 1 \ 1 1 \ .
$$

From either the first or the third definition,it is obvious that $\mathscr { C } _ { 6 }$ has the following symmetries:

1) scalar multiplication by any power of $\omega$ ，   
2) flipping of the two digits in any two of the couples,   
3) bodily permutation of the three couples in any way.

# 4. Completing a hexacodeword

In the application,one is often faced with the problem of determining a hexacodeword from some partial information about its digits.In many cases this reduces to one of two standard problems:

The 3-problem: determine a hexacodeword from any three of its digits.

The 5-problem: determine a hexacodeword from any five of its digits,one of which may be mistaken.

In either case,the answer is unique,and so we earnestly recommend that you use

The Best Method: guess the correct answer,and then justify it.

This is both easier and quicker than the methods that follow. But if you're stuck,you can always solve such problems like this:

The 3-problem: If the given digits are from distinct couples (such as $\scriptstyle { a , c , e } )$ ，use the $\omega \cdot$ or $\overline { { \omega } }$ -rule to find $s$ ，and then the 1-rule for the remaining digits (here $^ { b , d , f ) }$ ：

Example. $\omega ? ~ 1 ? ~ 0 ? \Rightarrow \omega s = \omega + 1 + 0 = \overline { { { \omega } } }$ so $s = \omega$ ， $W = \omega 0 ~ 1 \overline { { \omega } } ~ 0 \omega$ ，with signs $-- +$ ．(Although the answer must be right if we've calculated correctly,the reader is recommended always to check the answers by the shape and sign rules.)

# 5. The Golay code $\pmb { \mathcal { C } } _ { 2 4 }$ and the MOG

The Golay code $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ has already been mentioned several times (see in particular $\ S 2 . 8 . 2$ of Chap.3 and $\ S 2$ of Chap.1O)．In this chapter we shall often use blank and non-blank symbols instead of the digits O and 1. Robert Curtis [Cur2l found that the easiest way to compute with words of $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ is to arrange their digits in a $6 \times 4$ array,called by him the Miracle Octad Generator,or MOG.

Words of $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ in this notation are readily obtained from hexacodewords by

$? \omega \ ? 1 \ \omega ?$ $? \omega \ : 0 ? \ : \omega ?$ 112022 21701011 ？

eitheri) replacing each digit by an odd interpretation, in any way such that the top row becomes odd;   
or i) replacing each digit by an even interpretation,in any way such that the top row becomes even.

A row or column is called odd or even according as it contains an odd or even number of non-zero digits. The odd and even interpretations of the digits are shown in Fig.11.1. Note that the odd interpretations have either just one non-zero digit,or just one zero digit,in each column,while the even interpretations differ from the odd ones only in their treatment of the top row.

Justifying $\pmb { \mathcal { C } }$ -sets.The following procedure can therefore be used to verify that a given set is a $\mathscr { C }$ -set (i.e. the set of places where a codeword of $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 }$ is non-zero).

1）For each column,and for the top row,compute its count (the number of non-zero digits it contains).

2）For each column,compute also its score,obtained by adding $0 , 1 , \omega , \widetilde { \omega }$ for any non-zero digit in the first,second,third,fourth row,respectively. (Alternatively,a column has a given score digit if and only if it is one of the four interpretations of that digit).

Then the set is a $\mathscr { C }$ -set if and only if the counts have allthe same parity, while the scores form a hexacodeword. We shall call this process justifying the $\mathscr { C }$ -set.

In Fig.l1.2 we have given several interpretations of the standard hexacodeword $0 1 \ 0 1 \ \omega \overline { { \omega } }$ .We recommend to the beginner our practice of writing counts above,and scores below,the MOG diagram.
