# Even Unimodular 24-Dimensional Lattices

B. B.Venkov

Niemeier's classification of even unimodular 24-dimensional lattices is simplified. The methods involve the theory of modular forms,algebraic coding,and root systems.

# 1． Introduction

We consider even unimodular Euclidean lattices A in $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ or，in more classical terminology，classes of integral,positive definite,even quadratic forms of determinant 1 in $\pmb { n }$ variables. Such lattices exist only if $ \pmb { n } = 8 k$ ： A complete classification of such lattices is known only for $k = 1 , 2 , 3$ ： When $k = 4$ there are already more than 8O million lattices (see Table 16.5.)．When $k = 1$ or 2 the classification is very simple: there are precisely one 8-dimensional and two l6-dimensional lattices of the above type.A complete classification of the 24-dimensional lattices was obtained in 1968 by Niemeier [Nie2l.According to Niemeier, there are precisely 24 classes of even unimodular lattices. Each lattice $\pmb { \Lambda }$ isuniquely determined by its set of minimal vectors $\Lambda \left( 2 \right) = \left\{ \lambda \in \Lambda : \left( \lambda , \lambda \right) = 2 \right\}$ which form root systems of the following types:

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } & { 2 4 A _ { 1 } , \ 1 2 A _ { 2 } , \ 8 A _ { 3 } , \ 6 A _ { 4 } , \ 4 A _ { 6 } , \ 3 A _ { 8 } , \ 2 A _ { 1 2 } , \ A _ { 2 4 } , \ } & \\ & { 6 D _ { 4 } , \ 4 D _ { 6 } , \ 3 D _ { 8 } , \ 2 D _ { 1 2 } , \ D _ { 2 4 } , \ } & \\ & { 4 E _ { 6 } , \ 3 E _ { 8 } , \ } & \\ & { 4 A _ { 5 } + D _ { 4 } , \ 2 A _ { 7 } + 2 D _ { 5 } , \ 2 A _ { 9 } + D _ { 6 } , \ A _ { 1 5 } + D _ { 9 } , \ E _ { 8 } + D _ { 1 6 } , \ 2 E _ { 7 } + D _ { 1 0 } , \ E _ { 7 } + A _ { 1 7 } , \ } & \\ & { \ } & { \ ( 1 5 , \ 6 ) , \ } & { \ ( 3 A _ { 1 1 } ) . } \end{array}
$$

The lattice corresponding to the empty root system is the Leech lattice. Niemeier obtained his classification by Kneser's method [Kne4l,which involves studying lattices that are“neighbors”of a given one (see the previous chapter),requires extensive calculations,and in no way explains the appearance of the strange list (1） of root systems. Here we offer another approach to the classification of the even unimodular 24- dimensional lattices,based on an ä priori proof of the fact that the root system of a 24-dimensional lattice is one of the systems in (1） and that each root system in (1） can be realized in one and only one way. In $\ S 2$ we prove that the root system $\Lambda \left( 2 \right)$ of an even unimodular lattice $\pmb { \Lambda }$ in $\pmb { R } ^ { 2 4 }$ possesses the following properties:(i) either $\Lambda \left( 2 \right) = \emptyset$ or rank $\Lambda \left( 2 \right) = 2 4$ ， (ii) all irreducible components of $\Lambda \left( 2 \right)$ have the same Coxeter number $h$ ， (ii) $\left| \Lambda \left( 2 \right) \right| = 2 4 h$ ，where $\left| \Lambda \left( 2 \right) \right|$ is the number of elements in $\Lambda \left( 2 \right)$ .This is proved by means of modular forms (using theta series with spherical coefficients). It is easy to show that the only root systems possessing properties (i)-(i) are those in the list (1).

We then show that each root system in (1) can be realized as $\Lambda \left( 2 \right)$ for a unique lattice.This is actually a problem in algebraic coding theory (see $\ S 3$ ,and the existing literature on algebraic coding quickly enables us to obtain the final answer (\$4)．The last section is devoted to the Leech lattice.

# 2.Possible configurations of minimal vectors

Suppose $\Lambda \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 4 }$ isanevenunimodularlattice， $\Lambda \left( 2 n \right) =$ $\{ \lambda \ \in \Lambda : \left( \lambda , \lambda \right) = 2 n \}$ ,and $\Lambda \left( 2 \right)$ is the root system of $\mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \Lambda }$

Proposition 1． 1f $\alpha \in \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 4 }$ ,then

$$
\sum _ { y \in \Lambda \left( 2 \right) } \left( y , \alpha \right) ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { 1 2 } ( \alpha , \alpha ) \big | \Lambda \left( 2 \right) \big | .
$$

Proof. We use the classical result (see [Hec2l or $\scriptstyle [ 0 _ { \mathbf { g } \mathbf { g } 1 }$ ,Chap. VIl) which says that,for an even unimodular lattice $\Lambda$ in $V = \mathbf { R } ^ { f }$ ，the theta series with spherical coefficients

$$
f _ { \nu , p } = \sum _ { n } \biggl ( \sum _ { \chi \in \Lambda ( 2 n ) } P _ { \nu } \left( \chi \right) \biggr ) q ^ { n } , q = e ^ { 2 \pi i z } , \mathrm { I m } z > 0 ,
$$

is the Fourier expansion of a modular form for $P S L \left( 2 , \mathbf { Z } \right)$ of weight $\not { p } _ { 2 } f + \nu $ This form is a cusp form if $\nu > 0$ Here $P _ { \nu }$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $\pmb { \nu }$ which isa $\pmb { \Lambda }$ -spherical function,i.e. $\Delta _ { \Lambda } P _ { \nu } = 0$ where $\Delta _ { \Lambda }$ is the Laplace operator in a coordinate system in $V$ in which the inner product $( \mathbf { \epsilon } , )$ reduces to a sum of squares.The 2-dimensional $\Lambda$ spherical polynomials have a very simple form:they are linear combinations of polynomials

$$
P _ { 2 , \alpha } ( x ) = ( x , \alpha ) ^ { 2 } - \frac { 1 } { f } ( \alpha , \alpha ) ( x , x ) ,
$$

where $\alpha \in V$ (see [Hec2])． Thus,for any $\alpha \in V$ ，

$$
\sum _ { n } \left( \sum _ { x \in \Lambda ( 2 n ) } \ \left( ( x , \alpha ) ^ { 2 } { - } { \frac { 1 } { f } } ( \alpha , \alpha ) ( x , x ) \right) \right) q ^ { n }
$$

is a cusp form of weight $\% f + 2$ for the full modular group. In particular, for $f = 2 4$ the series (3) is a cusp form of weight 14; but such a form is equal to zero,since any modular form of weight $k$ is a polynomial in two modular forms, $E _ { 2 }$ and $E _ { 3 }$ ,of weights 4 and 6,and the cusp forms in this polynomial ring constitute the principal ideal generated by the unique parabolic form $\Delta$ of weight 12 (see [Ser1l)．Thus

$$
\sum _ { x \in \Lambda ( 2 n ) } \ O \left( x , \alpha \right) ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { 2 4 } 2 n \left( \alpha , \alpha \right) \left| \Lambda \left( 2 n \right) \right| ,
$$

which for $n = 1$ yields (2).

Corollary 1． Either $\Lambda \left( 2 \right) = \infty$ or rank $\Lambda \left( 2 \right) = 2 4$

Proof. Indeed, suppose rank $\Lambda \left( 2 \right) < 2 4$ , i.e. the vector subspace generated by $\Lambda \left( 2 \right)$ hasdimension $< 2 4$ Then $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 4 }$ contains a vector $\nu \neq 0$ orthogonal to all of $\Lambda$ (2). Putting $\alpha = \nu$ in (2),we see that $\left| \mathbf { A } \left( 2 \right) \right| = 0$

Corollary 2. All irreducible components of the root system $\Lambda \left( 2 \right)$ have the same Coxeter number $\pmb { h }$ ，and $\left| \Lambda \left( 2 \right) \right| = 2 4 \bar { h }$ ：

We now make use of the following property of the Coxeter number[Bou1, Chap.VI,\$1.11,Proposition 32l: if in an irreducible root system $R$ all roots have the same length,then the number of elements of $\pmb { R }$ not orthogonal to a fixed $\alpha \in R$ is equal to $4 h \ : - \ : 6$ .We take the usual normalization for an invariant inner product,where $( \alpha , \alpha ) = 2$ for $\alpha \in R$ Now if $\alpha , \alpha ^ { \prime } \in R$ ，then $( \alpha , \alpha ^ { \prime } )$ can assume only the values $0 , \pm 1 , \pm 2$ ,and $( \alpha , \alpha ^ { \prime } ) = \pm 2$ only if $\alpha ^ { \prime } = \pm \alpha$ .Therefore $4 h - 6 = 2 + 2 \beta ( R )$ ，where $\beta ( R )$ is the number of roots ${ \boldsymbol { \alpha } } ^ { \prime } \in R$ such that $( \alpha ^ { \prime } , \alpha ) = 1$ for a fixed $_ \alpha$ This does not depend on the choice of $_ { \alpha }$ ，since the Weyl group $W ( R )$ acts transitively on the roots．Thus $\beta ( R ) = 2 h \left( R \right) - 4$

Proof of Corollary 2. If $\alpha \in \Lambda \left( 2 \right)$ ,then,according to (2).

$$
\sum _ { y \in \Lambda ( 2 ) } { ( y , \alpha ) ^ { 2 } } = \frac { 1 } { 6 } \vert \Lambda \left( 2 \right) \vert ,
$$

It is clear that only the elements of that irreducible component $R _ { \alpha }$ containing $_ \alpha$ make a contribution to the left-hand side of the equality,and that

$$
\sum _ { y \in \Lambda ( 2 ) } { ( y , \alpha ) ^ { 2 } } = 2 \cdot 2 ^ { 2 } + 2 \beta ( R _ { \alpha } ) .
$$

Proposition 2． If $\Lambda \left( 2 \right) \neq \infty$ ，then the root system $\Lambda \left( 2 \right)$ in $\pmb { R } ^ { 2 4 }$ possesses the following properties:

Conditions (i)-(ii) are very strong,and it is not difficult to find all root systems in $\pmb { R } ^ { 2 4 }$ satisfying them.

# 3. On lattices with root systems of maximal rank

The aim of this section is to make several general observations about even unimodular lattices having a root system of maximal rank and about the connection between such lattices and algebraic codes. In what follows we will consider only those root systems in which all roots have the same length, i.e. those root systems whose irreducible components have types $A , D$ ,or $E$ ：

The invariant meaning of this triple is the following: $T ( R ) = P / Q$ ， where $\boldsymbol { Q }$ is the root lattice and $\pmb { P }$ the weight lattice for $R$ ； $G \left( R \right)$ is isomorphic to the quotient group of the automorphism group $A \left( R \right)$ of the root system $R$ by the Weyl group $W ( R )$ with the natural faithful action of $\scriptstyle A \left( R \right) / W \left( R \right)$ on ${ \cal P } / { \cal Q } ; l$ is the norm of the microweight lying in a given coset with respect to $Q$ ． Recall that an element $p \in P$ is called a microweight if $( p , r ) = 0 , \pm 1$ for all $r \in R$ ．In each coset in $P / Q$ there is precisely one orbit under the Weyl group $W ( R )$ consistingof microweights,and $l$ on a coset with respect to $Q$ is the norm of any microweight lying in this coset.

If a root system consists of $\pmb { n }$ isomorphic components $\yen 123$ ,i.e. has the form $^ { n R }$ ， then we put $T ( n R ) = T ( R ) ^ { n }$ ，we define $G \left( n R \right)$ to be the natural semidirect product

In the general case,i.e. for any root system $R$ ，the problem of classifying the even self-dual subgroups of $T ( R )$ relative to $G \left( R \right)$ can also be viewed as a problem of coding theory. In the sequel, self-dual subgroups of $T ( R )$ will often be called codes.

Remarks (i） The usual concept of isomorphism in considering codes over commutative rings is defined by monomial matrices (\$2.2 of Chap.3). Proposition 4 shows that to classify lattices with root system of maximal rank of type $n R$ (where $R$ is an irreducible root system) in most cases it is necessary to classify codes relative to monomial groups in which the nonzero elements are equal to $\pm 1$ Only lattices of type $n D _ { 4 }$ lead to complete monomial groups.

(ii) The classification of lattices with root systems of maximal rank of type $n D _ { 2 k }$ depends very weakly on $k$ :in the corresponding code only the function $l$ depends on $k$ ．This enables us to reduce the problem of classifying such lattices of type $n D _ { 2 k }$ to the case of small $k$ ． An analogous remark holds for other cases of isomorphisms between the $T ( R _ { i } )$ .For example $T ( D _ { 2 i + 1 } ) = T ( D _ { 5 } ) = T ( A _ { 3 } )$ ， $T ( E _ { 6 } ) = T ( A _ { 2 } )$ ， and $T ( E _ { 7 } ) = T ( A _ { 1 } )$ ：

(iii) Codes corresponding to lattices of maximal rank and of type $n D _ { 2 k }$ are not necessarily linear codes over $\mathbf { F } _ { 4 }$ ；that is，self-dual subgroups of $T ( n D _ { 2 k } ) = T ( D _ { 2 k } ) ^ { n } = { \bf F } _ { 4 } ^ { n }$ need not be invariant under multiplication by scalars of $\mathbf { F _ { 4 } }$ .For example,this occurs in the 24-dimensional lattice with root system $3 D _ { 8 }$ (see case XI in $\ S 4 )$ ；if the corresponding self-dual subgroup were a linear subspace,it would have dimension 3/2.

# 5.A characterization of the Leech lattice

To complete the proof of the main theorem it remains to consider the case of an empty root system,i.e.we must consider a lattice $\Lambda$ is in which $( x , x ) \neq 2$ for $x \in \Lambda$ ．In this case there also exists a lattice and it is unique: it is the remarkable Leech lattice.A characterization of Leech's lattice as the unique even unimodular lattice in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 4 }$ with $( x , x ) \neq 2$ was given by Conway (see Chap.12)． Conway's proof is very pretty and can hardly be improved. However，if we assume (as is natural in our approach） that the classification of lattices with nontrivial root systems is already known,then the characterization of Leech's lattice can be obtained more simply as follows.

Suppose $\Lambda \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 4 }$ is an even unimodular lattice with $\Lambda \left( 2 \right) = \infty$ We want to prove that $\pmb { \Lambda }$ is isomorphic to Leech's lattice. From Theorem 17 of Chap.7,the condition $\Lambda \left( 2 \right) = \emptyset$ implies that the theta series of $\Lambda$ is the same as the theta series of Leech's lattice,in particular, $\Lambda \left( 8 \right) \neq \infty$ Let $u \in \Lambda \left( 8 \right)$ and consider the lattice $\Gamma = \Lambda ^ { u } = \Lambda ^ { \prime } \cup ( u / 2 + \Lambda ^ { \prime } )$ ，where $\Lambda ^ { \prime } = \left\{ \lambda \in \Lambda : \left( \lambda , u \right) \equiv 0 \right.$ (mod 2)). Then $\mathbf { \Gamma } ^ { \Gamma }$ is an even unimodular lattice in $\pmb { R } ^ { 2 4 }$ (it is a neighbor of $\Lambda$ in the sense of the previous chapter)．The lattice $\Gamma$ has a nonempty root system, since $u / 2 \in \Gamma ( 2 )$ .We shall prove that the root system for $\mathbf { \Gamma } ^ { \mathbf { \Gamma } }$ is $k A _ { 1 }$ .It suffices to show that nonproportional rootsof $\Gamma \left( 2 \right)$ areorthogonal.Thisisveryeasy.Suppose $x , y \in \Gamma ( 2 ) , x \ne \pm y$ ，so that $x , y \in u / 2 + \Lambda ^ { \prime }$ ，and suppose $( x , y ) \neq 0$ Changing the sign of $y$ if necessary,we may assume that $( x , y ) = - 1$ ,but then $x \mathrm { ~ - ~ } y$ is a root,i.e. $( x - y , x - y ) = 2$ But $x - y \in \Lambda ^ { \prime } \subset \Lambda$ and $\Lambda \left( 2 \right) = \emptyset$ ，which is impossible.Thus $\Gamma ( 2 ) = k A _ { 1 }$ ；but then,scanning the list (1),we see that $k = 2 4$ and $\mathbf { \Gamma } ^ { \Gamma }$ is described in paragraph Iof $\ S 4$ i.e.in $\pmb { R } ^ { 2 4 }$ wecan chooseabasis $e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { 2 4 }$ suchthat $( e _ { i } , e _ { j } ) = 0$ if $i \neq j$ ， $( e _ { i } , e _ { i } ) = \mathbb { 1 } _ { 2 }$ and $\Sigma n _ { i } e _ { i } \in \Gamma$ if and only if $n _ { i } \in Z$ and $\{ \dot { \boldsymbol { i } } : \boldsymbol { n } _ { i } \equiv 1$ (mod 2)) is a codeword in the binary Golay code.Since the property of being adjacent lattices is symmetric, there is a $\nu \in \Gamma$ such that $\Lambda = \Gamma ^ { \nu }$ Suppose $\nu = \Sigma m _ { i } e _ { i } , m _ { i } \in \mathbf { Z }$ ：we will prove that all of the $m _ { i }$ are odd. Indeed,if some $m _ { \alpha }$ is even，then $( \nu , 2 e _ { \alpha } ) = m _ { \alpha } \equiv 0$ (mod 2)；hence $2 e _ { \alpha } \in \Gamma ^ { \nu } = \Lambda$ ，which is impossible,since $\Lambda \left( 2 \right) = \infty$ .Thus each $m _ { i } \equiv 1$ (mod 2). Since $\nu$ is defined mod 2r,we may assume that $m _ { i } = \pm 1$ ,and the action of the Weyl group $W ( \Gamma ( 2 ) )$ allows us to assume that $m _ { 1 } = 1$ ， i.e. as $\pmb { \nu }$ we can choose $e _ { 1 } + \ \cdots \ + e _ { 2 4 }$ For such a $\nu , \Gamma ^ { \nu }$ is the Leech lattice,as required. This completes the proof of the main theorem.

We saw in Chapter 7 that the minimal norm of a unimodular lattice in $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ does not exceed $\left[ n / 8 \right] + 1$ .If the minimal norm is equal to this quantity the lattice is called extremal. In this chapter we show that there are unique extremal lattices in dimensions 1, 2,3,4,5,6,7,8,12,14,15, 23, 24,and no other such lattices.

We will show that $a _ { \alpha } < 0$ and $a _ { \alpha - 1 } < 0$ for $\alpha \geqslant 6$ ，from which the negative coefficient is apparent. Applying the Burmann-Lagrange theorem to (1) and (2) we obtain,exactly as in [Mal1,Eq.(6)],

$$
a _ { s } = -  \frac { n } { s ! } \frac { d ^ { s - 1 } } { d q ^ { s - 1 } } \{ \frac { d \theta _ { 3 } } { d q } \cdot \theta _ { 3 } ^ { 8 s - n - 1 } \cdot h ^ { s } \} _ { q = 0 } ,
$$

for $0 \leqslant s \leqslant \alpha$ ,where,from Eq.(33) of Chap.7,

$$
h = \prod _ { m = 1 } ^ { \infty } \{ ( 1 - q ^ { 2 m - 1 } ) ( 1 - q ^ { 4 m } ) \} ^ { - 8 } .
$$

Now $d \theta _ { 3 } / d q$ has non-negative coefficients in its $q$ -expansion. When $s = \alpha$ or $\alpha { - } 1$ we have

$$
- 1 \geqslant 8 s - n - 1 \geqslant - 1 6 .
$$

Let $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 1 6$ ．Then,from Eq.(35) of Chap.4,

$$
\theta _ { 3 } ^ { - k } = \prod _ { m = 1 } ^ { \infty } \ : \left( 1 - q ^ { 2 m } \right) ^ { - k } \ : \prod _ { m = 1 } ^ { \infty } \ : \left( 1 + q ^ { 2 m - 1 } \right) ^ { - 2 k } .
$$

The first product has non-negative coefficients. On the other hand,

$$
\begin{array} { r c l } { { } } & { { } } & { { \displaystyle h ^ { s } \prod _ { m = 1 } ^ { \infty } ( 1 + q ^ { 2 m - 1 } ) ^ { - 2 k } = \prod _ { m = 1 } ^ { \infty } ( 1 - q ^ { 2 m - 1 } ) ^ { - ( 8 s - 2 k ) } } } \\ { { } } & { { } } & { { \displaystyle \times \prod _ { m = 1 } ^ { \infty } ( 1 - q ^ { 4 m - 2 } ) ^ { - 2 k } \prod _ { m = 1 } ^ { \infty } ( 1 - q ^ { 4 m } ) ^ { - 8 s } . } } \end{array}
$$

If $n \geqslant 4 8 , \alpha \geqslant 6 , s \geqslant 5$ ，then every product on the right-hand side has non-negative coeffcients and the first has strictly positive coefficients. Therefore the expression in braces in (8） has strictly positive coeffcients, showing that $a _ { \alpha } < 0$ and $a _ { \alpha - 1 } < 0$ ．This completes the proof of Theorem 3.

# 20

# Finding the Closest Lattice Point

J. H. Conway and N. J. A. Sloane

This chapter describes algorithms which,given an arbitrary point of $\pmb { { \mathbb { R } } } ^ { n }$ find the closest point of some given lattice.The lattices discussed include the root lattices $A _ { n } , D _ { n } , E _ { 6 } , E _ { 7 } , E _ { 8 }$ and their duals. These algorithms can be used for vector quantizing or for decoding lattice codes for a bandlimited channel.

# 1． Introduction

As discussed in $\ S 3$ of Chap.2 and $\ S 1$ of Chap.3,lattices are practically important because they can be used as vector quantizers and as codes for a bandlimited channel. For these applications it is essential that there exist fast “decoding”algorithms which, given an arbitrary point of the space, find the closest lattice point.

In this chapter we describe such algorithms for the lattices $A _ { n } ( n \geqslant 1 )$ ， $D _ { n } ( n \geqslant 3 ) , E _ { 6 } , E _ { 7 } , E _ { 8 }$ and their duals.This chapter is based on [Con29] and [Con4o]. The latter reference also gives an algorithm for decoding the Leech lattce (omitted here because of its length),algorithms for finding the closest codeword to various binary codes including the Golay code ("soft” decoding algorithms-see $\ S 4$ below)，and an extensive bibliography．See also [Ado1],[Bud1],[Che2],[Con26],[Con38],[For2], [Gor0],[Wol2].

Practical applications of these lattices also require algorithms for labeling lattice points. Suppose our code or quantizer uses a set $C = \bigl \{ c _ { 1 } , \ldots , c _ { m } \bigr \}$ of lattice points.Effcient “encoding”algorithms are needed which map $i$ $( 1 \leqslant i \leqslant M )$ into $c _ { i }$ ,and vice versa．The first problem can be solved using the algorithms described in this chapter,and the second by using a dual basis for the lattice - see [Con35].

The problem discussed in the following sections is this: for a lattice A in $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ ,find a decoding algorithm which,given an arbitrary point $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ ， finds a lattice point $\textbf { \em u } \in { \Lambda }$ that minimizes the distance from $_ x$ to $\pmb { u }$ .We shall use the descriptions of the latices and their duals given in Chap.4. Asusual it easier to work with the squared distance or norm $N ( x - u ) = ( x - u ) \cdot ( x - u )$ than with the distance itself.

# 2. The lattices $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n } , D _ { n }$ and $A _ { n }$

The algorithm for finding the closest point of $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ to an arbitrary point $\mathbf { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ is particularly simple.For a real number $x$ ,let

$$
f ( x ) = { \mathrm { c l o s e s t ~ i n t e g e r ~ t o ~ } } x .
$$

In case of a tie,choose the integer with the smallest absolute value. For $x = ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) \in \mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ ,let

$$
f ( x ) = \left( f ( x _ { 1 } ) , \ldots , f ( x _ { n } ) \right) .
$$

For future use we also define $g ( x )$ ，which is the same as $f ( x )$ except that the worst coordinate of $x \_ -$ that furthest from an integer - is rounded the wrong way. In case of a tie,the coordinate with the lowest subscript is rounded the wrong way.

More formally, for $x \in \mathbb { R }$ we define $f ( x )$ and the function $w \left( x \right)$ which rounds the wrong way as follows.(Here $m$ is an integer.)

$$
\begin{array} { c c c } { { } } & { { \mathrm { I f ~ } x = 0 \mathrm { t h e n ~ } f ( x ) = 0 , } } & { { w ( x ) = 1 . } } \\ { { } } & { { \mathrm { I f ~ } 0 < m \leqslant x \leqslant m + \vert _ { 2 } \mathrm { t h e n ~ } f ( x ) = m , } } & { { w ( x ) = m + 1 . } } \\ { { } } & { { 0 < m + \vert _ { 2 } < x < m + 1 \mathrm { t h e n ~ } f ( x ) = m + 1 , } } & { { w ( x ) = m . } } \\ { { } } & { { - m - \vert _ { 2 } \leqslant x \leqslant - m < 0 \mathrm { t h e n ~ } f ( x ) = - m , } } & { { w ( x ) = - m - 1 . } } \\ { { } } & { { \lceil - m - 1 < x < - m - \vert _ { 2 } \mathrm { t h e n ~ } f ( x ) = - m - 1 , \ w ( x ) = - m . } } & \end{array}
$$

(Ties are handled so as to give preference to points of smaller norm.） We also write

$$
x = f ( x ) + \delta \left( x \right) ,
$$

so that $\left| \delta \left( x \right) \right| \leqslant 1 / _ { 2 }$ is the distance from $_ x$ to the nearest integer.

Given $x = ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ ,let $k$ $( 1 \leqslant k \leqslant n )$ be such tha1

$$
\left| \delta \left( x _ { k } \right) \right| \leqslant \left| \delta \left( x _ { i } \right) \right| { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ a l l ~ } } 1 \leqslant i \leqslant n
$$

and

$$
\left| \delta ( x _ { k } ) \right| = \left| \delta ( x _ { i } ) \right| \Rightarrow k \leq i .
$$

Then $g \left( x \right)$ is defined by

$$
g ( \boldsymbol { x } ) = \left( f ( x _ { 1 } ) , f ( x _ { 2 } ) , \ldots , w ( x _ { k } ) , \ldots , f ( x _ { n } ) \right) .
$$

Algorithm 1．To find the closest point of $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ to $x$ ：

Given $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ ，the closest point of $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ is $f ( x )$ (If $x$ is equidistant from two or more points of $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ ，this procedure finds the one with the smallest norm.)

To see that the procedure works, let $u = ( u _ { 1 } , \ldots , u _ { n } )$ be any point of $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ Then

$$
N ( u - x ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( u _ { i } - x _ { i } ) ^ { 2 } ,
$$

which is minimized by choosing $u _ { i } = f ( x _ { i } )$ for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ .Because of (1） ties are broken correctly,favoring the point with the smallest norm.

Next we consider $D _ { n }$ (87.1 of Chap. 4).

Algorithm 2. To find the closest point of $D _ { n }$ to $x$

Given $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ ,the closest point of $D _ { n }$ is whichever of $f ( x )$ and $g ( x )$ has an even sum of coordinates (one will have an even sum,the other an odd sum).If $_ x$ is equidistant from two or more points of $D _ { n }$ this procedure produces a nearest point having the smallest norm.

This procedure works because $f ( x )$ is the closest point of $\mathbf { Z } ^ { n }$ to $_ x$ and $g \left( x \right)$ is the next closest. $f ( x )$ and $g ( x )$ differ by 1 in exactly one coordinate,and so precisely one of $\Sigma f ( x _ { i } )$ and $\Sigma g ( x _ { i } )$ is even and the other is odd.

Example: Find the closest point of $D _ { 4 }$ to

$$
x = \left( 0 . 6 , - 1 . 1 , 1 . 7 , 0 . 1 \right) .
$$

We compute $f ( x ) = \left( 1 , - 1 , 2 , 0 \right)$ and $g \left( x \right) = \left( 0 , - 1 , 2 , 0 \right)$ ，since the first coordinate of $x$ is the furthest from an integer.The sum of the coordinates of $f ( x )$ is $1 - 1 + 2 + 0 = 2$ ，which is even，while that of $g ( x )$ is $0 - 1 + 2 + 0 = 1$ ，odd.Therefore $f ( x )$ is the point of $D _ { 4 }$ closest to $x$ To illustrate how ties are handled,suppose

$$
x = \left( { \sqrt [ [object Object] ] { 2 } } , { \sqrt [ [object Object] ] { 2 } } , { \sqrt [ [object Object] ] { 2 } } \right) .
$$

In fact $x$ is now equidistant from eight points of $D _ { 4 }$ , namely (0,0,0,0),any permutation of (1,1,0,O),and (1,1,1,1). The algorithm computes

$$
\begin{array} { r } { f \left( x \right) = \left( 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 \right) , \ s \mathbf { u m } = 0 , \ \mathrm { e v e n } } \\ { g \left( x \right) = \left( 1 , 0 , 0 , 0 \right) , \ s \mathbf { u m } = 1 , \ \mathrm { o d d } , } \end{array}
$$

and selects $f \left( x \right)$ .Indeed $f ( x )$ does have the smallest norm of the eight neighboring points.The algorithm takes about $_ { 4 n }$ steps to decode $D _ { n }$ ：

Thelattice $A _ { n }$ （\$6.1ofChap.4）consistsofthepoints$u = ( u _ { 0 } , u _ { 1 } , \ldots , u _ { n } ) \in { \bf Z } ^ { n + 1 }$ with $\Sigma u _ { i } = 0$ ：

Algorithm 3.To find the closest point of $A _ { n }$ to $_ { x }$

Step $\boldsymbol { { l } }$ Given $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n + 1 }$ , compute $\boldsymbol { s } = \boldsymbol { \Sigma } \boldsymbol { x } _ { i }$ and replace $x$ by

$$
x ^ { \prime } = x - { \frac { s } { n + 1 } } \left( 1 , 1 , . . . . , 1 \right) .
$$

Step 2.Calculate $f ( x ^ { \prime } ) = ( f ( x _ { 0 } ^ { \prime } ) , \dots , f ( x _ { n } ^ { \prime } ) )$ and the deficiency $\Delta = \Sigma f ( x _ { i } ^ { \prime } )$

Step 3.Sort the $\pmb { x } _ { i } ^ { \prime }$ in order of increasing value of $\delta ( \boldsymbol { x } _ { i } ^ { \prime } )$ (defined in (2)).We obtain a rearrangement of the numbers $0 , 1 , \ldots , n$ ，say $i _ { 0 } ,$ $i _ { 1 } , \ldots , i _ { n }$ ,such that

$$
- 1 / _ { 2 } \leqslant \delta \left( x { ' } _ { i _ { 0 } } \right) \leqslant \ldots \leqslant \delta \left( x { ' } _ { i _ { n } } \right) \leqslant { \mathrm { \% } } .
$$

Step 4.If $\Delta = 0 , f ( x ^ { \prime } )$ is the closest point of $A _ { n }$ to $_ x$

If $\Delta > 0$ ，the closest point is obtained by subtracting 1 from the coordinates $f ( x _ { \ i _ { 0 } } ^ { \prime } ) , \dots , f ( x _ { \ i _ { \Delta - 1 } } ^ { \prime } )$ ：

If $\Delta < 0$ ，the closest point is obtained by adding 1 to the coordinates $f ( x _ { ~ i _ { n } } ^ { \prime } ) , f ( x _ { ~ i _ { n - 1 } } ^ { \prime } ) , . . . . , f ( x _ { ~ i _ { n - \Delta + 1 } } ^ { \prime } )$

Remarks.Step 1 projects $_ { x }$ onto a point $x '$ in the hyperplane $\Sigma x _ { i } = 0$ containing $A _ { n }$ .Then $f ( x ^ { \prime } )$ is the closest point of ${ \mathbf Z } ^ { n + 1 }$ to $x '$ ,and Steps 3 and 4 make the smallest changes to the norm of $f ( x ^ { \prime } )$ needed to make $\Sigma f ( x _ { i } ^ { \prime } )$ yanish.

The most time-consuming step is the sorting operation，which takes $O \left( n \log n \right)$ steps [Knu1],[Rei5]. As pointed out to us by A.M.Odlyzko, this can be reduced to a constant times $\pmb { n }$ ，by using the Rivest-Tarjan algorithm [Knu1,p.216] to find the $| \Delta |$ largest (if $\Delta > 0 ,$ ）or smallest (if $\Delta < 0 ,$ ）of the numbers $\delta ( { \boldsymbol { x } } _ { i } ^ { \prime } )$ ：

For $\pmb { n } = 2$ and 3 there are better algorithms. $\ b { A } _ { 2 }$ is the hexagonal lattice (Fig.1.3a),and is best decoded using the fact that it is the union of arectangular lattice and a translate,as suggested by Gersho ([Ger3, p.165],[Con38,p.299]). $\boldsymbol { A } _ { 3 }$ is equivalent to $D _ { 3 }$ ，and is best decoded by the $D _ { 3 }$ algorithm.

# 3．Decoding unions of cosets.

A procedure $\Phi$ for finding the closest point of a lattice $\pmb { \Lambda }$ to a given point $_ x$ can be easily converted to a procedure for finding the closest point of a coset $r + \Lambda$ to $_ x$ .For if $\Phi \left( x \right)$ is the closest point of $\Lambda$ to $_ x$ ，then $\Phi \left( x - r \right) + r$ is the closest point of $r + \Lambda$ to $x$ ：

Suppose further that $\pmb { L }$ is a lattice (or in fact any set of points） which is a union of cosets of $\pmb { \Lambda }$

$$
L = \bigcup _ { i = 0 } ^ { t - 1 } \left( r _ { i } + \Lambda \right) .
$$

(if $L$ is a lattice, $t = [ L : \Lambda ] = ( \operatorname* { d e t } \Lambda / \operatorname* { d e t } L ) ^ { 1 / 2 }$ is the index of $\pmb { \Lambda }$ in $\pmb { L }$ .）Then $\Phi$ can be used as the basis for the following procedure for finding the closest point of $\pmb { L }$

Algorithm 4. To find the closest point of $L$ (a union of cosets of a lattice) to a given point $_ x$

Given $_ x$ , compute

$$
y _ { i } = \Phi \left( x - r _ { i } \right) + r _ { i }
$$

for $i = 0 , 1 , . . . , t - 1$ .Compare each of $y _ { 0 } , \ldots , y _ { t - 1 }$ with $_ x$ and choose the closest.

Examples (a) $E _ { 6 }$ and $E _ { 6 } ^ { * }$ (in the complex versions defined by (120),(126) of Chap.4） both contain a sublattice equivalent to $\boldsymbol { A } _ { 2 } ^ { 3 }$ ，spanned by the vectors $\omega ^ { \nu } \left( \theta , 0 , 0 \right)$ ， $\omega ^ { \nu } ( 0 , \theta , 0 )$ ， $\omega ^ { \nu } ( 0 , 0 , \theta )$ ．This has index3 in $E _ { 6 }$ and index 9 in $E _ { 6 } ^ { * }$ .Explicit coset representatives $r _ { i }$ are given in [Con38].

(b) The versions of $E _ { 7 }$ and $\boldsymbol { E } _ { 7 } ^ { * }$ defined in $\ S 2 . 5$ of Chap.5 contain a sublattice $2 \mathbf { Z } ^ { 7 }$ ，to index 8 and i6 respectively. The coset representatives form the[7,3,4] and[7,4,3] Hamming codes respectively [Con38].

(c） $E _ { 8 }$ contains $D _ { 8 }$ as a sublatice of index 2,leading to the fast decoding algorithm for $E _ { 8 }$ described in [Con26],[Con29]．This decodes $E _ { 8 }$ in about 104 steps.An even faster algorithm is given in $\ S 6$

(d) $K _ { 1 2 }$ has several possible sublattices,but the best seems to be the one equivalent to $\boldsymbol { A } _ { 2 } ^ { 6 }$ ，of index 64，with coset representatives forming the hexacode [Con38].

(e) $\Lambda _ { 2 4 }$ has a sublattice of index 8192 that is equivalent to $D _ { 2 4 }$ ，which leads to a relatively_slow_ decoding algorithm. Faster algorithms are described in [Con40l,[For2].

(f) $D _ { n }$ has index 4 in $D _ { n } ^ { * }$ and $A _ { n }$ has index $n + 1$ in $A _ { n } ^ { * }$ ，so Algorithm 4 can be applied to ${ \boldsymbol { D } } _ { n } ^ { * }$ and $A _ { n } ^ { * }$ Coset representatives (the glue vectors for $D _ { n }$ and $A _ { n }$ ）are given in Chap.4.

# 4.“Soft decision” decoding for binary codes

Let $C$ be an $[ n , k ]$ binary code. By replacing the O's and 1's of the codewords by the real numbers $+ 1$ and $^ { - 1 }$ we may regard $C$ as embedded in $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ ．A“soft decision”(or“maximum likelihood"） decoder for $c$ isan algorithm which,when presented with an arbitrary point $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ ，finds a codeword $c \in C$ that minimizes the Euclidean distance from $_ x$ to $c$ .Note that

$$
N ( x - c ) = ( x - c ) \cdot ( x - c ) = x \cdot x - 2 x \cdot c + n ,
$$

since the components of $c$ are $\pm 1$ ，so it is enough to find a $c \in C$ that maximizes the inner product $x \cdot c$ .Many examples (including_the Golay codes $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 3 }$ and $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 4 } )$ and an extensive bibliography are given in [Con40].

Here we just give one example,for use in $\ S 6$ A first-order ReedMuller code $( \ S 2 . 7$ of Chap.3） has parameters $[ n , k ] = [ 2 ^ { m } , m + 1 ]$ and may be decoded in about $m 2 ^ { m }$ steps using the fast Hadamard transform. (The so-called “Green machine”described in [Gre2],[Gre3],[Har8], [Mac6,Chap.14], [Pos1]. Litsin and Shekhovtsov [Lit2] have recently shown that even this algorithm can be speeded up.)

# 5.Decoding lattices obtained from Construction A

If $C$ is an $[ n , k ]$ binary code,written in $\pm 1$ notation, Construction A(§2.1 of Chap. 5, $\ S 2$ of Chap.7） produces a lattice $\Lambda ( C )$ consisting of the vectors of the form

$$
c + 4 z , \quad c \in C , \ z \in { \bf Z } ^ { n } .
$$

(The set of points (7) is strictly speaking not a latice,but the translate of a lattice by the vector $( 1 , 1 , \ldots , 1 ) .$ ）

The following lemma makes it possble to use a decoding algorithm for $C$ to decode $\Lambda \left( C \right)$ ：

Lemma. Suppose $x = ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ lies in the cube $- 1 \leqslant x _ { i } \leqslant 1$ $( i = 1 , \ldots , n )$ ．Then no point of $\Lambda \left( C \right)$ is closer to $_ x$ than the closest codeword of $c$

Proof.Suppose the contrary,and let $\boldsymbol { u } = \left( u _ { 1 } , \ldots , u _ { n } \right)$ be a closest lattice point to $_ x$ .By hypothesis some $x _ { i } { ' } s$ are neither $+ 1$ nor $^ { - 1 }$ By subtracting a suitable vector $_ { 4 z }$ ,we may change these coordinates to $+ 1$ or $^ { - 1 }$ (depending on their parity） to produce a point of $\Lambda \left( C \right)$ that is in $C$ ， and is at least as close to $x$ as $\pmb { u }$ is,a contradiction.

Algorithm 5.To find the closest point of $\Lambda \left( C \right)$ to a given point $_ x$ (i)Given $x = ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ ， we first reduce all $x _ { i }$ to the range $- 1 \leqslant x _ { i } < 3$ by subtracting a vector $_ { 4 z }$ ：

(ii)Let $s$ denote the set of $i$ for which $1 < x _ { i } < 3$ For $\textit { i } \in S$ ，replace $x _ { i }$ by $2 - x _ { i }$ ：

(i)Since $_ x$ is now in the cube $- 1 \leqslant x _ { i } \leqslant 1 ( i = 1 , . . . , n )$ ，by the Lemma we are justified in applying the decoder for $C$ to $_ x$ , obtaining an output $c = ( c _ { 1 } , \ldots , c _ { n } )$ say.

(iv）For $\textit { i } \in S$ change $c _ { i }$ to $2 - { \boldsymbol { c } } _ { i }$ Then $c + 4 z$ is a closest point of $\pmb { \Lambda } \left( C \right)$ to the original vector $_ x$ ：

The total number of steps required is roughly $5 n$ plus the number to decode $c$ ：

# 6. Decoding $E _ { 8 }$

Since $E _ { 8 } = \Lambda \left( \mathcal { H } _ { 8 } \right)$ , and the Hamming code $\pmb { \mathcal { H } } _ { 8 }$ (\$2.4.2 of Chap.3） is a first order Reed-Muller code, $E _ { 8 }$ can also be decoded by this algorithm. $\pmb { \mathcal { H } } _ { 8 }$ can be decoded in about $3 \cdot 8 + 8 = 3 2$ steps by the fast Hadamard transform (\$4),and so $\scriptstyle { E _ { 8 } }$ can be decoded in about 72 steps. It is worth noting that this is faster than the more obvious algorithm given in Example (c) of the previous section.

# 21

# Voronoi Cells of Lattices and Quantization Errors

J. H. Conway and N. J. A. Sloane

In $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional space,what is the average squared distance of a random point from the closest point of the lattice $A _ { n }$ (or $D _ { n }$ ， $E _ { n }$ ， $A _ { n } ^ { * }$ or ${ \boldsymbol { D } } _ { n } ^ { * }$ )？Ifa point is picked at random inside a regular simplex,octahedron,6oo-cell or other polytope,what is its average squared distance from the centroid? The answers are given here,together with a description of the Voronoi cells of the above lattices.The results have applications to quantization and to the design of codes for a bandlimited channel．For example,a quantizer based on the eight-dimensional lattice $E _ { 8 }$ has a mean squared error per symbol of O.O717...when applied to uniformly distributed data,compared with O.o8333... for the best one-dimensional quantizer.

# 1． Introduction

Let $\boldsymbol { \Lambda }$ be an $_ n$ -dimensional lattice in $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ ．The Voronoi cells (81.2 of Chap.2） around the latice points are congruent polytopes,and we denote by $V ( 0 )$ the Voronoi cell around the origin. Then,as we saw in Eq.(87) of Chap.2,the normalized,dimensionless,second moment of inertia of $V ( 0 )$ ，

$$
G \left( \Lambda \right) = \frac { 1 } { n } \left( \operatorname * { d e t } \Lambda \right) ^ { - \frac { n + 2 } { 2 n } } \int _ { { \cal V } \left( 0 \right) } { x \cdot x } d x ,
$$

is equal to the mean squared error per symbol when the lattice is used as a vector quantizer for uniformly distributed inputs.If instead the lattice is used as a code for a bandlimited channel, the integral of $\exp ( - x \cdot x / 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ over $V ( 0 )$ gives the probability of correct decoding (\$1.3 of Chap.3). Furthermore the vertices of $V ( 0 )$ furthest from $\Lambda$ are the deep holes in $\Lambda$ ， and their distance from $\Lambda$ is the covering radius $R$ of $\Lambda$ (\$1.2 of Chap. 2). Spheres of radius $R$ around the lattice points just cover $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ ，so $R$ determines the thickness of A (\$1.1 of Chap.2).

For all these applications it is important to understand the structure of the polytope $V ( 0 )$ .In this chapter we give fairly explicit descriptions of $V ( 0 )$ for the root lattices $A _ { n } ( n \geqslant 1 )$ ， $D _ { n } ( n \geqslant 3 )$ ， $E _ { 6 }$ ， $E _ { 7 }$ ， $E _ { 8 }$ （ $\mathfrak { s } _ { 2 }$ of Chap.4) and their duals (except for $E _ { 6 } ^ { * }$ and $\boldsymbol { E } _ { 7 } ^ { * }$ )．Furthermore it will turn out that for these lattices it is possible to evaluate (1） exactly.

In $\ S 2$ we study the second moment of an arbitrary polytope $P$ ，not necessarily the Voronoi cell of a lattice.Of course Voronoi cells $V ( 0 )$ have the special property of being space-filling polytopes: the whole space $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ can be tiled by translated copies of $V ( 0 )$ ．In three dimensions polytopes with the latter property are called parallelohedra． (See [McM1],[VenO].)

If $P$ is a polytope with centroid $\hat { x }$ ，then its volume,unnormalized second moment and normalized second moment are

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { V o l \left( P \right) = \displaystyle \int _ { P } d x , ~ U ( P ) = \displaystyle \int _ { P } | | x - \hat { x } | | ^ { 2 } d x , } } \\ { { I ( P ) = \displaystyle \frac { U ( P ) } { V o l \left( P \right) } , } } \end{array}
$$

respectively,and its dimensionless second moment is

$$
G \left( P \right) = \frac { 1 } { n } \frac { U ( P ) } { V o l \left( P \right) ^ { 1 + 2 / n } } = \frac { 1 } { n } \frac { I ( P ) } { V o l \left( P \right) ^ { 2 / n } } .
$$

For applications to quantizing we are interested in the minimal value of $G \left( P \right)$ taken over all polytopes $P$ that tile by translation (cf.[Bar16]).

Summary of results. In $\ S \ S 2$ and 3 we compute $G \left( P \right)$ for a number of important polytopes,including all the regular polytopes (see Theorem 4).

The three- and four-dimensional polytopes are compared in Tables 21.1 and 21.2.The chief tools used are Dirichlet's integral (Theorem 1),an explicit formula for the second moment of an $n$ -simplex (Theorem 2),and a recursion formula giving the second moment of a polytope in terms of its cells (Theorem 3).

In $\ S 3$ we consider the lattices $A _ { n } , D _ { n } , E _ { n }$ and their duals,determine their Voronoi cells $V ( 0 )$ ,the second moments $G \left( \Lambda \right) = G \left( V ( 0 ) \right)$ ,and their covering radii $R$ ．The second moments of these and other lattices are summarized in Table 2.3and Fig.2.9of Chap.2.It is worth emphasizing the remarkably low value of the mean squared error for the lattice $E _ { 8 }$ (see (28)and Fig.2.9).Fast algorithms for quantizing with this lattce were described in the preceding chapter.

# 2．Second moments of polytopes

A polytope in this chapter means a closed and bounded convex region of $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ that is the intersection of a finite number of half-spaces (cf. $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { [ } \mathsf { C o x 2 0 } }$ $\ S 7 . 4 ] )$ .If we use a minimal collection of such half-spaces then the part of the polytope that lies in one of the bounding hyperplanes is called a face. If all edge-lengths are equal this length will usually be denoted by 2e.The main source for information about polytopes is Coxeter [Cox20l,but there is an extensive literature,particularly for low-dimensional figures.See for example[Ale1]，[Cox1]，[Cox5]-[Cox7]，[Cox10]，[Cox14]，[Cox18], [Cox22],[Cox23],[Cox25]，[Cox27]，[Cox28],[Cun1],[Elt1],[Fej9], [Fej10],[Grü1],[Hil2]，[Hol1],[Loe1]，[McM2],[Pug1]，[Wen1], [Wen2l. Second moments about an axis are tabulated for many simple polyhedra in standard engineering handbooks (see also [Sat1l),but these references do not give the values for $G \left( P \right)$ ：

2.A.Dirichlet's integral. A few special figures can be handled using Dirichlet's integral.

Theorem 1[Wht1, $\ S 1 2 . 5 1$ Let $f$ be continuous and $\alpha _ { 1 } , . . . , \alpha _ { n } > 0$ Then

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle \int f ( x _ { 1 } + \cdots + x _ { n } ) ~ x _ { 1 } ^ { \alpha _ { 1 } } \cdots x _ { n } ^ { \alpha _ { n } } ~ \frac { d x _ { 1 } } { x _ { 1 } } \cdots \frac { d x _ { n } } { x _ { n } } } } \\ { { = \frac { \Gamma ( \alpha _ { 1 } ) \cdots \Gamma ( \alpha _ { n } ) } { \Gamma ( \alpha _ { 1 } + \cdots + \alpha _ { n } ) } \displaystyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } f ( \tau ) ~ _ { \tau } \Sigma ^ { \alpha _ { i } - 1 } d \tau ~ , } } \end{array}
$$

where the integral on the left is taken over the region bounded by $x _ { 1 } \geqslant 0 , . . . , x _ { n } \geqslant 0$ and $x _ { 1 } + \cdots + x _ { n } \leqslant 1$

2.B.Generalized octahedron or crosspolytope.Consider for example the $_ n$ -dimensional generalized octahedron or crosspolytope $\beta _ { n }$ $\mathfrak { h } \ [ \mathrm { C o x } 2 0 , \ \ S 7 . 2 ]$ of edge-length $2 \ell$ Taking $f { = } 1$ ， $\alpha _ { 1 } { = } 1$ (to get the volume) or $\alpha _ { 1 } { = } 3$ (to get the second moment） and $\alpha _ { i } = 1$ for $i \geqslant 2$ in Theorem 1 we find

$$
\begin{array} { c } { { \displaystyle \frac { V o l ( \beta _ { n } ) } { ( 2 \ell ) ^ { n } } = \frac { 2 ^ { n / 2 } } { n ! } \ , \displaystyle \frac { I ( \beta _ { n } ) } { ( 2 \ell ) ^ { 2 } } = \frac { n } { ( n + 1 ) \ ( n + 2 ) } \ , } } \\ { { G ( \beta _ { n } ) = \displaystyle \frac { ( n ! ) ^ { 2 / n } } { 2 ( n + 1 ) \ ( n + 2 ) } } } \\ { { \displaystyle  \frac { 1 } { 2 e ^ { 2 } } = 0 . 0 6 7 6 6 7 6 . . . \ \mathrm { a s } \ n  \infty \ . } } \end{array}
$$

2.C.The $_ n$ -sphere.As a second application,for the $_ n$ -dimensional solid sphere (or ball) $S _ { n }$ of radius $\pmb { \rho }$ it is easy to deduce from Theorem 1 that

$$
{ \frac { V o l \left( S _ { n } \right) } { \rho ^ { n } } } = { \frac { \pi ^ { n / 2 } } { \Gamma \left( 1 / _ { 2 } n + 1 \right) } }
$$

(which establishes (16),(17) of Chap.1), $I ( S _ { n } ) = n \rho ^ { 2 } / ( n + 2 )$ ,and

$$
{ \begin{array} { l } { G \left( S _ { n } \right) = { \frac { \Gamma \left( 1 / _ { 2 } n + 1 \right) ^ { 2 / n } } { \left( n + 2 \right) \pi } } } \\ { \qquad \to { \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi e } } = 0 . 0 5 8 5 4 9 8 . . . { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } n \to \infty } \end{array} }
$$

It is clear from the definition that the sphere has the smallest value of $G \left( P \right)$ of any figure,so (8） establishes Zador's lower bound,the sphere bound (the left side of Eq.(82),Chap.2)．Unfortunately quantizers cannot be built with either spheres (unless $n = 1 )$ orgeneralized octahedra (unless $n = 1$ ,2 or 4) as Voronoi cells,since these objects do not fill space.

2.D. $_ n$ -Dimensional simplices.The next result makes it possible to find the second moment of any figure,provided it can be decomposed into simplices (cf.[Hoh1]).

Theorem 2.Let $P$ be an arbitrary simplex in $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ with vertices $\nu _ { i } = ( \nu _ { i 1 } , . . . , \nu _ { i n } )$ for $0 \leqslant i \leqslant n$ .Then $( a )$ the centroid of $\pmb { P }$ isthe barycenter

$$
{ \hat { \nu } } = { \frac { 1 } { n + 1 } } \left( \nu _ { 0 } + \cdots + \nu _ { n } \right)
$$

of the vertices,

$$
V o l \left( P \right) = \frac { 1 } { n ! } d e t \left[ \begin{array} { c } { { 1 \nu _ { 0 1 } \ldots \nu _ { 0 n } } } \\ { { 1 \nu _ { 1 1 } \ldots \nu _ { 1 n } } } \\ { { \ldots \ldots } } \\ { { 1 \nu _ { n 1 } \ldots \nu _ { n n } } } \end{array} \right] ,
$$

$( \boldsymbol { c } )$ the normalized second moment about the origin O is

$$
I _ { 0 } = \frac { n + 1 } { n + 2 } \| \hat { \nu } \| ^ { 2 } + \frac { 1 } { ( n + 1 ) \ ( n + 2 ) } \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { n } \| \nu _ { i } \| ^ { 2 } \ .
$$

In other words $\boldsymbol { I } _ { 0 }$ is equal to the second moment of a system of $n + 1$ particles each of mass $1 / ( ( n + 1 ) \left( n + 2 \right) )$ placed at the vertices and one particle of mass $( n + 1 ) / ( n + 2 )$ placed at the barycenter.

Proof.(a) is elementary，(b) iswell-known (cf.[Alll],[Gool,p.349]), and (c) follows from [Goo1,Eq.(24),the case $n = 2 ]$

2.E.Regular simplex.For example if $P$ is a regular $\pmb { n }$ -simplex of edgelength $2 \ell$ then

$$
\begin{array} { c } { { \displaystyle \frac { V o l ( P ) } { ( \sqrt { 2 } \ell ) ^ { n } } = \frac { \sqrt { n + 1 } } { n ! } ~ , \displaystyle \frac { I ( P ) } { ( \sqrt { 2 } \ell ) ^ { 2 } } = \frac { n } { ( n + 1 ) ~ ( n + 2 ) } ~ , } } \\ { { G \left( P \right) = \displaystyle \frac { ( n ! ) ^ { 2 / n } } { ( n + 1 ) ^ { 1 + \frac { 1 } { n } } ( n + 2 ) } } } \\ { { \longrightarrow e ^ { - 2 } = 0 . 1 3 5 3 3 5 . . . ~ \mathrm { a s } ~ n \longrightarrow \infty ~ . } } \end{array}
$$

For $n { = } 1 , 2$ and 3 the values of $G ( P )$ are 1/12, $1 / ( 6 \sqrt { 3 } ) = 0 . 0 9 6 2 2 5 0 . . . ,$ and $3 ^ { 2 / 3 } / 2 0 = 0 . 1 0 4 0 0 4 . . .$ ,and $G \left( P \right)$ increases monotonically with $\pmb { n }$ ：

2.F. Volume and second moment of a polytope in terms of its faces. Instead of decomposing a figure into simplices one may proceed by induction, expressing the volume and second moment of a polytope in terms of the volume and second moment of its faces,then in terms of its $\left( n - 2 \right)$ dimensional faces,and so on.Theorem 3 is the basis for this procedure.

Suppose $P$ is an $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional polytope with $N _ { 1 }$ congruent faces $F _ { 1 } ,$ $F _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , F _ { 1 } ^ { \prime \prime } , \ldots , N ;$ congruent faces $F _ { 2 } , F _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } , F _ { 2 } ^ { \prime \prime }$ ....，and so on. Suppose also that $P$ contains a point O such that all of the generalized pyramids $0 F _ { 1 }$ ， $0 F _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } { \mathrm { , } } \dots$ are congruent,all of $0 F _ { 2 } , \ 0 F _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } , . . .$ . are congruent,.. Let $a _ { i } \ \in \ F _ { i }$ be the foot of the perpendicular from O to $F _ { i }$ , let $h _ { i } = | | 0 a _ { i } | |$ ,and let $V _ { n - 1 } ( i )$ be the volume of $F _ { i }$ and $U _ { n - 1 } ( i )$ the unnormalized second moment of $F _ { i }$ about $a _ { i }$

Theorem 3. The volume and unnormalized second moment about O of $P$ are given by

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle V o l \left( P \right) = \sum _ { i } \frac { N _ { i } h _ { i } } { n } V _ { n - 1 } ( i ) \ , } } \\ { { \displaystyle U ( P ) = \sum _ { i } \frac { N _ { i } h _ { i } } { n + 2 } \left[ h _ { i } ^ { 2 } V _ { n - 1 } ( i ) + U _ { n - 1 } ( i ) \right] . } } \end{array}
$$

Proof. Follows from elementary calculus by dividing each generalized pyramid $O F _ { 1 }$ into slabs parallel to the face $F _ { i }$ ：

2.G.Truncated octahedron. For example let $P$ be the truncated octahedron with vertices consisting of all permutations of $\sqrt { 2 } \ell ( 0 , \pm 1 , \pm 2 )$ ： $P$ has $N _ { 1 } = 6$ square faces and $N _ { 2 } = 8$ faces which are regular hexagons, all with edge-length $_ { 2 \ell }$ .The second moments of these faces can be calculated directly,or else found in $\ S 2 . 1$ ，Then from the theorem we find that

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { V o l \left( P \right) = \displaystyle \frac { 6 \cdot \ell \sqrt { 8 } } { 3 } 4 \ell ^ { 2 } + \frac { 8 \cdot \ell \sqrt { 6 } } { 3 } 6 \sqrt { 3 } \ell ^ { 2 } = 6 4 \sqrt { 2 } \ell ^ { 3 } \ , } } \\ { { U ( P ) = \displaystyle \frac { 6 \cdot \ell \sqrt { 8 } } { 5 } \left[ 8 \ell ^ { 2 } \cdot 4 \ell ^ { 2 } + \frac { 8 \ell ^ { 4 } } { 3 } \right] + \frac { 8 \cdot \ell \sqrt { 6 } } { 5 } \left[ 6 \ell ^ { 2 } \cdot 6 \sqrt { 3 } \ell ^ { 2 } + 1 0 \sqrt { 3 } \ell ^ { 4 } \right] } } \\ { { \displaystyle = 3 0 4 \sqrt { 2 } \ell ^ { 5 } \ , } } \end{array}
$$

hence

$$
G \left( P \right) = { \frac { 1 } { 3 } } { \frac { I ( P ) } { V o l ( P ) ^ { 2 / 3 } } } = { \frac { 1 9 } { 1 9 2 ^ { 3 } \sqrt 2 } } = 0 . 0 7 8 5 4 3 3 . . . \ .
$$

2.H. Second moment of regular polytopes. The next theorem gives an explicit formula for the second moment of any regular polytope. Suppose $P$ is an $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional regular polytope $\left\{ \mathbf { C o x } 2 0 \right\}$ For $0 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ choose a $j$ -dimensional face $F _ { j }$ of $P$ so that $F _ { 0 } \subseteq F _ { 1 } \subseteq \dots \subseteq F _ { n } = P$ ,and let $0 _ { j }$ be the center of $F _ { j }$ ， $R _ { j } = | | 0 _ { n } 0 _ { j } | |$ ,and for $j \geqslant 1$ let $r _ { j } = | | 0 _ { j - 1 } 0 _ { j } | |$ . Thus $r _ { j }$ is the inradius of $F _ { j }$ measured from $0 _ { j }$ ,and $r _ { j } ^ { 2 } = R _ { j - 1 } ^ { 2 } - \dot { R } _ { j } ^ { 2 }$ Let $N _ { j , j - 1 }$ be the number of $( j - 1 )$ -dimensional faces of $F _ { j }$ ．Then it is known that the symmetry group of $\pmb { P }$ has order

$$
g = N _ { n , n - 1 } N _ { n - 1 , n - 2 } . \cdot \cdot N _ { 2 , 1 } N _ { 1 , 0 }
$$

[Cox20,\$7.6],and the volume of $\pmb { P }$ [Cox20,\$7.9] is

$$
V o l ( P ) = N _ { n , n - 1 } \cdots N _ { 2 , 1 } N _ { 1 , 0 } \cdot { \frac { r _ { 1 } r _ { 2 } \cdots r _ { n } } { n ! } } .
$$

Theorem 4. The second moment of any $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional regular polytope $P$ about its center $0 _ { n }$ is given by

$$
I ( P ) = \frac { 2 } { ( n + 1 ) \ ( n + 2 ) } \ ( R _ { 0 } ^ { 2 } + 2 R _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + 3 R _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + \cdots + n R _ { n - 1 } ^ { 2 } ) \ ,
$$

or equivalently

$$
I ( P ) = \frac { 2 } { ( n { + } 1 ) \ ( n { + } 2 ) } \ ( r _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + 3 r _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + 6 r _ { 3 } ^ { 2 } + \cdots + \frac { n ( n { + } 1 ) } { 2 } r _ { n } ^ { 2 } ) \ .
$$

Proof.The proof is by induction,the 1-dimensional case being immediate. From Theorem 3we have

$$
U ( P ) = \frac { N _ { n , n - 1 } r _ { n } } { n + 2 } ( r _ { n } ^ { 2 } V _ { n - 1 } ( P ) + U _ { n - 1 } ( P ) ) \ ,
$$

where (from (14) and the induction hypothesis)

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { { \cal V } _ { n - 1 } ( P ) = N _ { n - 1 , n - 2 } \cdots N _ { 2 , 1 } N _ { 1 , 0 } \cdot { \frac { r _ { 1 } r _ { 2 } \cdots r _ { n - 1 } } { ( n - 1 ) ! } } , } } \\ { { { \cal U } _ { n - 1 } ( P ) = V _ { n - 1 } ( P ) \cdot { \frac { 2 } { n ( n + 1 ) } } ( r _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \cdots + { \frac { n ( n - 1 ) } { 2 } } r _ { n - 1 } ^ { 2 } ) . } } \end{array}
$$

Then

$$
I ( P ) = \frac { U ( P ) } { V o l ( P ) } = \frac { n } { n + 2 } \{ r _ { n } ^ { 2 } + \frac { 2 } { n ( n { + } 1 ) } ( r _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \cdots + \frac { n ( n { - } 1 ) } { 2 } r _ { n - 1 } ^ { 2 } ) \} ,
$$

which simplifes to (16).

The values of g, Vol(P) and Rj are tabulated for allregular polytopes in $\scriptstyle { \left[ \mathbf { C o x } 2 0 \right. }$ ,Table I,pp.292-295l.We have already dealt with the simplex and generalized octahedron. For an $\pmb { n }$ -dimensional cube $G ( P ) = 1 / 1 2$ for all $_ n$ (since the cube is a direct product of line segments). We now treat the remaining regular polytopes.

2.1．Regular polygons.If $P$ is a regular $p$ -gon of edge-length $\scriptstyle 2 \ell$ ，then from Theorem 4 we find

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { { \displaystyle V o l \left( P \right) = p \ell ^ { 2 } c o t \ \frac { \pi } { p } } , \quad { \displaystyle I \left( P \right) = \frac { \ell ^ { 2 } } { 6 } ( 1 + 3 c o t ^ { 2 } \frac { \pi } { p } ) } \ , } } \\ { { { \displaystyle G \left( P \right) = \frac { 1 } { 6 p } ( c o s e c \ \frac { 2 \pi } { p } + c o t \ \frac { \pi } { p } ) } . } } \end{array}
$$

For $p = 3 , 4$ and 6 $, G ( P ) = 1 / ( 6 \sqrt { 3 } )$ ,1/12 and ${ \mathfrak { S } } / ( 3 6 { \sqrt { 3 } } )$ ：

$$
V o l = \frac { 2 0 \ell ^ { 3 } \tau ^ { 2 } } { 3 } , G = \frac { 1 } { 2 0 } \left( \frac { 6 \tau } { 5 } \right) ^ { 2 / 3 } = 0 . 0 7 7 8 1 8 5 . . . ,
$$

2.K. The exceptional 4-dimensional polytopes.There are three “exceptional" regular polytopes in four dimensions,the 24-cell, the 120-cell and the 600-cell． For the 24-cell

$$
V o l = 3 2 \ell ^ { 4 } , \ G = { \frac { 1 3 } { 1 2 0 \sqrt 2 } } = 0 . 0 7 6 6 0 3 2 . . . \ ;
$$

V o l = 1 2 0 \sqrt { 5 } \ell ^ { 4 } \tau ^ { 8 } , G = \frac { 4 3 \tau + 1 3 } { 3 0 0 \sqrt { 6 } \ 5 ^ { 1 / 4 } } = 0 . 0 7 5 1 4 7 0 . . . \ ;
$$

V o l = 1 0 0 \ell ^ { 4 } \tau ^ { 3 } , G = \frac { ( 3 \tau + 4 ) \ \tau ^ { 1 / 2 } } { 1 5 0 } = 0 . 0 7 5 0 8 3 9 . . . \ .

# 3.Voronoi cells and the mean squared error of lattice quantizers

3.A． The Voronoi cell of a root lattice. The Voronoi cells of the root lattices $A _ { n } ( n \geqslant 1 )$ ， $D _ { n } ( n \geqslant 3 )$ ， $E _ { 6 } , \ E _ { 7 }$ and $E _ { 8 }$ may be obtained in a uniform manner. The method is based on finding a fundamental simplex for the affine Weyl group of the lattice (S2 of Chap.4)． We denote the (finite） Weyl group of $\Lambda$ by $W ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ ,and the (infinite) affine Weyl group by $W _ { a } ( \Lambda )$ ：

The affine Weyl group $W _ { a } ( \Lambda )$ is described by the extended CoxeterDynkin diagram shown in Figs.21.1-21.3 (and in the last column of Table 4.1)． This diagram can be read in several different ways ([Bou1], [Cox20],[Gro3],[Haz1])．First,it provides a presentation for $W _ { a } ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ ， defining the group in terms of generators and relations (see $\ S 2$ of Chap. 4); however we shall not make use of this interpretation here. Second,it can be used to specify a fundamental simplex $s$ for $W _ { a } ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ .This is an $\pmb { n } -$ dimensional closed simplex whose images under the action of $W _ { a } ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ are distinct and tile $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ .In other words we can write

$$
\mathbf { R } ^ { n } = \bigcup _ { g \in W _ { a } ( \Lambda ) } g ( S ) \ ,
$$

where (except for the boundaries of $g ( S )$ ，a set of measure zero） each point $\mathbf { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ belongs to a unique image $g ( S )$ .In this interpretation the nodes of the diagram represent the hyperplanes that are the walls of the fundamental simplex [Cox20,\$11.3]. The angle between two walls or hyperplanes is indicated by the branch of the diagram joining the corresponding nodes. If the hyperplanes are at an angle of $\pi / 3$ the nodes are joined by a single branch,if the angle is $\pi / 4$ they are joined by a double branch (see Fig. 21.4),if the angle is $\pi / p$ with $p > 4$ they are joined by a branch labeled $p$ ，and finally if the hyperplanesare perpendicular the nodes are not joined by a branch. The nodes in Figs.21.1-21.3 have been labeled with the equations to the corresponding hyperplanes.

![](images/fef18af1eb3a5f9083ff440d3f3e219ab17a05aded9b00d7e62fcfc926205880.jpg)  
Figure 21.1． Extended Coxeter-Dynkin diagram for $W _ { a } ( A _ { n } )$ .The extending node is indicated by a solid circle.The $n { + 1 }$ nodes are labeled with the equations to the hyperplanes that are the walls of the fundamental simplex. The labelings in Figs.21.1-21.3 are based on [Boul,pp.250-270] and [Con25].

![](images/31e4f527791f2a1b647ce1d2354e3963f5d1a8f8b17b60a1a0ea5eb48aff38a8.jpg)  
Figure 21.2. Extended Coxeter-Dynkin diagram for $W _ { a } ( D _ { n } )$ .There are $n { + 1 }$ nodes.

In the third interpretation the nodes in the extended Coxeter-Dynkin diagram are taken to represent the vertices of a fundamental simplex, rather than the bounding hyperplanes. Each node represents the vertex opposite to the corresponding hyperplane (some examples are shown in Figs.21.6-21.8)- cf.[Cox20,\$11.6].

One of the nodes in the diagram is indicated by a solid circle.This is an extending node; removing it leaves an (ordinary） Coxeter-Dynkin diagram for the Weyl group $W ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ . Of the $n { + 1 }$ hyperplanes represented by the extended diagram,all except that corresponding to the extending node pass through the origin．It is helpful to think of the latter hyperplane as forming the roof of the fundamental simplex. The vertex of the fundamental simplex opposite the roof is the origin.

For later use we remark that the finite Weyl group $W ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ also has a fundamental domain, consisting of an infinite cone centered at the origin. A fundamental simplex for $W _ { a } ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ is obtained by taking the finite part of the cone beneath the roof. The intersection of this cone with the roof,or more precisely with a unit sphere centered at the origin,is a spherical simplex. The ordinary Coxeter-Dynkin diagram for $W ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ describes this spherical simplex in the same way as the extended diagram describes the fundamental simplex for $W _ { a } ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ .These spherical simplices and (ordinary) Coxeter-Dynkin diagrams can be used to define the Weyl groups of all the root systems (and not just the root lattices $A _ { n } , D _ { n }$ and $E _ { n }$ .In \$\$3.E,3.F we shall require the spherical simplices corresponding to $W ( A _ { n } )$ and $W ( C _ { n } )$ ,shown in Fig.21.4. The Weyl group $W ( A _ { n } )$ is usually writen as $[ 3 ^ { n - 1 } ]$ and is isomorphic to the symmetric group on $n { + 1 }$ letters. $W ( C _ { n } )$ is written $[ 3 ^ { n - 2 } , 4 ]$ and has order $2 ^ { n } n !$ (See $\ S 2$ of Chap. 4.)

Lemma.The origin is the closest lattice point to any interior point of the fundamental simplex.

Proof. Let $\pmb { u }$ be the closest lattice point to $x \in S$ . Suppose $u { \ne } 0$ Then $\textbf { \em u } \not \in \textbf { \em S }$ ，and $\pmb { u }$ and $_ { x }$ are on opposite sides of a reflecting hyperplane of

![](images/394db1d565f109ffa3eddbb71cc6e61a726218b4410849822549c2deab15dc09.jpg)  
Figure 21.3. Extended Coxeter-Dynkin diagramsfor(a) ${ \cal W } _ { a } ( E _ { 8 } )$ (b) $W _ { \pmb { a } } ( E _ { 7 } )$ and (c) $W _ { a } ( E _ { 6 } )$ ：

$W _ { a } ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ .Let $\pmb { u } ^ { \prime } \in \Lambda$ be the image of $\pmb { u }$ in this hyperplane,and let $y$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $\pmb { x }$ to the line ${ \bf \chi } _ { u u ^ { ' } }$ (see Fig.21.5).Then

$$
| | x u ^ { \prime } | | ^ { 2 } = | | x y | | ^ { 2 } + | | y u ^ { \prime } | | ^ { 2 } < | | x y | | ^ { 2 } + | | y u | | ^ { 2 } = | | x u | | ^ { 2 } ,
$$

and $_ x$ is closer to $\pmb { u } ^ { \prime }$ than to $\pmb { u }$ ,a contradiction． Therefore $u = 0$

Figure 21.4．Coxeter-Dynkin diagrams for the spherical simplices of (a) $W ( A _ { n } )$ and (b) $W ( C _ { n } )$ ．(The labeling of the nodes is for convenience only and has no geometrical significance.)

The connection between the fundamental simplex and the Voronoi cell is given by the following theorem.

Theorem 5. For any root lattice △,the Voronoi cell around the origin is the union of the images of the fundamental simplex under the Weyl group $W ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ ：

Proof. Let $_ x$ be any point of the Voronoi cell around the origin．From (23), $x \in g ( S )$ for some $g \in W _ { a } ( \Lambda )$ . Suppose $_ x$ is an interior point of $g ( S )$ .By the lemma,the closest lattice point to $x$ is $g \left( 0 \right)$ .Therefore $g \left( 0 \right) = 0 , g \in W \left( \Lambda \right)$ ,and

$$
x \in \bigcup _ { g \in W ( \Lambda ) } g ( S ) ~ .
$$

We omit the discussion of the case when $_ x$ is a boundary point of $g ( S )$ The converse statement, that $x \in \cup g ( S )$ implies $_ { x }$ is in the Voronoi cell, follows by reversing the steps.

It follows from Theorem 5 that the Voronoi cell is the union of $\left| W ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } ) \right|$ copies of the fundamental simplex $_ s$ .Furthermore the faces of the Voronoi region are the images of the roof of the fundamental simplex under $W ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ ．Thus the Voronoi cell is bounded by hyperplanes which are the perpendicular bisectors of the lines joining O to its nearest neighbors in the lattice.

Corollary. The number of $( n - 1 )$ -dimensional faces of the Voronoi cell of a root lattice is equal to the kissing number of the lattice.

This is not true for all lattices,as we shall see in $\ S 3 . G$ .The second moment of the Voronoi region can now be obtained from that of the fundamental simplex.

3.E．Voronoi cell for $D _ { n } ^ { * }$ ，In order to determine the Voronoi cells for the dual lattices $A _ { n } ^ { * }$ and $D _ { n } ^ { * }$ we shall use Wythoff's construction,as described in[Cox5] and [Cox20,\$11.6]. The idea is to construct new polytopes out of the spherical simplices described in $\ S 3 . A$ ，the vertices of the new polytope being indicated by drawing rings around certain nodes in the ordinary Coxeter-Dynkin diagram. More precisely，let $\nu _ { 1 } , \ldots , \nu _ { n }$ be the vertices of a spherical simplex for a Weyl group $W ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ ．If a single node of the diagram is ringed,say that corresponding to $\nu _ { i }$ ,the vertices of the new polytope are the images of $\nu _ { i }$ under the Weyl group. If two or more nodes are ringed,say those corresponding to $\nu _ { i } , \nu _ { j } , \dots$ ，the symbol represents a polytope whose vertices are the images under $W ( \boldsymbol { \Lambda } )$ of some interior point of the spherical subsimplex with vertices $\nu _ { i }$ ， $\nu _ { j } , \dots$ .We can adjust the metrical properties of the polytope (for example,equalize its edge lengths) by choosing this interior point suitably. Some 1-,2-and 3-dimensional examples are shown in Fig.21.9;others may be found in [Cox5],[Cox20l.

We now use this construction to find the Voronoi cell for ${ D } _ { n } ^ { * } , n \geqslant 3$ We change the scale so that $\smash { D _ { n } ^ { * } }$ becomes the union of $( 2 \mathbf { Z } ) ^ { n }$ and $( 1 ^ { n } ) + ( 2 \mathbf { Z } ) ^ { n }$ . The closest points to the origin in the first set consist of $_ { 2 n }$ points of the form $( \pm \ 2 , 0 ^ { n - 1 } )$ ,and the closest in the second set consist of $2 ^ { n }$ points of the form $( \pm 1 ^ { n } )$ ．The Voronoi cell $V ( 0 )$ is the intersection of the Voronoi cells determined by these two sets.The first of these, $\pmb { P }$ say, is a cube centered at O with vertices $( \pm 1 ^ { n } )$ .The second, $Q$ say，is a generalized octahedron with vertices $( \pm n / 2 , 0 ^ { n - 1 } )$ .Furthermore $\boldsymbol { Q }$ can be obtained by reciprocating $P$ in a sphere of radius $\rho = \sqrt { n / 2 }$ centered at the origin.

Thus the Voronoi cell $V ( 0 )$ is the intersection of $\pmb { P }$ and a reciprocal polytope $Q { = } P ^ { * }$ .In other words $V ( 0 )$ is obtained by truncating $\pmb { P }$ in the manner described on page 147 of $\left[ \mathsf { C o x } 2 0 \right]$ ，and is therefore specified by ringing one or two nodes of the Coxeter-Dynkin diagram (Fig.21.4b) for the spherical simplex of $P$ ([Cox5],[Cox20,\$\$8.1,11.7]).

The radii $R _ { j }$ (defined in $\ S 2 . \mathbf { H } )$ for the cube $P$ are given by $R _ { j } = { \sqrt { n - j } }$ [Cox20,TableI,p.295]．If $\pmb { n }$ is even the radius $\pmb { \rho }$ of the sphere of reciprocation is equal to $R _ { n / 2 }$ ，and we must ring the node labeled $n / 2$ in

Theorem 6. The Voronoi cell around the origin of the lattice $D _ { n } ^ { * }$ isthe polytope defined by the diagrams in Fig.21.10.

The coordinates for $\beta \left( n , k \right)$ and $\delta \left( n , k \right)$ given below show that the edge-lengths of the Voronoi regions are all equal. In Coxeter's notation [Cox20,S8.1] the Voronoi cell for $D _ { 2 t } ^ { * }$ is

We shall determine the second moments of these Voronoi cells recursively,using Theorem 3. In order to do this it will be necessary to find the second moments of all the polytopes $\alpha \left( n , k \right) , \beta \left( n , k \right) , \gamma \left( n , k \right)$ and $\delta \left( n , k \right)$ defined as in Fig.21.11． In this notation the Voronoi cell of $D _ { n } ^ { * }$ is (up to a scale factor) equal to $\beta \left( n , n / 2 \right)$ if $_ n$ is even and to $\delta \left( n , \left( n - 1 \right) / 2 \right)$ if $_ n$ is odd.Let $R _ { \alpha } ( n , k )$ ， $V _ { \alpha } ( n , k )$ and $U _ { \alpha } ( n , k )$ denote respectively the circumradius,volume and unnormalized second moment about the center of $\alpha ( n , k )$ ,with a similar notation for $\beta ( n , k )$ ， $\gamma ( n , k )$ and $\delta \left( n , k \right)$ ：

Figure 21.11． The polytopes $\alpha ( n , k ) , \beta ( n , k ) , \gamma ( n , k )$ and $\delta ( n , k )$ In general $\alpha ( n , k )$ has $_ n$ nodes with the $\pmb { k }$ -th node from the right ringed, and $\gamma ( n , k )$ has $_ n$ nodes with the $\pmb { k }$ -th and $( k + 1 ) \mathsf { s t }$ ringed (except that $\gamma ( n , 0 ) = \alpha ( n , 1 )$ and $\gamma ( n , n ) = \alpha { \left( n , n \right) } )$ ： $\beta ( n , k )$ and $\delta ( n , k )$ are the same as $\alpha ( n , k )$ and $\gamma ( n , k )$ respectively,except that the left branch is a double bond．By convention $\alpha ( 0 , 0 )$ and $\gamma ( 0 , 0 )$ represent a point.

For the vertices of the polytope $\alpha ( n , k )$ it is convenient to take the points in $\mathbf { R } ^ { n + 1 }$ whose coordinates are all the permutations of $( 0 ^ { n - k + 1 } , 1 ^ { k } )$ [Cox20,S8.7]. The centroid of $\alpha ( n , k )$ is the point

$$
{ \frac { k } { n + 1 } } \ ( 1 ^ { n + 1 } ) ,
$$

and so the circumradius is

$$
\begin{array} { r } { R _ { \alpha } ( n , k ) = \sqrt { \frac { k ( n - k + 1 ) } { n + 1 } } . } \end{array}
$$

Similarly

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \beta \left( n , k \right) \mathrm { ~ h a s ~ v e r t i c e s ~ } \left( 0 ^ { n - k } , \pm 1 ^ { k } \right) , R _ { \beta } ( n , k ) = \sqrt { k } , } \\ & { } \\ & { \gamma ( n , k ) \mathrm { ~ h a s ~ v e r t i c e s ~ } ( 0 ^ { n - k } , 1 , 2 ^ { k } ) , R _ { \gamma } ( n , k ) = \sqrt { \frac { 4 k ( n - k ) + n } { n + 1 } } , } \end{array}
$$

(These polytopes appear with different names in $\left[ \mathbf { C o x } 2 2 \right] .$ ）Each of these polytopes has two kinds of faces,obtained by deleting either the left or the right node of its diagram [Cox20,\$\$7.6,11.6,11.7].For example deleting the left node of the $\alpha ( n , k )$ diagram produces an $\alpha ( n - 1 , k - 1 )$ ，while deleting the right node produces an $\alpha ( n { - } 1 , k )$ .Thus in general $\alpha ( n , k )$ has faces of type $\alpha ( n { - } 1 , k { - } 1 )$ and $\alpha ( n { - } 1 , k )$ .(If $k = 0$ the first type is absent,while if $k = n$ the second type is absent.） The number of faces of each type is given by the ratio of the orders of the underlying Weyl groups (obtained by ignoring the rings on the diagram)． Thus the number of $\alpha \left( n - 1 , k - 1 \right)$ -type cells of an $\alpha ( n , k )$ is

$$
\frac { \left| [ 3 ^ { n - 1 } ] \right| } { \left| [ 3 ^ { n - 2 } ] \right| } = \frac { ( n + 1 ) ! } { n ! } = n + 1 \ .
$$

This is also the number of $\alpha ( n { - } 1 , k )$ -type faces. We represent this process of finding the faces by the graph shown in Fig.21.12.

Theorem 7. The Voronoi cell for the lattice $\boldsymbol { A } _ { n } ^ { * }$ is the polytope $\scriptstyle P _ { n }$ defined in Fig.21.16. If we rescale $A _ { n } ^ { * }$ by multiplying it by $n + 1$ , the vertices of the Voronoi cell consist of the $\left( n + 1 \right) !$ points obtained by permuting the coordinates of

G. The walls of the Voronoi cell. As explained in $\ S 1 . 2$ of Chap.2,the walls of the Voronoi cell $V ( 0 )$ for a lattice $\Lambda$ are defined by the relevant vectors of $\Lambda$ ．For a root lattice we saw in the Corollary to Theorem 5 that the relevant vectors in a root lattice are precisely the minimal vectors.In this case there is a simple description of $V ( 0 )$ ：

Theorem8. If the relevant vectors are precisely the minimal vectors,then $V ( 0 )$ is the reciprocal of the vertex figure of $\Lambda$ at the origin. Equivalently, $V ( 0 )$ is (on a suitable scale) the reciprocal of the polytope whose vertices are the minimal vectors ofA.

Proof. This follows immediately from the definitions of vertex figure and reciprocal polytope - see [Cox20].

The following is a useful sufficient condition for a lattice to have this property. Let us write $\Lambda = \Lambda _ { 0 } \cup \Lambda _ { 1 } \cup \mathbf { \Lambda } \cdot \mathbf { \mu } \cdot \mathbf { \mu } .$ ，where the ith shell $\Lambda _ { i }$ consists of all $\nu \in \Lambda$ with $\pmb { \nu } \cdot \pmb { \nu } = \lambda _ { i }$ (say),and $0 = \lambda _ { 0 } < \lambda _ { 1 } < \mathbf { \rho } \cdot \mathbf { \sigma } \cdot \mathbf { \sigma } \cdot$

Theorem 9. Suppose that (i) $\Delta _ { r } \subset \Lambda _ { 1 } + \Lambda _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \Lambda _ { 1 }$ (r times),and (i) $r \lambda _ { 1 } \leqslant \lambda _ { r }$ ，for all $r = 1$ ,2,.. Then the relevant vectors are precisely the minimal vectors.

Condition (i) states that $\Lambda _ { 1 }$ spans $\Lambda$ ,and moreover does it economically in the sense that any vector in $\Lambda _ { r }$ is the sum of not more than $r$ vectors of $\mathbf { \Lambda } _ { \mathbf { \Lambda } } ^ { \mathbf { \Lambda } }$ ： In practice this condition is very easily checked by induction. An important class of latices satisfying (i) are those obtained by applying Construction A to a linear binary code with minimal distance $\leqslant 4$ thatis spanned by the codewords of minimal weight,and if $d \textless 4$ has the additional property that no coordinate of the code is always zero.

Proof of Theorem 9. Suppose the contrary,so that there is a point $u ~ \in ~ \Lambda _ { r }$ with $r > 1$ and a point $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ suchthat $x \cdot u > \mathbb { \ Y } _ { 2 } \mathbb { \lambda } _ { r }$ ，but $x \cdot \nu \leqslant / _ { 2 } \lambda _ { 1 }$ for all $\nu \in \Lambda _ { 1 }$ .From (i), $u = \sum n _ { i } \nu _ { i }$ with $\nu _ { i } ~ \in \Lambda _ { 1 }$ ， $n _ { i } > 0$ and $\textstyle \sum n _ { i } \leqslant r$ .Then $\begin{array} { r } { \boldsymbol { x } \cdot \boldsymbol { u } = \sum n _ { i } \left( \boldsymbol { x } \cdot \boldsymbol { \nu } _ { i } \right) \leqslant { } ^ { 1 / 2 } \lambda _ { 1 } \sum n _ { i } \leqslant { } ^ { 1 / 2 } r \lambda _ { 1 } \leqslant { } ^ { 1 / 2 } \lambda _ { r } } \end{array}$ ,a contradiction.

Voronoi has given a simple characterization of the relevant vectors in any lattice (see [Vor1,Vol.134 (1908),p.277] and [Ven5]).

Theorem 10. A nonzero vector $\nu \in \Lambda$ is relevant if and only $i f \pm \nu$ are the only shortest vectors in the coset $\nu + 2 \Lambda$

Proof. Note that each nonzero vector $\nu \in \Lambda$ determines a half-space $H _ { \nu } = \{ x \in \mathbf { R } ^ { n } : x \cdot \nu \leqslant \mathbb { \breve { / } } 2 \nu \cdot \nu \}$ ，and $V ( 0 )$ is the intersection of these halfspaces.(Only if） Suppose $\nu , w$ satisfy $\nu \equiv w$ (mod $2 \Lambda )$ ， $\nu \neq \pm \ w _ { w }$ ， $N ( \boldsymbol { w } ) \leqslant N ( \boldsymbol { \nu } )$ .Then $t = \ V _ { 2 } \left( \nu + w \right)$ ， $u = \mathbb { V } _ { 2 } \left( \nu - w \right)$ are nonzero vectors in $\pmb { \Lambda }$ If $x \ \in \ H _ { t }$ n $H _ { u }$ then $x \cdot t \ \leqslant \ \ V _ { 2 } t \cdot t$ ， $x \cdot u \leqslant \sqrt [ 1 ] { 2 \boldsymbol { u } \cdot \boldsymbol { u } }$ ，implying $x \cdot \nu \ \leqslant \ \Vdash \nu \cdot \nu$ ，and so $H _ { \nu }$ is not needed to define $V ( 0 )$ ,i.e. $\nu$ is not relevant. (If) Suppose $\nu$ is not relevant．In particular,the point $_ { 1 / 2 \nu }$ must lie on or outside some $H _ { w }$ for $w \ne 0$ ， $w \ne \nu$ ，i.e. $1 / 2 \nu \cdot w \ \geqslant \ 1 / _ { 2 } w \cdot w$ .Therefore $N ( \nu - 2 w ) \leqslant N ( \nu )$ .Furthermore $\nu - 2 w \ne \pm \nu$ and is also in the coset $\nu + 2 \Lambda$ ，

For example,for the Leech lattice we see from Theorem 2 of Chap.12 that the Voronoi cell is bounded by the $1 9 6 5 6 0 + 1 6 7 7 3 1 2 0 = 1 6 9 6 9 6 8 0$ hyperplanes corresponding to the vectors of norm 4 and 6.
